News.title: 'No terminally ill person should be dying in a hospital corridor while in pain or distress'
News.content:
'No terminally ill person should be dying in a hospital corridor while in pain or distress'

Nurses have told of treating patients receiving end-of-life care in 'unsafe' corridors or makeshift spaces - including one woman who died on a bathroom floor

View 2 Images Sarah Williamson, director of nursing and quality at Marie Curie, said "no terminally ill person should die in a corridor (Image: Marie Curie)

Reacting to their 'harrowing' survey which revealed more than half of nurses taking part had treated patients in a makeshift area, Sarah Williamson, director of nursing and quality at Marie Curie, said "no terminally ill person should be dying in a corridor or a waiting room."

‌



Speaking to the Mirror, she said: "Today, a new survey of more than 1,100 nurses has revealed the front-line experiences of clinical practitioners caring for dying people across the UK. The results were alarming. 55% of nurses have treated patients in a corridor or non-designated clinical area such as a waiting room. More than 70% of nurses said staffing levels are a constraint or barrier to providing end of life care. More than half said a lack of time is a constraint to giving people end of life care.

‌



"The survey also told us stories of confusion when a dying patient's wishes could not be verified due to an over reliance on paper files, and care providers and the NHS using different electronic systems. One nurse recalled a terminal metastatic cancer patient who died on the bathroom floor after a CPR attempt: 'We were never going to get her back. She died on the floor in the bathroom, undignified, family hysterical, staff all left traumatised.'

‌



"Another nurse described an older man carrying his paper care plan in his pocket at all times so that he wasn’t subjected to intervention against his wishes.

View 2 Images One woman died on a bathroom floor leaving her family 'hysterical' (Image: Getty Images)

AI could diagnose heart disease and high blood pressure after five-second face scan READ MORE :

"These harrowing stories have been incredibly difficult to read, but it's so important that we are aware of the stark reality facing nurses, clinical teams, families and patients every day.

‌



"As Director of Nursing and Quality at the UK's leading end of life care charity Marie Curie, unfortunately, these testimonies feel all too familiar.

"A host of pressures on staffing, time and care planning are putting end of life care at risk, leaving some dying people facing distressing and undignified deaths. This is a symptom of a system under strain, but also lack of access to 24/7 support for people at the end of life with A&E often becoming a default in moments of crisis when there is nowhere else to turn.

"The nurses I work with everyday work hard to deliver the highest quality care possible, but right now the reality is that care is not up to scratch.

‌



'That's what it means to die in dignity'

"No terminally ill person should be dying in a corridor or waiting room. No one should be receiving inappropriate CPR during their final moments against their wishes. And, when someone has taken the time to think about how they want to die, that decision should follow them, wherever they are and to whoever is caring for them. That's what it means to die in dignity, and it should be a standard level of care.

"Marie Curie is currently trialling new ways of working with the NHS in hospital emergency departments and GP practices, to identify people approaching the end of life earlier and put the right support in place, including Advance Care Plans.

"But the issue runs much deeper. This autumn the UK Government is expected to publish a plan for England to overhaul end of life care, called the Modern Services Framework for Palliative and End of Life Care.

Article continues below

"We need to make sure the scope of this opportunity is not missed. We are calling for this to be a fully funded plan to deliver a 24/7 palliative care helpline to ensure there is access to round the clock care, medication and coordinated support to reduce the numbers being forced to turn to A&E.

"Everyone agrees that no one should die in pain or distress, something needs to change to make that happen. "

News.title: No 10 Downing Street advertised as holiday let in fake listing on travel giant Booking.com
News.content:
No 10 Downing Street advertised as holiday let in fake listing on travel giant Booking.com

Consumer group Which? says it was able to advertise the Prime Minister's 10 Downing Street for let on Booking.com for several months - raising big concerns about the online giant's safeguards

View 4 Images Consumer group Which? was able to create a fake holiday let for 10 Downing Street on Booking.com (Image: Which?)

Online travel giant Booking.com has been accused of exposing customers to “glaring” security flaws after researchers were able to list 10 Downing Street as a holiday let.

‌



Consumer watchdog Which? said it was allowed to set-up a fake listing for the PM’s official home - complete with the address and even a photo of the famous black front door - within minutes. Which? said the website processed a payment from one of its researchers using a different account for a week-long.

‌



The ease in setting-up the bogus listing comes despite Booking.com claiming it uses advanced AI and multiple security controls. Which? said it had repeatedly exposed Booking.com’s security gaps and received dozens of complaints from people receiving scam messages on the platform, plus heard of hundreds of travellers arriving at properties to discover that the listing was fake.

‌



View 4 Images Which? says details about a fake listing for 10 Downing Street should have been spotted by Booking.com's systems (Image: Which?)

Argos reveals top 20 toys for Christmas 2026 featuring Lego, Toy Story and Peppa Pig READ MORE :

Premium Bond results for September 2026 announced including £1million prizes READ MORE :

Those trying to contact Booking.com to complaint or for help were initially directed to what Which? said was an ineffective AI chatbot.

To test the website’s systems, a Which? researcher listed a property on Booking.com in mid-June, headlined ‘1 bedroom apartment in the heart of London’, including the exact address - 10 Downing Street, London - its location on a map, and a photo of the most famous front door in Britain. The listing was set so users had to request a stay, so nobody could book automatically without being approved.

‌



View 4 Images Booking.com has hit back at findings by consumer group Which? (Image: Getty Images)

Which? was also able to add a fake review, giving it 10/10. After writing the review, Booking.com sent a message saying that it would be ‘checked by our team of moderators’ - but the review appeared almost immediately, despite what Which? said was was obviously a joke, including a reference to how enjoyable it was hanging out with Larry The Cat.

The listing was not removed until August 27, even after Which? said it had made Booking.com aware of its findings. It warned it showed "glaring gaps in Booking.com's security".

‌



Rory Boland, editor of Which? Travel said: “If Booking.com’s so-called sophisticated AI systems can’t spot that 10 Downing Street is not a holiday rental, then it’s no wonder scammers can exploit the platform so easily.

“It would be laughable that we were able to list the UK’s most famous address for rent, if the consequences weren’t so devastating for holidaymakers, who risk losing thousands of pounds to bogus listings and phishing links.

View 4 Images Fake review of 10 Downing Street even referred to hanging out with Larry the cat (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

‌



“Booking.com’s checks are clearly unfit for purpose, and the Prime Minister must now urge Ofcom to use the Online Safety Act to crack down on irresponsible online platforms that leave consumers wide open to fraud.”

A spokesperson for Booking.com said: “This limited test is not a true reflection of the experience of millions of listings or reviews published on our platform.

“The property added by Which? was not visible and ‘live’ for the time period referenced*, and as it was not open and bookable, some of our automatic fraud controls were not triggered to completely remove the closed listing.

Article continues below

“Of the other examples shared by Which?, not all listings have been proven to be fraudulent.”

It added: “We can confirm that we use a range of checks and verification measures to help protect our platform, alongside technologies including artificial intelligence.

“Together, these measures help us detect and remove the majority of fraudulent listings within 24 hours.”

News.title: Met Office humidity warning as parts of UK facing muggy weather while temperatures climb
News.content:
Met Office humidity warning as parts of UK facing muggy weather while temperatures climb

The forecast suggests the muggy air will be most apparent ahead of, and along, weather systems pushing in from the Atlantic — with spells of rain and showers at times

View 2 Images The south of England is set to see humid weather return as temperatures rise (Image: ANDY RAIN/EPA/Shutterstock)

The Met Office has warned that humid air will return to parts of the UK this week, with the muggy conditions most likely to be felt in the south and the South East as temperatures rise.

‌



Met Office meteorologist Greg Dewhurst said on the Met Office Youtube channel a “southwesterly breeze” would help pull in moisture-laden air again, making it feel uncomfortable for some as the week progresses.

‌



“A southwesterly breeze here is drawing in the humid air once more,” he said in the latest week-ahead forecast.

‌



After the week began with a changeable picture, the Met Office forecaster said humidity could become more noticeable midweek, particularly in southern areas. He said there may be “a fairly humid start to the day in the south” and later added: “A rather humid feeling day where the sun does come out,” with temperatures “25, possibly 26 Celsius towards the southeast.”

The forecast suggests the muggy air will be most apparent ahead of, and along, weather systems pushing in from the Atlantic — with spells of rain and showers at times.

The meteorologist added: “This weather front becomes the dividing line between warm and humid air to the south and something a little fresher to the north.”

‌



View 2 Images Temperatures are set to rise to the mid-20s across the south of England on Thursday, bringing muggy humid conditions (Image: Met Office)

Although the rest of the week looks uncertain, temperatures are expected to rise overall, to the mid-20s with brighter spells, especially in the south, while the north stays closer to average.

The news comes as the Met Office announced that new provisional figures show summer 2026 was the warmest in the UK since records began nearly 150 years ago.

‌



The forecaster found that the country warmed to an average of 16.5C in June, July and August, a significant 0.4C warmer than the previous record, set just last year.

Figures from the agency, which date back to 1884 show that the top six warmest summers on record have all occurred this century, including three this decade: 2026 in first place, followed by 2025, 2018, 2006, 2003 and 2022.

On several occasions this summer temperatures nearly reached 40C with five distinct heatwaves and drought conditions declared across much of the UK.

Article continues below

Figures from the agency revealed that England and Wales had their driest Julys on record, and southern England the driest month ever recorded since 1836.

News.title: Two killed at a wedding as US bomb strikes hit civilian areas in Iran - reports
News.content:
Two killed at a wedding as US bomb strikes hit civilian areas in Iran - reports

Iranian officials say that four people, including one child, have been killed in US airstrikes on the south of the country

View 2 Images Prior to the weekend here had been a month without US strikes in the Middle East (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

A US strike hit a home where a wedding ceremony was being held in southern Iran, Iranian officials have said. Ahmad Nafisi, deputy governor of the region told Iranian state television that two people were killed and others wounded at the celebration which was being held in a home.

‌



Explosions have been reported across southern Iranian coastal areas, including Kuhestak where the wedding was taking place and the port city of Bandar Abbas which is home to naval and air force facilities. Iranian state media reported that civilian sites and a civilian airport had been hit.

‌



A US strike hit a home where a wedding ceremony was being held in Kuhestak in southern Iran, killing two people and wounding at least 50 others, Ahmad Nafisi, Hormozgan Province's deputy governor, told Iranian state television in a phone call. Red Crescent rescue officials in the province said the death toll had risen to four, including a child.

‌



The deadly strikes come after the US restarted attacks on Sunday following a month without military action. Witnesses in the area said that the explosions today were stronger than those on Sunday and smoke can be seen rising from areas on the Strait of Hormuz.

The US and Iran are both seeking control over the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway off Iran's coast through which 20% of the world's oil normally flows. Tehran effectively closed it after the war began.

View 2 Images Vessels are seen in the Strait of Hormuz, off the port city of Bandar Abbas in southern Iran which has reportedly come under attack from US air strikes (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



The renewed fighting comes as American citizens in the Middle East have been warned by the US government to expect to see flight cancellations in the region. Just hours after the Consular warning was issued, Trump took to his own social media platform, Truth Social to threaten escalation.

"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings," Trump warned on social media.

US Central Command has said the latest strikes were in response to Tehran trying to attack commercial ships and American forces in the Middle East.

Article continues below

Iranian semi-official media said the country began firing missiles and drones in response to U.S. strikes. News agencies reported late Tuesday that it had launched operations and Iran's military command said the armed forces would deliver what they described as "crushing and devastating blows" against the United States.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had said earlier Tuesday, before the latest strikes, that the Islamic Republic would be ready to return to the interim ceasefire deal reached with the US in June if Washington does the same. "If the U.S. returns to its commitments in the memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate," state media reported.

News.title: Bristol fire live: 'Explosions' heard as hundreds of firefighters tackle major blaze
News.content:
A huge fire has broken out in Brislington this afternoon

There are reports of hundreds of firefighters tackling a massive blaze at an industrial unit in the south of Bristol after crews from nine fire stations were scrambled to the incident

Hundreds of firefighters have descended on a trading estate in south Bristol this afternoon after a massive fire broke out.

Emergency crews scrambled to Dixon Road in the Brislington neighbourhood with roads cordoned off and reports from the scene of “hundreds” of firefighters.

Avon Fire and Rescue Service has said that crews from nine different stations have attended the incident.

News.title: 'Andy Burnham strikes hopeful note in first Commons test but difficult choices loom'
News.content:
After a long hot summer, it was back to reality for Andy Burnham.

The new Prime Minister faced his first Commons test as Labour MPs finally got to see their new leader in action, six weeks after he swept to power to become Britain's sixth PM in a decade.

Despite 16 years away from the Commons front bench, the PM appeared unfazed by spending more than three hours answering 125 questions on his agenda.

He sought to strike a more collegiate tone with Kemi Badenoch, and said he wanted to ditch political point scoring in favour of getting things done. It's a stark contrast from Nigel Farage, who was back in Parliament after spending the summer arguing with a man dressed as a bin to distract from questions about his finances.

‌



The exchanges were pure Burnham. Big on ambition, peppered with hope and optimism, but also highly political. There was no repeat of the doom and gloom warnings from the early months of Keir Starmer's premiership, a mistake the new PM is determined not to repeat.

Keir Starmer to step down as Labour MP after resigning as PM in July READ MORE :

Nigel Farage heckled as he returns to Parliament after Clacton by-election READ MORE :

View 2 Images Keir Starmer announced his plans to step down as an MP hours before Andy Burnham's big Commons moment (Image: Stefan Rousseau/PA Wire)

Ukraine, defence spending, taxes, welfare, hospitality, social care, even the Jodrell Bank telescope. Burnham engaged with everything, dropping hints left, right and centre on what he plans to do with power.

Here lies the tension. Burnham has huge ambitions and he knows he has to make a real impact to persuade voters to give Labour another term in office. But he won't be able to do everything, and there will be times when he has to make difficult and unpopular choices.

‌



The row over the early release of prisoners shows how problems will erupt that consume the PM's attention. There are tricky issues on his desk, including the Budget, major reviews on welfare, a decision on North Sea oil and gas, immigration reforms, and defence spending.

The problems are not just at home. While he was speaking, Germany accused Russia of an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport, in a stark reminder of how turbulent the global picture is.

His predecessor also left him a parting gift - a by-election Burnham could do without. Keir Starmer's decision to quit as an MP - only weeks after pledging to serve out this Parliament - dominated the headlines ahead of the PM's big Commons moment.

It sets up an early test of Burnham's electoral appeal outside of the North West. Holborn and St Pancras has long been a Labour stronghold, but Starmer's majority was reduced to 11,572 in 2024, despite the party's landslide victory.

‌



Independents and the Greens were nipping at his heels back then, and the political picture has changed since the general election. It will be a tempting seat for Zack Polanski to contest, particularly if the Greens can form some sort of pact with local independents.

Labour will need to throw the kitchen sink at winning it to avoid putting a dampener on Burnham's good vibes.

News.title: UK steakhouse chain to close all 20 restaurants this week
News.content:
UK steakhouse chain to close all 20 restaurants this week

Whitbread, owner of the Bar + Block announced it was closing all 20 of its restaurants this week, leaving fans of the chain heartbroken

View 2 Images The well-loved chain is closing all of its outlets this week (Image: Getty Images)

A popular British chain of steakhouses is due to shut its doors this week- with the closure of all 20 of its restaurants.

‌



Fans were left devastated after Whitbread announced it was closing all 20 of its Bar + Block chains as of Thursday, September 3.

‌



The company said the move has come as part of a massive restructuring effort that will see a number of well-liked venues close their doors for good.

‌



The all-day steakhouses first opened back in 2016 with the aim of drawing in younger diners.

Fans of the eateries have been left heartbroken following the announcement, with one saying: “They do the best Sunday lunch here. Will miss it.”

While another said: “Never had a bad meal at Bar + Block in various locations, that’s a shame.”

‌



View 2 Images Bar and Block restaurants are operated by Whitbread Plc which also owns Premier Inn hotels and Costa Coffee (Image: Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The closures come as owners Whitbread will also close all of its Cookhouse + Pub and Table + Table brands to focus more on its Premier Inn brand.

In an announcement earlier this year Whitbread said: “This change will involve exiting all of our remaining branded restaurants, which trade under brands including Beefeater and Brewers Fayre, a number of which will be converted into approximately 600 additional Premier Inn rooms, with the remainder expected to be sold as going concerns,” the company added.

‌



The Beefeater and Brewers Fayre brands are set to close on September 10 and September 7 respectively. The plan will see a total of 261 restaurants shutter for good.

A number of the Beefeater and Brewers Fayre venues will be converted into approximately 600 additional Premier Inn hotel rooms while the others are expected to be sold as going concerns, the company announced in April.

This is the full list of all the Bar + Block locations closing

Bath

Belfast

Birmingham City Centre Exchange Square

Birmingham City Centre Waterloo Street

Edinburgh

Glasgow

Leamington Spa

London Aldgate

London Hammersmith

London Kings Cross

London Paddington

London Southwark

London Sutton

London Wimbledon

Milton Keynes

Newcastle

Nottingham

Portsmouth

Whiteley

Winnersh

Article continues below

In a farewell post on Instagram the Bar + Block chain said: "On the 3rd September, Bar + Block will officially close its doors across all locations.

"From evening cocktails and weekend brunches to indulging in a premium cut of steak, serving you has been an absolute privilege. We are immensely grateful to every guest who came through our doors, and to our passionate team who made every experience unforgettable.

"Before we mix our final drink and serve our last steak on the 3rd September, we’d love to welcome you back one last time. Come raise a glass, savour your favourite dish, and toast to the memories we’ve made together."

News.title: Trump threatens Iran with 'biggest attack of them all' as Americans in Middle East told to 'be aware'
News.content:
Trump threatens Iran with 'biggest attack of them all' as Americans in Middle East told to 'be aware'

Americans in the Middle East were told to be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions less than an hour before the president took to social media to threaten Iran with a fresh wave of attacks

View 2 Images President Donald Trump listens as a reporter asks a question in the Oval Office of the White House, Monday, Aug. 31, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin) (Image: AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)

Americans travelling or living in the Middle East have been warned of 'potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions' in the region as Trump threatens fresh attacks in Iran.

‌



Donald Trump issued stark warning to Iran following confirmation that the US has launched fresh strikes on Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz. The US President said American forces were "as we speak" hitting Iranian targets close to the vital shipping route, and threatened that "the biggest attack of them all is waiting in the wings".

‌



The President's Truth Social post came within hours of the US Consulate in the Middle East issuing a warning to Americans in the region. The US State Department said American citizens should be aware of potential flight disruption.

‌



The consular advice states: "Due to tensions in the Middle East, the security environment remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation. Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance and be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions."

Trump said that the current US strikes on Iran were a response to country's attempt to lay sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz and an attack on a US military base in Jordan which saw eight missiles launched.

View 2 Images The Strait of Hormuz is a crucial point of control in the region (Image: Getty Images)

‌



On Truth Social he said added: "If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran!" Trump also maintained the Strait of Hormuz presently has "no mines", claiming those positioned in the critical waterway had been "completely removed or detonated".

The President confirmed all eight missiles launched at the US military base in Jordan had been "successfully knocked down". His most recent remarks follow Iranian state television broadcasting what it claimed were ballistic missiles being fired towards US bases in Jordan.

Jordan's armed forces also reported that eight missiles entering its airspace early on Monday were intercepted. The US strikes targeted two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island, according to a US official cited by Axios.

‌



Trump subsequently told Fox News: "We're going to hit them hard. There will be a response."

He also branded Iran's leadership as "violent" and "evil" while issuing warnings over its nuclear ambitions.

Trump said: "If they had a nuclear weapon, Israel would be gone. If I weren't President, Israel would be gone and there would probably be no Middle East."

Article continues below

The US launched attacks on Larak Island on August 30. These attacks marked the first reported US strike on Iranian territory since late July.

The mounting tensions have also unsettled energy markets, with oil prices climbing by approximately three per cent in the wake of the previous strikes.

News.title: Burnham promises more devolution and public control of essential services
News.content:
Andy Burnham has promised to set out plans for "stronger public control" of essential services as he addressed the House of Commons for the first time since taking power.

The prime minister said "a series of wrong turns" since the 1980s had seen economic power in the UK privatised and pointed to the water industry as "a leaking monument to that approach - a country run in the private rather than public interest".

He reiterated his belief that political power had been centralised and announced he would be making devolution powers available to more areas in England.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of offering "more government control, more taxes and more politicians".

"His diagnosis is completely wrong, his theory of growth is completely wrong, he thinks that if government spends more money, we will all get richer - that is not how this works," she said.

Badenoch also warned the prime minister that his new job would be "very different" to his previous Greater Manchester mayoral role where he "did not have to make difficult trade-offs".

Burnham became prime minister on 20 July shortly after Parliament closed for the summer recess.

Tuesday marked the first day of the new parliamentary session and provided his first opportunity to address MPs and take questions.

He told the House of Commons that "Britain is not where we would wish it to be", but promised to "build a new sense of optimism around the country".

Following his 10 years away from Parliament, Burnham said he was returning with a "clear diagnosis" of what had gone wrong in the country.

"From the 1980s, this country took a series of wrong turns," he said.

"Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country deindustrialised, austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this.

"And then Brexit compounded the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration."

In the months before becoming prime minister, Burnham stopped short of calling for full nationalisation but said he wanted to see greater public control of water and energy.

On Tuesday, he promised that a plan to achieve this would be produced "later in the year".

Pressed on his plans for the water sector by Conservative MP Alison Griffiths, Burnham said it was important to "look at all possible solutions".

"It's a very regrettable situation that the privatisation of water has left us in a position where we're going to find it very difficult to reverse," he added.

News.title: UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget
News.content:
Long-term government borrowing costs have risen to a 28-year high, putting further pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham ahead of his first Budget next month.

The yield on a 30-year gilt â a loan to the British government â rose to 5.89% on Tuesday, the highest since 1998.

Borrowing costs in the US, Japan and Europe have hit similar highs in recent days, reflecting investors' concerns about inflation, state borrowing levels and spending levels by large tech companies on AI.

Burnham told the House of Commons his government's "bedrock", as it seeks to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, will be "fiscal responsibility".

All of those factors will make the Budget process trickier for Burnham, who on Tuesday addressed MPs for the first time as prime minister, and his Chancellor John Healey.

Burnham told the House of Commons the economy and the cost of living were "the biggest issues facing the country".

Higher borrowing costs will reduce the amount of headroom the government has against its self-imposed fiscal rules, limiting the amount Healey can spend on consumer-friendly measures to ease the cost of living.

Despite the squeezed public finances, Burnham said said he would bring about "more substantial change" to ease living costs.

"Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be," he added.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of "living in the past".

"His diagnosis is completely wrong," she told the House of Commons. "His theory of growth is completely wrong. He thinks that if Government spends more money, we will all get richer.

"That is not how this works."

The chancellor has previously said he will stick to a set of fiscal rules imposed by his predecessor Rachel Reeves that restrict borrowing. These rules are designed to help markets have clarity about the path of borrowing.

The more that is forecast to be spent on interest payments, the more likely that there will be a squeeze on spending or some form of tax rise to meet these rules.

On top of that, higher government rates can feed through to higher business and household borrowing costs, and so weigh on the economy.

Burnham was already facing a tough balancing act with taxing and spending, due to pressures on defence and the cost of living.

As well as the rise to 30-year gilt yields, the yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt rose to 5.22% on Tuesday. This is its highest rate since June 2008, at the height of the global financial crisis.

Gilt yields move counter to the value of the bonds, meaning their prices fall when yields rise.

News.title: Rising numbers of children in mental health crisis ending up in A&E
News.content:
There has been a sharp rise in children and young people attending A&E units in England in a mental health crisis, NHS doctors are warning.

The number of six to 17-year-olds turning up in significant distress for things like self-harm and eating disorders, or in emotional crisis, rose by 36% between 2019 and 2025, according to the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health analysis.

Some faced waits of more than 12 hours once there. The college said A&Es were not the best place for them, but a lack of support in the community meant they often had nowhere else to turn.

The government said it was looking to improve services and would be setting out plans soon.

The analysis â based on figures provided under the Freedom of Information Act by NHS England â found there were 75,491 attendances at A&E by children and young people for a mental health concern in 2025.

That is up from 55,525 in 2019 with some of the biggest rises seen in very young children aged six to nine. The increases far outstrip the overall jump in attendances, which has risen by just over 8% over the period.

Doctors said the cases included children and young people brought in by families, carers and police â some of those in emotional crisis become aggressive or have challenging behaviour.

In total, more than 6,200, around 8%, waited over 12 hours in A&E.

News.title: Baby girl who died at Sheffield house was stabbed, police say
News.content:
A newborn baby girl who was discovered fatally injured at a house in Sheffield died as a result of stab wounds, police have said.

The baby was found at a house on Holywell Heights in the Wincobank area on Sunday morning, after police were called to reports of concern for her safety.

South Yorkshire Police said despite the best efforts of police and paramedics, the baby died at the scene.

Seven people aged between 15 and 37 were arrested on suspicion of her murder. Two of them, aged 26 and 37, were later bailed, but police confirmed on Tuesday a warrant had been obtained to extend time in custody for the remaining five as inquiries continued.

Det Ch Insp Tom Woodward, leading the investigation, said: "We recognise this is deeply distressing for those who would have loved to have a chance to love this baby girl, for the emergency services who responded and for the community who will inevitably be shocked by this incident.

"Everyone involved in responding to this tragedy - from the first officers and paramedics on the scene to the detectives now leading the investigation - has felt the profound impact of this investigation."

He added: "Our commitment to this little girl is unwavering. We will confront every difficult and distressing challenge and pursue every line of inquiry with determination and care to secure justice for her.

"We know the local community will hold her in their thoughts and support us as we work through this complex investigation."

A South Yorkshire Police spokesperson said officers were continuing their investigations in the Holywell Heights area and asked anyone with information that might be useful to contact them.

News.title: Rybakina makes winning start in race to number one
News.content:
Elena Rybakina says she is "motivated" by the race to become world number one but is simply taking things "day by day" after getting her US Open campaign off to a winning start.

Playing for the first time since withdrawing midway through her Cincinnati Masters quarter-final with a heel injury last month, Rybakina showed no signs of discomfort as she eased to a dominant 6-3 6-2 win over 17-year-old wildcard Thea Frodin.

The 27-year-old second seed trails Aryna Sabalenka by just 434 points in the world rankings and will become number one for the first time by reaching the semi-finals in New York â even if Sabalenka defends her title.

Regardless of her performance, Rybakina will also secure the top ranking if none of Sabalenka, Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula lift the trophy.

"I'm definitely motivated [to become world number one]," said Rybakina, who trailed Sabalenka by more than 3,000 points in the spring before the Belarusian entered a mid-season slump.

"I feel like I had opportunities before and it didn't go my way. It will be an amazing achievement but it's still too far and I need to focus on my day off tomorrow, my recovery, and just keep on going."

News.title: Israel warns it will retaliate if UK imposes sanctions
News.content:
Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar has warned his country will retaliate if the UK imposes sanctions against it over the potential expansion of settlements in the West Bank.

Addressing Parliament for the first time as foreign secretary, Ed Miliband said he would introduce a "comprehensive reset" of policy on Israel "in the coming weeks".

He said the government would examine how to stop UK companies "financing, constructing or advertising new settlements" in the occupied West Bank.

Responding, Gideon Saar told Hebrew-language news website Ynet: "If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain."

"If they act, I think they will be making a big mistake," he said.

Last month, Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in the so-called E1 area - a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn widespread international condemnation.

The development would in effect divide the West Bank in two and isolate East Jerusalem.

Miliband said the plans are "illegal under international law" and called them "the crossing of a red line, as it cuts through the heart of the West Bank and risks making a Palestinian state unviable".

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also warned that Israel's statement about the E1 area could "imperil or end" the two-state solution in the Middle East.

All settlements are illegal under international law and, under global pressure, Israel held off for decades on plans to build in the area.

News.title: Watch: Norway's new king takes oath as mourners pay respects to his late father
News.content:
Norway's Haakon VIII has sworn an oath before parliament in Oslo in the first major step of his reign as King.

During Tuesday's ceremony, parliament also held a minute's silence for Haakon's father, the late King Harald V, who died on Friday.

Haakon's wife, Queen Mette-Marit, was absent from the formalities as she continues to recover from a lung transplant.

Following the ceremony, mourners began paying their respects at the late King's coffin, which is lying in state at the Royal Palace until 8 September.

News.title: Soft launches and late sittings - six ways to get cheaper meals out
News.content:
Restaurants often want to fill seats outside of peak lunch and dinner hours so opting for earlier or later sittings can be rewarded by a cheaper bill.

Apps such as First Table, which operates across 21 UK cities, as well as Ireland, New Zealand and Australia, give diners 50% off food when they book a participating restaurant's first or last dining slot. In exchange, diners pay a small booking fee.

EatClub is another, giving walk-ins up to 50% off the whole bill at thousands of venues when they redeem an offer within its app. The biggest discounts are at off-peak times.

Shokofeh Hejazi, director of foresight and innovation at global trends agency The Food People, says earlier dining appeals because it tends to be quieter and calmer, people drink less and it allows them to get home sooner.

Meeting up for breakfast also tends to be a bit more wallet-friendly as it's usually just one course and diners get the same catch-up time with friends and family, she adds.

News.title: Range Rover launches first fully electric model
News.content:
Range Rover has unveiled its first fully electric model, after a yearâlong delay to its planned launch.

The Range Rover Electric, to be built in Solihull, marks a major shift in its electrification programme, backed by largeâscale upgrades across its West Midlands sites.

Parent company JLR said it had up-skilled 10,500 workers for electric production as it pushes ahead with modernisation despite recent financial pressures and planned job cuts.

The launch comes as the Coventryâbased carmaker faces falling profits, supply chain disruption and restructuring following a cyber attack last year.

The company said the launch was being supported by new battery and electric drive unit production lines as well as training around 9,000 employees in Solihull for electrification and a further 1,500 trained across the region.

JLR's Electric Propulsion Manufacturing Centre in Wolverhampton is now producing battery packs and electric drive units alongside internal combustion engines.

Martin Limpert, managing director of Range Rover, called the new model the result of a decade of "considered engineering".

JLR's electric roll-out comes after a turbulent year with profits dropping to Â£66m in the first quarter after a fire at a key Norwegian supplier.

The business is also undergoing restructuring, confirming that fewer than 300 roles will go less than a year after a cyber attack halted production for more than a month.

At the time of the results, the firm said new product launches would leave "JLR in good shape whilst acknowledging the continuing geopolitical, inflationary and regulatory challenges the industry faces".

News.title: More than 110 rescued a week after Nepal deadly floods, army says
News.content:
One hundred and nineteen people have been rescued using air resources in Nepal following deadly floods, a spokesperson for the country's army said.

It comes nearly a week after the disaster that hit both Nepal and neighbouring Tibet, killing more than 1,000 people, with more than 3,900 still missing.

A Nepali army spokesperson earlier said a British male was among those rescued, along with 118 Nepalese people, of whom 44 were female and 74 male.

Later on Tuesday, the British man, Alastair Chambers, told the Telegraph and PA Media he was not rescued and had travelled to the region to help with aid efforts.

The BBC has contacted the UK Foreign Office for comment.

On Tuesday, Foreign Office minister Lord Wood of Anfield confirmed 36 British people remain unaccounted for - an increase from the 33 previously reported.

More than 600 are workers believed to be trapped in a vast network of mud-filled tunnels at hydropower sites along Trishuli River are among the thousands who are still missing.

Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Monday that 279 people had been rescued from the sites.

The rescue operation is being spearheaded by an international team made up of Chinese and Nepalese military personnel, while experts from India, Korea and Australia are also involved.

On Tuesday, the Nepalese Tourist Board said it had rescued 330 foreign nationals in total.

Saturday saw a rapid development team from the UK arrive in Nepal to provide support for Britons and their families.

News.title: Family mourn 'deeply loved' girl killed in Middlesbrough fire
News.content:
The family of a seven-year-old girl killed in a house fire said their lives had been changed forever by her "devastating loss".

Valentina Foster died alongside her aunt Natalie McDonald, 34, in the blaze at Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of 26 August. A man has been charged with their murders.

In a tribute, the youngster's parents said their daughter would "always be in our hearts, and her memory will live with us forever".

"She was deeply loved and will be missed beyond words by her family, friends, and everyone whose life she touched," they said.

"Our lives have changed forever, and we are struggling to come to terms with this devastating loss."

They added she would be "forever missed" by her brothers and sisters.

News.title: Keir Starmer announces he is standing down as MP
News.content:
Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has announced he is to stand down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs.

The move will trigger a by-election in the London seat of Holborn and St Pancras, long a Labour stronghold, which he has represented since 2015.

Sir Keir, who left Downing Street in July, had previously said he would stay on as an MP until the next UK general election, which is not due until 2029.

But in a surprise statement hours before his successor Andy Burnham made his debut in the House of Commons, he said he was resigning to work on issues such as international affairs and violence against women and girls.

Paying tribute to his predecessor, Burnham highlighted Sir Keir's work with Ukraine and the Hillsborough Law drawn up under his government to improve the accountability of public officials, which is going through Parliament.

"He has given this country a lifetime of public service, particularly for those fighting for justice," he added.

"His leadership took our party from one of its worst defeats to its best victories and created a platform to change this country for the better. We will use it well, and we wish his family the very best for the future."

Announcing his resignation, Sir Keir told the Camden New Journal, external it had been a "huge honour and privilege" to represent the London constituency for 11 years, ending weeks of speculation about whether he would remain an MP.

He added he was ready to "pass the baton to a successor", telling the newspaper it was the "right time" for him to leave Parliament.

He said: "I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world.

"I will also continue, as I have done for a long time now with others, to work on combating violence against women and girls; that is an issue that matters to me hugely.

"It's work I started before I became an MP and it's work I'm keen to continue after I'm an MP. So international affairs on the one hand, and continuing my work on violence against women and girls on the other."

Sir Keir became prime minister after winning a landslide majority at the 2024 election, but quit No 10 after pressure from Labour MPs to stand aside.

News.title: Spaces in male prisons fall to lowest level of year, sources say
News.content:
An investment of Â£110m, which will come from existing budgets, will be used to convert unused office space, laundry rooms and storage space into cells, the MoJ said.

Speaking in the Commons on Tuesday, the justice secretary told MPs the government's plan to free up capacity in the UK's male prison estate will ensure the justice system "commands the confidence of the British public"

"This is the right thing to do, and I pay tribute to his wife Lissie and mother Debbie (Adlam), who campaigned for this," he said.

"We would like to have gone further, but due to the lack of investment in the previous government's 14 years, we are unable to do so."

He added Labour has been forced to take "tough decisions" because it had inherited a justice system "on the brink of failure".

Norris also told MPs the government plans to "bring forward legislation" to end Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences "once and for all â by the end of this Parliament".

IPPS sentences were used where prisoners were considered to pose a significant risk of causing serious harm to the public. Once they had served a minimum term they could only be released if the Parole Board was satisfied they no longer posed a risk to the public.

Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy called plans to end IPP sentences a "fag packet policy".

He said: "This is the Government's fifth early release policy in just six weeks since the prime minister took office.

"At every stage, we were told ministers had no choice but to include dangerous criminals, because the alternative would be the collapse of the entire system.

"Now the plan is to stop one group of dangerous criminals leaving prison early by letting a different group of dangerous criminals out instead."

Earlier, Norris told the BBC prisoners being released early did not mean "freedom" and victims would have a say in restrictions placed on those criminals.

Asked where clothes would be washed if laundry rooms were converted into cells, Norris told BBC Breakfast: "Of course we're going to make sure that the prisons can still function properly.

"This is a creative look, as I say, around our estate and being able to use some space that we can re-prioritise."

Norris said he suspected the number of extra prison spaces created from freeing up existing space within prisons would be "landing somewhere in the middle" of 200 and 900.

But the chairman of the Prison Officers' Association, Mark Fairhurst, said: "You can create as much additional space as you like, and build as many new prisons as you like, but where are the staff coming from to supervise people? Nobody wants to be a prison officer anymore."

Prisons in England and Wales are running at 97% capacity.

Under the early release scheme some 4,500 prisoners are now expected to start being let out of prison in tranches from October.

On Sunday, the prime minister told BBC Breakfast anyone convicted of manslaughter would be excluded from the scheme, following a campaign from PC Andrew Harper's family to block the release of two men convicted over his killing in 2019.

Extra prison space would also be created by deporting more foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.

Government figures show there were 10,134 foreign nationals held in custody on 30 June, 3,283 of whom were on remand and would not be eligible for deportation.

In the year to June, 5,962 foreign offenders were sent back to their home countries - the highest rate of deportations since 2017 and a 12% increase on the previous year.

News.title: Summer 2026 was UK's hottest on record, Met Office says
News.content:
In a rapid attribution study - which looks at how much of a role climate change plays - the Met Office say the average temperature was made around 130 times more likely due to human-induced climate change.

And step back from this summer and there is clue to our changing climate in the temperature record itself.

In a climate that isn't changing, new records should become progressively rarer, because every time a record falls, it raises the bar for the next one.

Think about the 100m race. Each time someone sets a new record, it becomes harder to beat. And there's another thing. Typically records are only ever broken by a few fractions of a second â often just a millisecond or two.

In June 1991, for example, Leroy Burrell ran 9.90 seconds, beating Carl Lewis's 1988 world record of 9.92 seconds by just two hundredths of a second.

Now look at the UK summer temperature record. Until last year, the four hottest summers on record were separated by just five hundredths of a degree.

Then 2025 beat the previous record by 0.34C. And this summer has beaten that new record by another 0.40C.

So after years when the record moved by tiny fractions, in just two summers the bar has been raised by 0.74C.

Head of Climate Attribution at the Met Office, Dr Mark McCarthy said that summer 2026 was "remarkable" and we can expect to see extremes occurring more frequently in the future because of climate change.

So why is this happening so quickly here? The UK sits on the western edge of Europe, the fastest-warming continent on Earth - warming at roughly twice the global rate.

There are a few reasons for that. Land heats up faster than the oceans, parts of Europe stretch into the rapidly warming Arctic, and changes in weather patterns have favoured more frequent and intense summer heatwaves.

Scientists are still working out exactly how much each factor contributes, but the result is clear: the background climate in which British weather happens is getting warmer.

None of this means the UK will break its summer record every year. Weather will always give us cooler summers as well as hotter ones. But the pattern is becoming unmistakable: records that once marked the extreme edge of the UK's climate are being overtaken with remarkable speed.

So the question is not whether the UK will experience summers hotter than this one. It is how often they will come - and how much hotter they might be.

News.title: Trump says US position on Falklands 'one of many' under review
News.content:
Donald Trump has said the United States' position on the Falkland Islands is "one of many" under review, as he pressed the UK to increase military spending.

The US president said the UK has "got some problems, but they'll get solved" when asked about defence funding as a follow-up question to his response on the Falklands.

It comes after The Daily Telegraph reported, external US defence officials were drawing up proposals to incentivise Nato allies to meet their spending pledges, with a threat to oppose UK sovereignty over the Falklands among the possible options.

The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".

A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering."

The Falkland Islands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina.

The two countries waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim.

The 74-day conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

Previous US administrations have formally recognised the UK's de facto administration of the islands, but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump was asked by the BBC if he was reviewing the US position on the Falkland Islands.

The president replied: "I always review every position. That's just one of many."

Trump's remarks were labelled "nonsense" by Labour MP Dame Emily Thornberry, who chairs the Commons foreign affairs committee, as she asked the UK government to issue an official response in the House of Commons.

Foreign Office Minister Uma Kumaran replied: "The UK has no doubt about its sovereignty over the Falkland Islands.

"They are and will always remain a British overseas territory in line with the wishes of the Falkland islanders.

"The UK is steadfast in our support for the islanders' rights of self-determination."

Kumaran said she had seen Trump's comments, adding: "Our position remains unchanged."

News.title: Two-day sea search for missing teen on holiday is called off
News.content:
A major sea search for a missing 15-year-old boy has been called off after two days, the coastguard has said.

At about 15:30 BST on Sunday, HM Coastguard received a report that three people were experiencing difficulty in the water at Marloes Sands beach, Pembrokeshire.

Two managed to get out of the water, but the teenage boy, who was visiting the area on holiday from Yorkshire, was unaccounted for. The search was suspended at 19:30 BST on Monday.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency told the BBC that there were currently no plans to resume the search.

Pembrokeshire councillor Claire George said the community had been in shock.

She said: "We're absolutely distraught that somebody has come to harm when they've come to enjoy our wonderful coastline. It's most upsetting for all of us."

Marloes, she said, was remote and hard to access, adding that some beaches were safer than others.

She said: "It's a very dynamic environment. The sea can change at any minute, the weather can change at any minute, so people need to be aware of the risks."

On social media, Angle Lifeboat RNLI said its crew "worked tirelessly" for 22 hours at sea in a major, multi-agency search for the missing swimmer.

On Sunday, Broad Haven and Dale coastguard rescue teams were in attendance, alongside RNLI lifeboats from Angle, Tenby and St Davids and a pilot boat.

A coastguard helicopter and a HM Coastguard fixed wing aircraft were sent, along with the Welsh Ambulance Service.

The search was suspended at about 03:30 BST on Monday and started again later that morning, before being called off in the evening.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency said, despite an extensive search, "sadly, no sign of the missing person was found".

Angle Lifeboat RNLI added its crew had "shown immense dedication over the past two days".

It thanked the Milford Haven Coastguard for "their fantastic coordination and support" in what they said has been a "lengthy and tiring incident".

"Our thoughts are with the swimmer's family and friends at this difficult time," it added.

News.title: Transfer deadline day LIVE: Chelsea furious as Camara deal falls through, Balogun walks away from Everton, Man City sign Fernandez
News.content:
Manchester City have announced the record-equalling transfer of Enzo Fernandez for £125m - but Chelsea’s deal for Monaco’s Lamine Camara has dramatically fallen through after the transfer deadline. Chelsea are said to be furious after Monaco pulled out of a £47m deal for the 22-year-old midfielder at the last moment. They wanted to have a replacement for Fernandez lined up after City reached an agreement with Chelsea to sign the midfielder, matching the British record transfer fee Liverpool paid Newcastle United for Alexander Isak last summer.

Manchester City have meanwhile announced the £60m arrival of Iliman Ndiaye but Everton were dealt a bitter blow after the deadline as striker Folarin Balogun walked away from his £40m move from Monaco, after they had sold Beto to Fiorentina. The Toffees were left with Jack Grealish and Ainsley Maitland-Niles as their only replacements, while Tottenham have signed Mykhailo Mudryk on loan. Sunderland beat Crystal Palace to the signing of Malick Fofana after a dramatic tug-of-war for the £30m Lyon winger.

Manchester United did not sign a left back, despite being offered the chance to sign Rayan Ait-Nouri from rivals Manchester City. United were presented with a loan with obligation to buy but had no interest in a permanent move for the City defender. Liverpool’s business is over after signing Bradley Barcola for £120m and agreeing to sign 18-year-old Belgian goalkeeper Lucca Brughmans next summer. Harvey Elliot, meanwhile, has joined Valencia on loan.

Arsenal’s pursuit of Julian Alvarez has finally concluded with the forward remaining at Atletico Madrid, who refused to allow the Argentina international to join Barcelona. The Gunners have sold Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus and even allowed Ethan Nwaneri to depart on loan and the window closes without Mikel Arteta signing the marquee attacking signing he craved.

Vice President JD Vance said in a podcast released Tuesday that if a 2024 assassination attempt had killed Donald Trump, he would have always wondered if it was part of a conspiracy and might not have accepted even another Republican as the next president.

Vance made the statement during a conversation with Christian podcaster Bryce Crawford. The vice president, who recently released a book detailing his own journey to Catholicism, also defended President Trump for posting an image of himself as Jesus and mused about whether artificial intelligence was a sign of the end times.

The conversation kicked off with a discussion of faith and the rush to scientifically explain away events that may be divinely touched. Vance cited the July 2024 assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, during which a bullet nicked Trump's ear and a supporter was killed.

Trump has long talked about his survival as divinely guided, a theme Vance took up. The vice president said that if the bullet had killed Trump, “we would have had real civil strife in a way that I don’t know that the country could have ever come back from.”

Vance said many Trump supporters would have assumed a conspiracy had robbed them of their chosen president, and he said he would have also had those thoughts “in the back of my mind.”

“I would have assumed very dark forces had taken out Donald Trump, right as he was about to come back into the White House,” Vance said. “There would have just been an illegitimacy to our entire political system.”

Most of the hour-and-ten-minute conversation was an amiable chat about faith, Vance's own spiritual journey, his Easter meeting with Pope Francis the day before the pontiff's death last year, and human frailty and fallibility. But it occasionally touched on darker themes.

Crawford asked Vance whether, as vice president, he had ever been in a room that was “spiritually dark.”

“I've been in meetings with world leaders where various issues are being discussed, and somebody will say something or somebody will make an observation and I'll feel some darkness about it, it sets off every spiritual alarm bell in my body,” Vance said. He added he also felt “a very dark spiritual energy” in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, probably because of the carnage at the Civil War battlefield.

Vance cites AI during a discussion about ‘end times’

Crawford also asked Vance about his interest in the “end times,” which the vice president laughingly said had been more of an obsession in youth during the late 1990s, when people were abuzz about the possibility with the coming millennium. A chortling Vance recounted a story of a friend who was obsessed that the world would end in late 2007 and ran up major credit card debt.

“There are, like, things about the world that make me feel, like, not shocked if the antichrist was walking among us, but, again I try not to focus too much on it,” Vance said. He cited “IT companies” and the use of artificial intelligence as a substitute for human interaction.

“I think that’s kind of satanic,” Crawford said when Vance recounted the story of one acquaintance using AI as a marriage counselor.

“Yeah, when you completely divorce the human from the social element that God made us for, OK that's very, that's very bad,” Vance said.

Crawford asked Vance about Trump’s post on social media of an AI-generated image of himself as Jesus earlier this year, which Crawford said offended him. Trump initially contended he thought the image was of him as a doctor, then took down the post amid widespread criticism from even some of his own backers.

Vance defended the president. “He did not mean to, like, mock or mimic God, that's just not who he is,” Vance said, adding that the president often tries to keep things light and constantly makes jokes. “He's a bit of a ballbuster, for those of us who work with him, and he just likes to have a good time. And I think that if people appreciated that, they would recognize, he's not trying to offend people, he's trying to keep things light.”

Tiger Woods is set to appear in court on Wednesday for a change of plea hearing stemming from his car crash in Florida in March.

Woods, a 15-time major champion, was arrested and spent eight hours in jail before being bailed after the Land Rover he was driving rolled over in a collision with a pick-up truck towing a trailer.

He previously entered a written plea of not guilty via his lawyers to charges of driving under the influence, property damage and a refusal to submit to testing.

open image in gallery Tiger Woods is a 15-time major champion (Owen Humphreys/PA) ( PA Archive )

A court notice shows he is now slated to appear at Martin County Courthouse on Wednesday morning at 8.30am local time for a hearing, but it is unknown what Woods will change his plea to or if he has reached a plea deal with prosecutors.

Woods walked away unhurt from the crash, escaping out of his passenger door, and while he passed a breathalyser test for alcohol, the 50-year-old refused to submit to a urinary test for drugs.

According to a police affidavit, Woods was observed by the investigating officers to be “sweating profusely” while acting “lethargic and slow” with eyes that were “bloodshot and glassy”.

He admitted he “was looking down at his cell phone and changing the radio station” in the moments before the crash and “did not notice the vehicle in front of him had slowed down”.

Woods told the authorities he had not consumed any alcohol but admitted to taking “a few” prescription medications and had done so earlier in the morning while insisting he had not had any illegal drugs.

open image in gallery Woods was charged with driving under the influence, property damage and a refusal to submit to testing (Jane Barlow/PA) ( PA Archive )

Woods, who was also charged with property damage and refusal to submit to a lawful test, was observed to be “extremely alert and talkative” and had “hiccups during the entire investigation”.

Multiple sobriety exercises were conducted, where he struggled to follow instructions, leading a deputy to conclude: “How he performed on the exercises and based on my training, knowledge and experience, I believe Woods’ normal faculties were impaired and he was unable to safely operate the motor vehicle”.

During a search of his vehicle, investigators found two white pills, which were identified as hydrocodone, a prescription opioid used to treat severe, chronic pain.

Woods underwent emergency surgery after suffering multiple leg injuries following a serious car accident in California in February 2021. He has not competed on the PGA Tour since July 2024.

The affidavit stated Woods said he had 20 surgeries on his leg as a result of that crash, plus seven operations on his back, while the report also noted Woods was “limping and stumbling”.

Woods later wrote on X: “I know and understand the seriousness of the situation I find myself in.

“I am stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health. This is necessary in order for me to prioritise my wellbeing and work toward lasting recovery.”

Woods was also arrested on suspicion of DUI offences in 2017 after being found asleep at the wheel of his car in Jupiter, Florida.

He later pleaded guilty to reckless driving after it emerged he had had five prescription drugs in his system at the time.

In 2009, he crashed his car into a fire hydrant and tree outside his home in an incident that led to a spectacular unravelling of his private life.

News.title: What is the ‘Cat in the Hat’ viral trend that is landing teens in trouble with the law?
News.content:

A viral social media trend has landed teens in trouble with police in at least two states as authorities warn students about threats to school safety.

The so-called Cat in the Hat trend has spread across the country as young people share AI-generated content of someone wearing a costume of the famous Dr. Seuss character and appearing to be coming after people at their schools or homes.

Authorities in Kentucky and Colorado are among those to have cracked down on the trend.

The Allen County-Scottsville Crime Task Force in Kentucky opened an investigation last Thursday after it said multiple local students reported receiving threatening messages through Snapchat and other social media platforms from someone who identified themselves as the “Cat in the Hat.”

The task force said in a Facebook post Saturday that it had identified the minor behind a TikTok account involved in the investigation and that “the matter is being handled accordingly.”

open image in gallery A viral ‘Cat in the Hat’ social media trend has landed teens in jail in a couple of states as local authorities warn students about threats to school safety ( Getty Images/iStock )

The task force told The Independent that the minor “came forward to law enforcement and fully cooperated with the investigation,” adding that they were cited and released.

“The ‘Cat in the Hat’ accounts are part of a viral social media trend that has spread well beyond Allen County.

“Young people have been creating accounts and using AI-generated images and videos to make it appear that the character is coming to their town, school, neighborhood, or even after specific people,” the task force explained in a statement shared by WKRN.

“What may start as an internet trend or prank can quickly cross the line when it causes students to genuinely fear for their safety.”

open image in gallery The trend has spread across the country as young people share AI-generated content of someone wearing a costume of the famous Dr. Seuss character and appearing to be coming after people at their schools or homes ( Getty Images )

A 14-year-old student from Grand Junction High School in Colorado was arrested Monday in connection with the viral trend.

Last Friday, local police were made aware of a social media post referencing the “Cat in the Hat” trend on TikTok and suggesting someone may appear at a local middle school and at random houses.

“The posts are intended to cause alarm and fear in individuals,” Grand Junction Police said in a Facebook post.

The 14-year-old was charged with Interference with Staff, Faculty, or Students of Educational Institutions and Harassment and released to his parents.

“GJPD takes reports involving school safety seriously and will continue working closely with our community partners to prioritize the safety and security of our students, staff, and schools,” the Facebook post read.

Items linked to music legends such as Queen, The Beatles and Michael Jackson are set to go under the hammer in an auction with an estimated total value of £3 million.

The Propstore sale will feature 800 lots, including a black and gold military jacket worn in public by Jackson between 1994 and 1996, and a Pan American Airways menu autographed by all four members of The Beatles during their inaugural flight to the US.

Detailed with 24-carat gold braiding, the jacket worn by the “Thriller” singer is expected to fetch between £180,000 and £360,000, while the Beatles menu, dated 7 February 1964, is expected to make between £40,000 to £80,000.

Additionally, the auction includes a stage-worn, embellished black wrap top and flared trousers belonging to Queen frontman Freddie Mercury from the Sheer Heart Attack tour, valued between £60,000 and £120,000.

open image in gallery Propstore's music specialist Mark Hochman looks at Michael Jackson´s black-and-gold military-style jacket ( PA )

Noel Gallagher’s autographed Takamine FP460SC acoustic guitar, one of two identical guitars used during Oasis’s 1996 MTV Unplugged performance at London’s Royal Festival Hall as well as the (What’s the Story) Morning Glory? and Be Here Now tours will also go on sale.

The instrument, which comes with a stencilled Oasis case, is expected to make between £75,000 and £150,000.

Other items include a pair of John Lennon’s tinted glasses, expected to fetch between £100,000 and £200,000, and glasses worn by George Michael during the Faith tour, which are valued between £15,000 and £30,000.

Sex Pistols guitarist Steve Jones’ Filthy Lucre Tour stage-worn Vivienne Westwood Kilt is also included in the auction along with a signed promotional photo of the band, with the pair expected to make between £5,000 and £10,000.

open image in gallery Mark Hochman holds a Vivienne Westwood kilt worn by Sex Pistols guitarist Steve Jones on the Filthy Lucre Tour ( PA )

Mark Hochman, Propstore’s music specialist, said: “This auction brings together remarkable pieces connected to defining moments in music history.

“From Michael Jackson’s extensively documented military-style jacket and Noel Gallagher’s MTV Unplugged guitar to The Beatles’ signed Pan Am menu, each has an extraordinary story behind it.

“With over 800 lots also featuring memorabilia from Freddie Mercury, Britney Spears, George Michael and many more, Propstore’s auction offers something for music fans across generations and genres.”

The auction will take place on 1 and 2 October with bidding available online from the auction company’s website and via telephone, as well as absentee bids.

There will also be a special public free exhibition at The Cumberland Hotel in London from 24-27 September.

Sir Michael Palin and historian David Olusoga are set to feature in a new documentary detailing the return of the Bayeux Tapestry to the UK after nearly 1,000 years.

Arriving from France at the British Museum in London in July, the 70-metre-long linen artwork features embroidered images depicting the Norman Conquest.

This marks the first time the tapestry has returned to the country since it was created roughly 960 years ago, with the museum's landmark exhibition running until next July.

TV presenter and comedian Sir Michael will lend his voice to Secrets Of The Bayeux Tapestry, a new BBC Two documentary which will explore the efforts to return the priceless work back to the UK.

open image in gallery The tapestry depicts the 1066 Norman invasion and Battle of Hastings ( British Museum )

The tapestry depicts the 1066 Norman invasion and Battle of Hastings, which saw William the Conqueror take the English throne from King Harold and become the first Norman king of England.

The 60-minute episode will feature Olusoga along with other historians and experts such as Professor Janina Ramirez and Dan Snow, as they examine what the item can reveal about the Norman invasion.

The documentary will also address the mysteries surrounding the tapestry, such as who commissioned the piece, its creators and its intended purpose, as it delves into what it can reveal about the country the UK has become.

Viewers will also meet the Franco-British team of experts who helped move the irreplaceable object from its former home at the Bayeux Tapestry Museum in Bayeux in Normandy, where it had been displayed since 1983.

Former politician and academic Rory Stewart is also involved with the documentary, and described it as “the best way of really understanding the depth and detail of what can otherwise be quite a perplexing line of images”.

“Something we often miss are the hidden details, particularly around the frames: leaves, mysterious figures and strange implications,” he added.

open image in gallery The 60-minute episode will feature Olusoga along with other historians and experts, as they examine what the item can reveal about the Norman invasion ( AFP/Getty )

Fellow collaborator Dr Millie Horton-Insch, the project curator of The Bayeux Tapestry exhibition at the British Museum, described the object as “the most incredible investment of time and labour”.

She added: “It was the thrill of a lifetime to watch the Tapestry arrive at The British Museum, quite literally a once in a millennium event.

“I think that audiences will be amazed to see the work that went into it and it’s wonderful that this documentary will allow them to.”

The tapestry is currently on display at the museum in Room 30, the Sainsbury Exhibitions Gallery.

The British Museum expects around 7.5 million visitors during its stay in London, and tickets for the exhibition are currently sold out until December.

The next wave of public tickets for The Bayeux Tapestry will go on sale on 21 October for visits between January and March next year, with further tickets to be released at a later date.

Secrets Of The Bayeux Tapestry will air on BBC Two and will also be available to watch on BBC iPlayer.

News.title: Man City sign Enzo Fernandez for £125m to end transfer saga of the summer
News.content:
It is expected to be another busy deadline day in the Premier League, with many clubs still hoping to finalise deals before the transfer window shuts at 11pm. Here, Telegraph Sport identifies 10 potential high-profile moves that could yet go through.

Julian Alvarez to Barcelona… or Arsenal

This has been the most dramatic and relentless saga of the European transfer window. The situation, as far as we understand it, is as follows: Barcelona want Alvarez and Alvarez wants Barcelona, but Atletico Madrid refuse to sell him to Barcelona. Arsenal want Alvarez, and Atletico are more open to selling him to Arsenal, but Alvarez only wants Barcelona. For a move to happen, it will require one party to change their mind. Either Atletico decides to sell to Barcelona, or Alvarez decides he will join Arsenal.

Enzo Fernandez to Manchester City

Another long-running saga. Chelsea are well aware of City’s interest in Fernandez but want a massive fee for the Argentina international, having initially valued him at £120m. City have the cash and the space in the squad after saying goodbye to Rodri, Tijani Reijnders, Nico Gonzalez and Bernardo Silva this summer. Fernandez has not featured in Chelsea’s last two games.

Lamine Camara to Chelsea

As reported by Telegraph Sport last week, Chelsea have identified Monaco midfielder Camara as a target amid the uncertainty over Fernandez’s future. French reports on Monday suggested the move may have stalled, however. The clock is ticking.

Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City

Spurs had been working on a deal to sign Ndiaye from Everton but they now appear to have fallen behind City in the race for the winger, as a consequence of City failing in their attempt to sign Cody Gakpo from Liverpool. City are ready to complete the hijack on deadline day.

Ismaila Sarr to Liverpool

A deal that, as of Monday night, is regarded as unlikely to happen. As with their interest in Brighton’s Yankuba Minteh, Liverpool have so far been unable to strike a deal with Crystal Palace for Sarr, who scored 21 goals in 45 games last season. Liverpool would only allow Gakpo to leave if a replacement, such as Sarr, can be signed.

News.title: Borrowing cost surge leaves Healey with £10bn headache
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs have surged at one of the fastest paces in the world in a move that threatens to blow a near £10bn hole in Chancellor John Healey’s fiscal plans.

Interest rates on 10-year gilts, a benchmark for Treasury borrowing costs, rose to the highest level since 2008 on Tuesday amid a global bond market rout.

Britain’s cost to borrow over 20 years rose to its highest level since 1998, signalling growing stress in the market.

Government borrowing costs around the world have climbed sharply in recent weeks, amid concerns about unsustainable debts and persistent inflation.

However, Britain suffered the biggest increase in bond yields in the G7 on Tuesday as economists warned that investors were particularly nervous ahead of Mr Healey’s first Budget.
