In a statement issued over the weekend, Cooper pointed out that all crimes, especially drug abuse, are serious national security threats, and if Liberians do not pay keen attention and work together, they could damage the future of the nation.

Cooper argued that the drugs law, which was signed into law in 2022, a first-degree felonious offense, is aimed to regulate, restrict, control, limit, or eradicate the illegal export and importation as well as the flagrant use, abuse, and proliferation of narcotic substances within the bailiwick of the Republic of Liberia and is not in any way designed to target any group of specific lawful persons.

“The drugs law should not be misconstrued and politicized as a witch-hunt or selective justice,’’ he stated.

However, the Liberian Law School student called on the government to remain within the confines of the rule of law in the fight against the deadly practices.

He added that the constitutional rights of all defendants are not negotiable and must be fully protected without any justification.

“As much as we all appreciate the government’s political will to fight drugs, or crimes in general, we are also keen to remind them to remain lawful, especially law enforcement officers, so that they themselves will not be the violators of law they are protecting or will not abuse others’ constitutional rights,’’ he said.

Cooper warned that “suspects are not convicts, and therefore should be treated as innocent until proven guilty, especially as regards their rights to due process, right to life, right to fair trial, right to a speedy and public trial, which are fundamental rights that must be protected at all times regardless of the persons before the law. ‘’

In an African legal system, “Taytay-mo-taytay” (the law is the law), Cooper intimated that all persons are equal before the law and must be treated equally, regardless of their status and capacity in society.

He encouraged Liberians to continue their advocacy for fair justice and respect for the rules of law.

‘‘Liberia deserves to be a crime-free society, and Liberians deserve to live a better life,’’ Cooper said.

“Drugs affect all citizens regardless of which party, religion, or community you are part of. Therefore, we call all well-meaning Liberians to support the Government of Liberia’s efforts in the fight against drugs, and desist from challenging law enforcement officers,’’ he added.

World.title: Liberia: Kogar’s MDR Expulsion Puts Koung, Unity Party’s Nimba Base Under Scrutiny
World.content:
MONROVIA — The expulsion last week of Senator Samuel Gongben Kogar from the Movement for Reconstruction and Democracy (MDR) may have been decided inside a party meeting room, but its political implications could extend far beyond the walls of the party’s headquarters in Monrovia.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

For the MDR, the decision represents the enforcement of party discipline and a reaffirmation of its alliance with President Joseph Boakai and the governing Unity Party. For Kogar, however, the expulsion creates a new political reality for a senator who has built an electoral identity that predates his most recent association with the party.

For Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung, the development could prove even more delicate.

Koung’s political strength has long been closely associated with Nimba County, while the Unity Party’s historic victory in the county in the 2023 presidential election was one of the strongest pillars of the Boakai-Koung ticket’s national success.

The question now emerging is whether the political disagreement between Kogar and the MDR can remain confined to the party or whether it will eventually begin to alter the political calculations surrounding Nimba ahead of the 2029 presidential election.

The MDR Executive Committee voted to expel Kogar after a disciplinary process that Chairman Cooper Kruah said was triggered by a complaint alleging violations of the party’s constitution and bylaws.

Kruah has insisted that Kogar was given an opportunity to defend himself and that the expulsion followed established party procedures rather than being an arbitrary political decision.

“Anybody who contravenes the Constitution and bylaws of the party, that person will be dealt with in keeping with what the law says,” Kruah said.

According to the MDR chairman, Kogar received a copy of the complaint and initially participated in the process but subsequently failed to appear for a further hearing.

“He was provided with a copy of the complaint, and he submitted himself to the investigation, but continued to ask for excuses, one excuse after the other,” Kruah said.

Kruah added that when the matter was scheduled for further hearing, neither Kogar nor his lawyer appeared, which he characterized as a waiver of their right to be heard.

The committee subsequently recommended Kogar’s expulsion and instructed that anything belonging to the MDR that remained in his possession be returned to the party.

“That means, for today, he is no longer a member of the party,” Kruah declared.

But the chairman’s explanation went beyond the disciplinary process and directly entered the broader political relationship between the MDR and the Unity Party.

Kruah accused Kogar of taking positions that were inconsistent with the governing coalition and argued that a politician cannot simultaneously participate in government while presenting himself as an opposition voice against that same government.

“This party is in collaboration with the Unity Party. We are part of the government. You cannot be part of the government and sit and play opposition in the same government that you are a part of,” he said.

Kruah was equally emphatic about the MDR’s continuing allegiance to President Boakai.

“This party stands with the Unity Party and stands with this president,” he said, adding that the party supported Boakai in the past, supports him presently and intends to support him in the future.

That position makes Kogar’s expulsion politically significant beyond the question of party membership.

The MDR is not simply another political organization in the Liberian landscape. It is the party founded by the late Senator Prince Y. Johnson, whose political influence transformed Nimba into one of the most closely watched electoral battlegrounds in the country.

And the response from Johnson’s family indicates that the dispute may increasingly become entangled with the unresolved question of who carries the political legacy of the late senator.

Amy Johnson, daughter of the late Prince Johnson, publicly came to Kogar’s defense following the expulsion. Her statement was sharply critical of individuals she accused of having betrayed her father while expressing sympathy and support for Kogar.

She argued that the senator’s expulsion was not necessarily an unexpected political development and warned him to be cautious, drawing comparisons with what she described as the treatment her late father received from people within his own political circle.

Her intervention was also framed around the history of the MDR and her father’s political legacy. She questioned why individuals who had previously left or opposed the party had returned following Prince Johnson’s death, while recalling earlier internal battles involving her father and Kogar.

At the heart of her message was a declaration of solidarity with the senator: “Da My Pa Party: We Will Stand By Kogar.”

The statement does not automatically translate into an electoral bloc for Kogar, but its political symbolism should not be underestimated. Prince Johnson spent decades constructing a political organization whose influence was particularly powerful in Nimba, and the question of what remains of that influence after his death is likely to become increasingly important as the 2029 election approaches.

That is where the history of Nimba becomes particularly relevant.

The county has repeatedly demonstrated that it can produce powerful political movements around individual leaders, but its electoral history also shows that no politician has been able to permanently command every voter.

In the first round of the 2017 presidential election, Prince Johnson demonstrated the scale of his political influence when he received 107,430 votes in Nimba, equivalent to 53.50% of the county’s presidential vote. Joseph Boakai received 39,964 votes, representing 19.90%, while George Weah secured 16,002 votes, or 7.97%, and Alexander Cummings received 12,548 votes, representing 6.25%.

The political importance of PYJ’s influence became even more evident in the runoff. Following his decision to support George Weah, Weah’s Nimba vote rose to 73,434, representing 57.14%, while Boakai received 55,083 votes, or 42.86%.

That election created a powerful precedent in Liberian politics: a dominant Nimba political actor could potentially move a substantial portion of the county’s electorate behind a national presidential candidate.

But subsequent elections have complicated the idea that Nimba’s vote belongs permanently to any one political leader.

When Koung contested the 2020 senatorial election on the MDR ticket, he won with 37,899 votes, representing 36.12% of the vote. Edith Gongloe-Weh received 34,153 votes, or 32.55%, while Garrison Yealue secured 15,607 votes, representing 14.87%.

Koung therefore became senator with considerably less than half of the countywide vote, demonstrating that even a strong political figure backed by an influential political machine could not automatically consolidate the entire Nimba electorate.

The political landscape changed dramatically in 2023 when Koung moved from the Senate to the national stage as Boakai’s running mate.

The Boakai-Koung ticket received 138,070 votes in Nimba in the first round of the presidential election, representing 59.53% of the county’s vote. George Weah received 50,427 votes, or 21.74%, while Tiawan Gongloe secured 17,024 votes, representing 7.34%.

In the runoff, the Boakai-Koung ticket increased its dominance, receiving 144,646 votes, or 74.14%, compared with Weah’s 50,453 votes, or 25.86%.

Those numbers established Koung as an exceptionally important electoral figure in Nimba and gave the Unity Party a political advantage that would be difficult for any rival to ignore.

But there is another way to read the same numbers.

Even when Nimba had a son of the county on the national ticket, approximately one-quarter of voters in the runoff still supported the opposing candidate.

That is perhaps one of the most important lessons for the Unity Party as it considers 2029. Nimba can strongly support a political ticket without becoming politically unanimous.

That distinction becomes even more important when examining what happened after Prince Johnson’s death.

The late senator died in November 2024, leaving behind not only a vacant Senate seat but also a political structure whose future was suddenly uncertain.

The April 2025 senatorial by-election therefore became an early test of the post-PYJ political order.

Kogar emerged as the MDR candidate and won decisively, receiving 62,136 votes, representing 52.08% of the countywide vote. Edith Gongloe-Weh received 40,506 votes, or 33.95%, while Mack Gblinwon secured 7,489 votes, representing 6.28%.

The significance of Kogar’s victory extends beyond the percentage. He crossed the 50% mark in a countywide election and accumulated more than 62,000 votes at a time when Nimba was still adjusting to the death of one of its most influential political figures.

Whether those votes represented Kogar personally, the MDR machinery, the continuing influence of the PYJ political network, support from Koung, or some combination of all four is difficult to establish with mathematical certainty.

But the result nevertheless demonstrated that Kogar possessed a substantial electoral constituency. That makes his expulsion from the MDR a political experiment of sorts.

The next question is whether Kogar’s support is attached primarily to the party, to the political establishment that backed him, to his own personality, or to a combination of those factors.

If the majority of his support was party-based, the MDR could potentially retain much of its political influence. If a significant portion was personally attached to Kogar, his departure could create a new political bloc.

If the 2025 victory was the product of several forces working together, then the outcome of the separation could depend on which of those relationships survive.

That uncertainty is precisely what makes the development important for Koung. Kogar is not an unknown political figure entering the electoral arena for the first time.

He has won four elections in Nimba, according to the political account surrounding his record, and has moved from the House of Representatives to the Senate. His political base is also described as extending across important parts of the county, including the Gbehlay-Geh and Buu-Yao areas, with maternal ties into the Mano belt.

Such a record does not guarantee future victories. But it does make the assumption that Kogar can simply be politically erased following an MDR expulsion difficult to sustain.

The danger for the Unity Party would be to confuse party membership with voter loyalty. A voter who supported Kogar in a senatorial election may not necessarily support him in a presidential election.

Similarly, a voter who supported Koung in 2023 may not automatically abandon the Unity Party because of a dispute between Koung and Kogar.

Liberian voters are not a single political constituency, and Nimba’s electoral history demonstrates that voters frequently make different calculations depending on the office being contested, the candidates involved and the alliances surrounding them.

Still, presidential elections are often decided by margins, and that is where Kogar’s political relevance could become significant. He does not have to take a majority of Nimba away from the Unity Party to affect the national equation.

If he were to move a meaningful portion of his supporters toward another political coalition, the effect could be enough to reduce the Unity Party’s margin in a county where the party might otherwise expect overwhelming support.

That is the political gamble.

In 2023, the Boakai-Koung ticket won 74.14% of Nimba’s runoff vote. If the Unity Party expects to reproduce that performance in 2029, it will have to contend with a political environment that may contain more competing centers of influence. The most important of those could be Kogar. There is also a generational dimension to the dispute.

For decades, PYJ represented the dominant political personality in Nimba. His death created space for other politicians to compete for influence. Koung is already one of the strongest beneficiaries of that transition, having moved from senator to vice president and becoming an important national figure.

Kogar’s rise represents another strand of the same transition. The two politicians are not politically identical, and their constituencies may overlap without being interchangeable.

If Kogar and Koung eventually reconcile, the episode could ultimately strengthen the governing coalition by bringing competing political interests back together.

If they remain divided, however, the dispute could evolve into a contest over who can mobilize the political constituency that once operated under the broader PYJ-MDR umbrella.

If Kogar aligns himself with an opposition presidential candidate in 2029, the calculation becomes even more serious for the Unity Party. And if he decides to become part of another presidential ticket—or pursues a presidential ambition himself—the potential for fragmentation could increase considerably.

But political analysis is not about predicting the future with certainty. It is about identifying the factors that could shape it.

Kogar’s political career has been shaped by battles over party structures, leadership and political loyalty, and his supporters now argue that he is once again being forced to fight for his political survival.

His critics, meanwhile, can point to Kruah’s explanation that Kogar was given due process and failed to appear for a scheduled hearing. Both narratives are likely to remain part of the political debate.

But the larger issue cannot be resolved by determining who won the argument inside the MDR meeting.

The real verdict will come from voters. If Kogar remains politically active, his next political move will provide an important indication of how much of his 2025 support was personal. If he can mobilize supporters outside the MDR structure, that would suggest that his political influence is broader than the party machinery.

If he struggles to reproduce that support, it would strengthen the argument that the MDR and the wider political coalition surrounding Koung were more important to his victory than his personal appeal.

For Koung and the Unity Party, therefore, the wisest response may not be to dismiss Kogar but to understand what his expulsion could mean.

Nimba politics has repeatedly punished those who assume that electoral loyalty is permanent. In 2017, PYJ demonstrated that his political influence could dramatically reshape a presidential contest.

In 2020, Koung won a competitive Senate election with 36.12% of the vote, demonstrating both his strength and the limits of political consolidation.

In 2023, the Boakai-Koung ticket transformed Nimba into one of its strongest political bases, winning 59.53% in the first round and 74.14% in the runoff. In 2025, Kogar demonstrated his own electoral strength by winning 52.08% and 62,136 votes in the senatorial by-election.

The numbers are different elections, under different circumstances, involving different candidates. They cannot simply be added together or treated as a direct projection of 2029.

Koung remains a formidable political figure in the county, but his political future will increasingly be judged against his ability to maintain the coalition that helped elevate him to the vice presidency.

Kogar, meanwhile, has been removed from the MDR, but he has not been removed from Nimba politics.

His 62,136 votes are not his permanent property. Neither are they irrelevant. Some belonged to the candidate, some may have belonged to the party, some may have been influenced by the broader political environment, and some may have reflected relationships built over years.

The challenge is determining how much of that coalition can travel with him. That is a question that cannot be answered by an MDR resolution.

It can only be answered through future political activity and, eventually, through votes. For now, the photograph of Kogar being removed from the MDR headquarters may be the most visible symbol of his political separation from the party.

But the more important picture may be the one voters will create in 2029.

World.title: Liberia: Fed, But Starving: Health Workers Say Misinformation, Fees and Aid Cuts are Causing a Dramatic Rise in Severely Malnourished Babies
World.content:
Summary:

21-year-old Lovetee did not know breast milk is all babies under six months can consume. She fed her four-month-old daughter, Princess, soft rice and well water, and the baby is now dangerously malnourished.

Health workers across the country say this is common. UNICEF found only about half of Liberian babies under six months are exclusively breastfed, and many caregivers wrongly believe infants need water or food to grow strong or stop crying.

The problem is getting worse. A 2025 study saw a nearly tripling in cases of acute malnutrition, alarming health officials. They say USAID cuts have left them without first-line tools to treat malnourished children, meaning more will die.

The introduction of fees for service at public facilities means many babies are born and die without ever being registered or getting any support.

By King Brown with New Narratives

BUCHANAN, Grand Bassa County— The sun is hot here in Big Joe Town, outside Grand Bassa’s capital city. Lovetee, 21, sits on a wooden chair watching her four-month-old daughter, Princess, lying weak on her lap, suffering from diarrhea. Princess’s ribs show through her skin, and her hair is thinning instead of growing.

Lovetee, a first-time mother, has not eaten properly in days and she says she barely sleeps because Princess cries until morning. She has been feeding Princess soft rice mixed with soup, plus water from the open community well, a practice she learned from her brother’s partner. Lovetee says no one ever told her a baby under six months cannot eat food or drink water. Mother and baby are paying for that lack of knowledge.

“When my baby crying, my breath can want cut off, because she can just be breathing fast, fast,” Lovetee says. “Her stomach just running. She weak, weak in her body. To even lift her, I have to balance her neck with my one hand and her waist with my other hand before she break.”

Experts say that knowledge gap, between what families believe and what a newborn’s body can process, sits at the center of a public health crisis playing out quietly in homes across Liberia. In 2020 – the most recent data – the Demographic and Health Survey found that 56 percent of young Liberians surveyed incorrectly believed babies needed water in their first six months, and 46 percent believed babies needed something beyond breast milk to grow strong. Only about half of Liberian babies under six months are exclusively breastfed.

A more recent survey is alarming public health experts. The 2025 Comprehensive Food Security and Nutrition Survey, not yet published online, found that 8.5 percent of children in Liberia, below the age of five years, suffer from acute malnutrition or wasting, a dramatic increase from the Demographic and Health Survey, which put the number at 3 percent.

Experts think the numbers are actually higher because they see women who have been told the dangers of giving infants food and water and do it anyway. Experts don’t trust that caregivers are telling survey takers the truth.

The problem is compounded by the introduction of fees and aid cuts. Lovetee wants to take Princess to the government hospital, but under the new policy, started in March, requiring all patients to pay for services at public health facilities that were previously free, she would need roughly L$500 upfront for a bed, plus money for medicine. Unemployed and single, she does not have the money.

Even if Lovetee got Princess to a health facility, nurses no longer have the “plumpy nut” nutrition boost and antibiotics that used to be provided with funding from USAID. All they can do is teach her to feed the baby breastmilk alone.

“If things are not handled within five to 10 years, it will lead to an outbreak [explosion of cases],” warns Samuel Moiwai, public health lecturer at Grand Bassa University.

A Body Not Yet Built for Food

According to the World Health Organization , for the first six months, an infant’s digestive system is built to process one thing: breast milk, since it supplies all the nutrients and fluids an infant needs. The only other thing they can take in is formula, but it must be prepared with sterilized bottles and clean water, often out of reach in rural areas.

But Debra Bah, a pediatric nurse in Buchanan, says she regularly sees babies under six months drinking plain water and eating softened family food, believing breast milk alone is not enough. It is a mistake, says Bah.

“When you give soft rice or water, the baby goes quiet for some time, so family believes the baby is satisfied, not knowing such silence can be very dangerous,” she says.

Solid food introduced too early can cause gas, diarrhea, a swollen abdomen, dehydration, respiratory infections and vomiting.

A father learns too late

Archiebald Moses, 33, says his partner grates and sun-dries eddoes bought at market, then cooks the powder as a daily meal for their five-month-old son, alongside breastfeeding. The baby is not doing well.

“I never heard from anybody before that giving young baby the food we are giving him is harming him,” Moses says. He says fathers should be included in nutrition education too.

Nurse Joyce Albert Mitchell looks for medication after screening an infant for signs of malnutrition. Photo By King Brown

Joyce Albert Mitchell has screened babies at Buchanan’s Well Baby Clinic for five years. About 50 infants pass through weekly, and staff logs one or two malnutrition cases almost daily. She says the real number is higher since many rural mothers never reach the clinic.

The number of women giving birth in health facilities has hit more than 80 percent – a record high. There they are educated about breastfeeding. But Joyce says that guidance is constantly undermined by relatives insisting babies need water and food.

“Giving water to a baby is very dangerous. The child’s immune system is very small and weak,” Joyce says. “If the mother forces water into the child’s stomach, the gut will get filled, and the child will be unable to suck the breast milk well; the water already filled the stomach, it can cause damage for the child.”

Eunice Feekpah Bundor, a community health services supervisor and clinic screener, says giving babies water and food early is common and getting worse. She says some mothers start giving water almost immediately after birth; by one, two or three months, caregivers add fufu, dumboy, rice and other foods.

“Yesterday I received a patient; you could see the spinal cord, the skin dry, the face looked almost like an oldman’s face,” Bundor says.

Nearby health worker Rebecca Karr recalls a three-month-old who died after weeks of eating rice and drinking well water that led to diarrhea and fever.

“By the time they brought the baby, she could not drink or breastfeed,” Karr says. “We tried, but we could not save her.”

The staff worry that numbers may be higher. The babies being born at home without ever having their births registered can die and no one ever knows they existed.

Malnutrition doesn’t only shrink bodies; it damages brain development, lowers IQ, and delays walking and learning, says Sundayway Vungee, Grand Bassa County’s Nutrition Supervisor and a ten-year veteran of the Liberia Government Referral Hospital’s maternity ward. She worries about the next generation of children.

“For Liberia to flourish, our young generation coming up, they have to be well-nourished. When they are well-nourished, they will be able to think well, go to school, and pick up well.”

Traditional misinformation persists

Oretha Tukpeh is a face of the problem. The 55-year-old grandmother of six says her own children were given water and family foods, country rice, plantain, eddoes, and creek water from a young age, and none died or needed hospital care.

“People can hear plenty funny things in the city,” she says, laughing. “But in the bush, you will not hear it, don’t give the baby this one, give the baby that one.”

Vungee says old habits are especially hard to change among teenage mothers as young as 12 who are too young to understand the gravity of raising a baby and are vulnerable to grandmother’s messages. (One in three Liberian girls is pregnant before 18, one of the highest rates in the world). Vungee says some discard the deep-yellow colostrum produced right after birth, believing it unclean, though it is dense with the antibodies newborns need most. Many lack support from the baby’s father, making breastfeeding harder.

Joanna Fahwor, who runs an organization supporting single mothers in Grand Bassa, says many mothers she works with were told by relatives that breast milk was “weak” and that water, rice, eddoes and oatmeal would make babies “strong.”

One case has stayed with her, a two-month-old girl who, within a week of starting solid food, developed severe diarrhea and skin sores, her weight dropping so fast her clothes hung off her. She says the baby later improved after clinic treatment.

The county runs nutrition programs at 18 health facilities and 25 mother-support groups around Buchanan. But programs have been crippled by aid cuts. The therapeutic food supplies known as “plumpy nut” and antibiotics supplied to treat severe malnutrition that used to be supplied by USAID have run out.

Joanna Fahwor, Executive Director of Single Mothers, a women based organization in Grand Bassa County. Photo By King Brown

“Most of the children are dying because of no product in the country,” she says.

Liberia is not alone in facing these challenges, but some countries have achieved far higher breastfeeding rates. UNICEF reported that up to 87 percent of Rwandan mothers exclusively breastfed in 2019, aided by national campaigns, evidence that public education and supportive policy can make a difference.

Back in Big Joe Town, Lovetee frets as she watches her daughter fade. The tragedy is that she along with thousands of other mothers, had the means to help her child thrive, for free, but for now, she lacks the knowledge.

World.title: Liberia: Charlyne Brumskine Becomes First Liberian Woman Appointed to Prestigious Post on West African Regional Court
World.content:
Cllr. Charlyne Brumskine speaking at an AMUJAR event in May at the Ellen Johnson Sirleaf Presidential Center in Monrovia.

Summary

Charlyne Brumskine is one of five judges selected for the prestigious role serving on the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) Community Court of Justice, which hears cases against regional governments, from 2026 to 2030.

The lawyer, who brings more than 23 years of legal experience to the court, is the first Liberian woman to serve in that role.

Brumskine says she wants more West Africans to understand and have access to the Court, including through proceedings outside its headquarters in Abuja, Nigeria.

By Joyclyn Wea, gender correspondent with New Narratives

When Charlyne Brumskine learned she had been selected to the coveted post as a judge on the Ecowas Community Court of Justice, her thoughts turned to her late father.

Charles Walker Brumskine, the prominent lawyer and four-time presidential candidate who died in 2019, had hoped to serve as vice president of the Economic Community of West African States Commission himself, his daughter said.

“My father did not get it. You can imagine how proud I feel to have been able to achieve that,” Brumskine said.

Brumskine is one of five judges selected to serve on the regional court from 2026 to 2030, alongside judges from Nigeria, The Gambia, Togo and Benin. The Court’s bench rotates among Economic Community of West African States member states every four years.

Brumskine is not the first Liberian to serve on the Court. Liberian judges Micah Wilkins Wright and Yussif D. Kaba previously served on the bench. But she is the first Liberian woman.

“Is a privilege that I do not take lightly,” Brumskine said. “I am continuing the legacy of Liberian women who came before me, those who plaited the mat on which I sit. But I am also a forebearer of those who will come after me. I am simply keeping the seat warm for them and providing a blueprint of how Liberian women must represent our country with dignity, excellence, and purpose.”

Based in Abuja, Nigeria, the Community Court of Justice is the judicial arm of the Economic Community of West African States. It interprets regional laws and treaties, settles disputes involving member states and Economic Community of West African States institutions, and hears human rights cases.

Its human rights jurisdiction gives the Court particular importance to ordinary citizens. Individuals can bring qualifying human rights complaints directly before it without first exhausting all remedies in their national courts.

One recent example saw a group of survivors of the 1990 St. Peter’s Lutheran Church massacre, in which up to 600 people were killed by Armed Forces of Liberia soldiers, sue the Liberian government, accusing successive administrations of failing to investigate and prosecute those responsible. But in October 2024, the court threw out the case, ruling it lacked jurisdiction because the violations fell before the court’s human rights mandate existed.

Brumskine said about 90 percent of the Court’s cases concern human rights, covering issues ranging from human trafficking and unlawful detention to freedom of expression and due process.

Liberians have used the Court in other cases. Kabineh Ja’neh, the former Supreme Court associate justice, challenged his impeachment there in 2020. The Court ruled in his favor, finding the government had violated his right to a fair hearing and ordering the government to pay him compensation and restore certain rights. Liberia later sought a review, but the Court rejected the application and ordered compliance with its original judgment.

In another recent case, the Court in July 2025 dismissed an application involving Abrahim Sheriff, raised in Guinea but claimed to be of Liberian origin, who brought a case against Liberia and Guinea at the Court, alleging both governments unlawfully arrested and detained him on unfounded claims of armed insurrection and mercenary activity, subjecting him to torture and enforced disappearance and confiscating $180,000.

Those cases, Brumskine said, demonstrate the breadth of issues that can reach the regional bench. But she said she hopes that Liberians will not have to go there.

“I hope that our government, our judicial system, affords our citizens the opportunity to fundamental rights so that no one appears before me or before any of the justices from Liberia,” she said.

Despite several landmark human rights rulings, the Court faces mounting criticism over poor compliance by member states, with enforcement of its binding judgments remaining one of its toughest challenges since it began operations in 2001. That weakness was on display in the Lutheran Church massacre case, where the court’s narrow reading of its jurisdiction let the Liberian government avoid accountability.

The Court’s independence is also being tested by politically sensitive cases, including a suit by Ghana’s suspended and later dismissed Chief Justice, Gertrude Torkornoo, who is seeking $10 million in damages over her removal. Most recently, the court has been drawn into regional migration politics, hearing a case accusing Ghana of unlawfully detaining and deporting refugees transferred from the US under a secret deportation agreement — the first case filed under the 1979 ECOWAS Free Movement Protocol.

Brumskine comes to the Court with more than 23 years of legal experience. She has also been active in politics and was Alexander Cummings’ running mate in the 2023 presidential election.

During the Ellen Johnson Sirleaf administration, Brumskine worked with the Ministry of Justice on Liberia’s anti-human trafficking framework and with the Ministry of Commerce as Liberia negotiated accession to the World Trade Organization. During the George Weah administration, her law firm served as external counsel to the Central Bank of Liberia.

She is founder of CMB Law Group and has taught at the Louis Arthur Grimes School of Law and the Liberian School of Law. She is licensed to practice law in Liberia, New York and Washington, D.C., and has worked across private practice, public policy and international negotiations.

That background differs from Economic Community of West African States judges who often reach the regional bench after careers in national judiciaries. But previous service as a judge was not required. Candidates could qualify with at least 20 years of relevant professional experience as a judge, lawyer or legal academic.

The selection process was competitive.

The Liberian government submitted three nominees after being allocated a seat on the rotating bench. The three were interviewed in Sierra Leone in April by the ECOWAS Community Judicial Council, made up of chief justices from across the region. Jutonu Kollie, Ministry of Justice communications officer, did not respond to questions about the identities of the other two finalists by deadline.

Brumskine recalled sitting before nine regional chief justices who were sitting as the Economic Community of West African States Community Judicial Council, the body responsible for screening and recommending candidates for the court judgeship as part of her interview panel, wearing headphones as interpreters translated among English, French, and Portuguese speakers. The questions ranged from Economic Community of West African States treaties and human rights protocols to regional affairs and legal philosophy.

The Judicial Council ranked the three candidates and sent its recommendations to the Economic Community of West African States Council of Ministers before the Authority of Heads of State and Government gave final approval.

Former president Sirleaf, Charlyne Brumskine, along with other influential Liberian women, at a dollar campaign in April 2025 to raise funds to support Edith Gongloe Weh’s Senatorial race.

Brumskine said one of her priorities will be helping ordinary West Africans better understand a Court many do not know exists. She wants the Court to become more visible outside Abuja, including by holding activities and proceedings in member states.

“Let the Court come to Monrovia,” she said. “Let people come and see and hear and feel what the Community Court of Justice is. Let’s take it to Accra. Let’s take it to all the different countries in the region.”

She said she believes that access matters particularly for women and other citizens seeking remedies for human rights violations, including human trafficking, which has been growing in Liberia and where the government has done little to protect victims. She stressed that the court is for all West African citizens, not just the elite, to hold governments to account.

“A woman in Buchanan can take her case to the Economic Community of West African States Court of Justice if she meets certain criteria,” Brumskine said.

Her appointment means yet another Liberian woman has attained a prestigious post outside the country while women in the country continued to struggle for representation in leadership. Women hold just 10 of 103 seats in the Legislature. Brumskine said progress has been slow, but she sees her own responsibility as extending beyond occupying a regional seat.

Bowoulo Taylor Kelley, vice president of the Association of Female Lawyers of Liberia, said Brumskine’s appointment demonstrates what Liberian women can achieve when given the opportunity. “These barriers do not reflect a lack of talent,” Kelley said. “Rather, they reflect systems that must be deliberately opened and made fairer.”

At her Monrovia law firm, she said she is mentoring three young women lawyers to take on greater responsibilities eventually. “It’s my role to train. It’s my role to mentor so that when Charlyne Brumskine goes out, they are stepping up to take my place locally,” she said.

For Brumskine, however, the immediate task is the Court and the four years ahead.

“To be a judge, it is the pinnacle, it is the height, it’s the peak of our professional career,” she said. “And not just a judge in Liberia. To be a regional judge.”

Brumskine’s term begins in Mid-October 2026.

World.title: Hichilema Begins Second Term, Pledges Growth-Focused Agenda
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema and Vice President Mutale Nalumango took the oath of office on Tuesday for a new five-year mandate running through 2031, committing to govern with honesty and accountability.

Addressing the crowd at Heroes Stadium in Lusaka, Hichilema reached out to his political rivals and asked citizens to accept differing political views, arguing that election outcomes shouldn’t drive Zambians apart permanently. He said his administration would make sure every citizen’s perspective counted and would push development that meaningfully improves daily life in communities across Zambia. He urged all Zambians, regardless of party, faith, tribe, gender, or economic standing, to unite behind both diligence and smart strategy in building the nation forward.

The centerpiece of his new term is what he’s calling the Grow Zambia Agenda, meant to carry forward the economic stabilization gains of his first term into a new phase centered on growth, wealth-building, employment, and broadly shared prosperity. He said his government would push harder on reform in mining, farming, tourism, and energy, paired with infrastructure and industrial development, to tap into the country’s economic capacity.

He also laid out a set of numeric targets guiding the term, dubbed 10-10-5-3-3-1-1-1, covering 10 million tonnes of maize production, 10,000 megawatts of power generation, five million annual tourist visits, three million tonnes each of copper and soybeans, a million tonnes each of wheat and sugar, and beef exports worth at least $1 billion.

He stressed that growth needs to show up concretely in people’s lives through employment for graduates, dependable markets for farmers, more room for business, and stronger revenue to fund ongoing development.

On social policy, Hichilema pointed to free schooling, better health services, a boosted Constituency Development Fund, and empowerment programs aimed at women and youth as key priorities. He noted that 2.6 million school-age children who had previously dropped out are now back in classrooms. He also promised to push more authority and funding down to local government so development reaches every part of Zambia, and he framed proportional representation as a way to bring more women, young people, and people with disabilities into governance.

Calling education the great equalizer, Hichilema called for continued investment in schooling, skills development, and healthcare, alongside a cultural shift that puts children and future generations at the heart of national planning. He also pledged continued modernization of the civil service, with better delivery, more digital tools, and stronger accountability and anti-corruption efforts, and told public officials to prioritize the national interest over personal gain.

On the international front, he said Zambia would keep pursuing economic diplomacy and regional stability while deepening ties with neighboring states, Africa, and the broader global community, positioning the country as a dependable, investment-friendly partner.

The inauguration unfolded against a tense backdrop. Hichilema had been declared the winner of the August 18 election with roughly 60% of the vote, per the Electoral Commission of Zambia, continuing the country’s largely peaceful electoral track record since multiparty rule returned in 1991. His closest rival, Brian Mundubile, took about 38% and disputed the outcome, alleging irregularities.

Days after the vote, security forces searched Mundubile‘s residence. He says he went into hiding fearing for his safety before he and running mate Makebi Zulu turned themselves in on August 24 after taking shelter at a United Nations building. Both are now held at Mukobeko Maximum Security Prison on treason allegations, with courts closed to legal challenges of the election result during this period.

Heads of state from across the continent attended the ceremony, including Kenya‘s William Ruto, Botswana‘s Duma Boko, and Zimbabwe‘s Emmerson Mnangagwa.

World.title: HH pledges to scale-up investments in all sectors
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has pledged to scale – up investment in education and skills development and health sectors, under his renewed mandate to govern Zambia.

He has noted that in his last term, reforms introduced in the education sector, notable among them, the introduction of signing of free education into law, saw about 2.6 million learners who had previously dropped out, return to school.

Guided by the ‘Go Zambia Agenda’ under his new mandate, President Hichilema has assured that his administration will therefore continue to build on the gains scored in his previous term.

Speaking shortly after his inauguration, the Head of State noted that continued investment in education will, therefore, ensure equal access to opportunities for all Zambians.

“Education remains the greatest equalizer, best investment and indeed inheritance that we can pass on to our children. Education gives them a lasting sense of value and protection for whatever else they are left with”, the President highlighted.

The President assured of increased economic empowerment for women and young people in order to enable them to contribute to job creation and economic growth.

He added that continued empowerment of young people will not only curb the culture of handouts but also enable them to contribute to economic growth, noting that social protection programmes are meant to uplift the livelihoods of vulnerable citizens.

President Hichilema further stated that his administration will expedite decentralisation, which saw the increase of the Constituency Development Funds (CDF) from 1.6 to 40 million kwacha in his previous term, in order to ensure development reaches all parts of the country.

Meanwhile, visiting Heads of State have pledged their countries’ support towards President Hichilema’s new developmental agenda.

President of Zimbabwe, Emmerson Mnangagwa assured that his country will continue to partner with Zambia to achieve mutual developmental targets.

He called for the two countries to harness regional opportunities for the benefit of citizens’ economic growth.

“The responsibility to build and industrialise our countries remains with us”, he stressed.

And President of Kenya, William Ruto expressed confidence in President Hichilema’s new mandate, further stressing the need for Zambia to maximise on its various resources, including a youthful population to create wealth.

“We have resources and the youngest population on earth. The challenge before us isn’t the absence of resources but how we use them”, President Ruto emphasised.

World.title: Tanzania, Eswatini dignitaries leave Zambia
World.content:
Tanzanian President Samia Hassan has left the country after witnessing the inauguration ceremony of President Hakainde Hichilema.

President Hassan was accorded a half-guard of honour, one of the highest military honours accorded to a visiting Head of State.

She was accompanied by Tanzanian Minister of Foreign Affairs Ngwapu Maghembe.

Meanwhile, Eswatini Deputy Prime Minister Tulusile Dladla has also left Zambia for her home country.

President Hassan and Ms Dladla were seen off at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport by Deputy Secretary to Cabinet Oliver Kalabo, Lusaka Province Permanent Secretary Joe Kalusa, Defence Attachés accredited to Zambia and other senior government officials.

Ms Dladla departed Zambia at 16:12 hours while Ms Samia left at 16:27 hours.

World.title: Presidents Boko, Ruto leave Zambia
World.content:
Botswana President Duma Boko has become the fourth African Head of State to leave Zambia after attending the inauguration ceremony of President Hakainde Hichilema, at the National Heroes stadium in Lusaka this afternoon.

President Boko, who was accompanied by Minister of Foreign Affairs Phenyo Butale and other senior government officials, left Kenneth Kaunda International Airport at 16:50 hours.

He was seen off at the airport by Deputy Secretary to Cabinet Oliver Kalabo, Lusaka Province Permanent Secretary Joe Kalusa, Zimbabwean Ambassador to Zambia Charity Chiramba, Defence Attachés accredited to Zambia and other senior government officials.

Meanwhile, President of Kenya William Ruto has also left the country.

The presidential plane carrying Mr Ruto left the country at 17:05 hours.

The two Heads of State are among other international dignitaries who attended President Hakainde Hichilema’s inauguration ceremony at the National Heroes stadium in Lusaka following his victory in the August 13 general elections.

World.title: President Hichilema emphasises inclusive development
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema says his administration intends to continue with inclusive development of not leaving anyone behind.

President Hichilema says that this is to ensure that every Zambian enjoys a share of the country’s social and economic growth, regardless of political or social standing.

The Head of State said this in a speech read on his behalf by Vice President Mutale Nalumango during the inauguration luncheon in Lusaka.

He reminded that Zambia was coming from a collapsing economy which was stabilised and the debt restructured in the last five years.

The Head of State indicated that Zambia was now moving from stability to prosperity and growth.

The President reiterated that part of the agenda in the new five-year mandate was to double the economy.

President Hichilema added that the government will also work with traditional leaders to advance peace and development.

Emphasising on the need to guard peace, the Head of State explained that peace is the greatest ingredient for development.

Meanwhile, the Head of State highlighted that Zambia will deepen global partnerships in trade, investment, technology and skills for youth and women empowerment.

“Zambia remains a reliable friend and constructive partner. We continue to promote peace, regional integration and economic cooperation,” he stated.

And he thanked the Zambian people for a renewed mandate, accepting it with humility to serve, deliver and remain accountable.

Mrs Nalumango led a toast to continued peace, unity and prosperity for all Zambians.

World.title: Kanchibiya council launches sports club registration exercise
World.content:
The Kanchibiya Town Council has launched an exercise which will see the registration of sports clubs in all sports disciplines across the district.

The local authority has since tasked sports coordinators to ensure that a minimum of two clubs are registered within their respective wards.

Speaking in a telephone interview today, Acting Kanchibiya Council Secretary Augustine Chanda said only registered clubs holding a valid Council Certificate of Registration will be permitted to participate in the community sports tournaments that would be organized by the local authority.

Chanda said only registered clubs will be eligible to contribute players for selection to district teams that will represent the province at national events.

He added that only registered clubs will receive support from the local authority in the form of sports materials and will be recognized by their respective Sports Federations and Associations at provincial and national levels.

Chanda disclosed that for a club to obtain a Certificate of Registration from the Local Authority, they are required to submit copies of their Club Constitution, Meeting Minutes, List of Members, and a TPIN certificate.

He said the registration fee for a club is K250 and shall be paid to the Department of Finance.

Meanwhile, Kanchibiya Town Council Community Development Officer Joseph Nkazi also stressed the importance of registration, urging clubs to complete the process to enable them to benefit from different incentives.

Nkazi said unregistered clubs risk missing out on significant opportunities including tournament participation, district team selection, sports materials support, and national federation recognition.

“We urge all sports clubs in the district to take advantage of this registration exercise. Registration opens doors to many opportunities that will benefit both the clubs and the players,” Nkazi said.

World.title: Power targets positive start  in Africa  ‎
World.content:
‎Power Dynamos coach Oswald Mutapa is seeking a positive start ahead of this weekend’s TotalEnergies CAF Champions League 2026/27 First Preliminary Round match against Al Merriekh SC of Sudan.

‎

‎The Zambian champions left for Rwanda on Tuesday, where the Sudanese giants are playing their home matches.

‎

‎Mutapa says the first leg is critical in setting the tone for the campaign.

‎

‎“This is an important assignment we are going into. From the first game you need to get a positive result and that makes you half way through to the next round,” Mutapa said before departure.

‎

‎“A positive result is important so that as we start the CAF Champions League campaign we will know where we are going. It is important that we start on a high and positive note,” he added.

‎

‎The coach urged his players to go to Rwanda with courage and intent.

‎

‎“We must go to Rwanda with courage, show intent from the word go so that even as we come to the return leg we would have done half of the job,” Mutapa said.

‎

‎The first leg is scheduled for September 4-6, with the return leg set for September 11-13.

‎

‎This is Power’s second consecutive appearance in the Champions League.

‎

‎The Second Preliminary Round will be played on October 16-18 and October 23-25, with the 16 winners advancing to the group stage at the end of November.

World.title: Zambians cautioned against looming El Nino
World.content:
The Restoration for Community Justice has urged Zambians to begin preparing now for a drier-than-normal 2026/27 rainy season, as scientists warn of a strengthening El Niño weather pattern expected to peak between October and December this year.

‎In a press release issued to the media today, Restoration for Community Justice Chief Executive Officer Mathews Mulenga says, according to reports, most of Southern Africa, Zambia included, is projected to receive below-normal rainfall between October 2026 and March 2027.

‎Mr Mulenga said this will be driven by the El Niño phenomenon in the tropical pacific.

‎Mr Mulenga said the country cannot afford to treat the warning casually, given that agriculture, energy and tourism, all climate-sensitive sectors, underpin the livelihoods of millions of Zambians.

‎”This is not a Kanchibiya problem or a Muchinga problem. This is a national emergency in the making and every Zambian, from the smallholder farmer in the village to the policymaker in Lusaka, has a role to play in preparing for it,” Mr Mulenga said.

‎He said over two million smallholder farmers nationwide are at risk and warned that this year’s record national maize harvest of five million metric tons should not create complacency, recalling that the drought of 2023/24 wiped out similar gains just as quickly as they were made.

‎Mr Mulenga has since called on farmers across the country to diversify into early-maturing and drought-tolerant crops and embrace alternative livelihoods such as beekeeping, fish farming, and small livestock rearing, which are less exposed to erratic rainfall.

‎He also urged the government to invest more in early warning systems and anticipatory action, further calling on farmers nationwide not to sell off their entire harvest but to retain some for reserves for the anticipated lean period.

‎And Kanchibiya District Co-operative Union Chairperson Robert Mushili said cooperatives across Zambia are willing to adopt early warning information but need it communicated in practical, timely terms.

‎”This message should reach every corner of Zambia, not just districts like ours. If farmers everywhere know in September what to expect, they can still make good decisions before it is too late,” Mr Mushili said.

World.title: Tanzania: Govt Announces Two-Month Illegal Firearms Amnesty
World.content:
Dodoma — THE government has announced a two-month amnesty for people possessing firearms illegally, giving them an opportunity to voluntarily surrender the weapons without facing prosecution.

The amnesty, which takes effect on September 1 and runs through October 31, this year, is part of a national campaign aimed at removing illegal firearms from communities and preventing their use in crime.

Minister for Home Affairs Patrobas Katambi said yesterday in Dodoma that the government had formally announced the amnesty through a government notice dated August 28, this year, as it seeks to strengthen peace and security in Tanzania.

Under the arrangement, people who surrender firearms they possess without the required permits or through unlawful means will not be prosecuted for the illegal possession.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Mr Katambi urged all people who possess firearms unlawfully or outside established legal procedures to take advantage of the opportunity and surrender the weapons.

He said the surrender exercise will be conducted at police stations, local government offices and ward executive offices, making it easier for illegal firearm holders to hand over the weapons without fear of prosecution during the amnesty period.

The minister, however, issued a strong warning to anyone who continues to possess an illegal firearm after the amnesty expires on October 31.

"Anyone found with a firearm after this amnesty period ends will have committed an offence and will face legal action as quickly as possible,"

Mr Katambi said, warning that continued possession would indicate malicious intent inconsistent with efforts to maintain a safe and peaceful nation.

The campaign is being implemented by the Tanzania Police Force in collaboration with other security and defence organs and will run throughout September and October. It will also involve the media and other key stakeholders in raising public awareness.

Inspector General of Police (IGP) Camillus Wambura said the amnesty was a deliberate government intervention designed to complement, rather than replace, police operations against illegal firearms.

"This campaign is not a substitute for police operations, but an additional tool to prevent these firearms from being used before crime occurs and before harm is caused," Mr Wambura said.

The IGP said Tanzania had continued to ratify and implement various regional and international agreements while strengthening its legal and operational systems for controlling the possession, use and distribution of firearms.

World.title: Libya: Can the African Union Remain Relevant in Libya?
World.content:
analysis

Unless the AU can help coordinate implementation of existing peace initiatives, its influence on the ground may continue to wane.

Fifteen years after the 2011 uprising that toppled Muammar Gaddafi, Libya remains fragmented. Rival eastern and western power centres prevent total collapse but block meaningful national reconciliation, institutional unification and democratic transition.

Instability fuels arms trafficking, organised crime, irregular migration, terrorism and foreign fighter movements across the Sahel and beyond. With Africa's largest oil reserves and about 150 armed groups, competition for resources exacerbates the crisis.

Libya has long been one of the African Union's (AU) most important files. The Peace and Security Council (PSC) has held at least 20 meetings on Libya since February 2011, and the AU High-Level Committee on Libya is the organisation's main vehicle for an African-led settlement.



In Libya's crowded mediation landscape, the AU stands out for its distinctive role in reconciliation. But can it use this position to align existing initiatives and ensure their implementation?

Recent developments suggest cautious but significant diplomatic progress in Libya. In January, the Presidential Council and the Government of National Unity in the west of the country signed the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation. Other groups had signed in February 2025 after the AU facilitated the charter.

Other advances this year are the 11 April approval by rival administrations of the country's first unified budget in more than a decade. In another first, a joint military exercise facilitated by the United States in March brought together top rival commanders.

On 30 August, adversaries agreed on a 'landmark' roadmap to national elections within two years, mediated by the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL). This follows a parallel, largely Libyan-led tripartite agreement signed on 16 June, which commits the parties to simultaneous presidential and parliamentary elections by 17 February 2027, establishes a sovereign oversight committee, and outlines steps to end the transition.

AU Commission Chairperson Mahamoud Ali Youssouf welcomed the June agreement as a step towards constitutional order and reconciliation. By contrast, UN Secretary-General Special Representative Hanna Tetteh didn't mention it in her 18 June remarks, instead prioritising the UNSMIL facilitate- roadmap.

In addition to Libya's overlapping peace processes, security and other concerns remain. At its 9 June meeting, the PSC reiterated calls for all foreign forces and mercenaries to withdraw and expressed concern over continued violations of the United Nations (UN) embargo, illicit fuel exports, armed clashes and deteriorating humanitarian conditions of African migrants in detention centres.

It recognised that Libya's core challenge was not a lack of peace efforts, but a persistent failure to implement existing agreements - at least nine major roadmaps or accords have been launched since 2011.

Libya's accords consistently collapse or stall at implementation. As the Tripoli-based Sadeq Institute's Anas El Gomati told ISS Today, 'Endorsement is not implementation.' The core obstacles are institutional and economic. Rival authorities in the east and west benefit politically and financially from maintaining parallel institutions - particularly through controlling oil revenues and state resources.

Oil revenues sustain competing security structures, administrations, judicial bodies and financial networks. El Gomati says elections won't resolve the crisis without deeper institution-building, public finance and security reforms.

External actors add to the complexity. El Gomati says the United Arab Emirates has faced little consequence or mediation attention despite being the primary external military patron of Khalifa Haftar's eastern-aligned Libyan National Army (LNA) since 2016. LNA-controlled territories also reportedly serve as a supply corridor for Sudan's Rapid Support Forces.

The PSC has rejected the presence of foreign forces, mercenaries and fighters. However, the 5+5 Joint Military Commission, comprising military negotiators representing both east and west, says fragmented security sector institutions hamper external force withdrawals.

In this environment, overlapping peace initiatives - the UN roadmap, AU efforts and the tripartite agreement - risk duplication and forum-shopping. Greater coordination is essential to turn recent diplomatic momentum into lasting impact.

Implementation of the AU's 2011 roadmap and high-level committee decisions has been slow due to external factors (foreign interference and competing mediation tracks) and internal constraints (limited follow-up capacity and resources, and competing continental priorities).

Nevertheless, a clear example of the AU's added value is the 2025 National Reconciliation Charter. The initiative brings together opposing power centres, has helped bridge Libya's political and geographical divide, and has contributed to diplomatic momentum. Unlike other actors in Libya focused on elections and institutions, the AU frames the crisis as both political and societal and prioritises national reconciliation, transitional justice and social cohesion.

The AU also collaborated with Africa's three UN Security Council members and the United Kingdom (as Libya's penholder) to secure the unanimous April 2026 adoption of Resolution 2819, which extended Libya's sanctions regime.

Close 

But unless the AU can help harmonise the implementation of existing peace initiatives, its influence on the ground may continue to wane.

The PSC should help coordinate action on the tripartite agreement, the UN roadmap and the reconciliation charter. This would reduce duplication and advance institutional reunification and the conduct of credible elections by the end of 2027. The PSC should also expedite its field mission to Libya and the relocation of the AU Liaison Office from Tunis to Tripoli, as agreed by the AU in 2022.

The AU's relevance in Libya will depend not on new initiatives, but on its ability to act as coordinator and guarantor of implementation in a landscape dominated by powerful external players and fragmented domestic interests.
