World.title: Africa: The Drylands Dividend - the Smart Investment for Powering a Water-Scarce World
World.content:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Sep 1 2026 (IPS) - Open a can of something fizzy and the reason the sugar doesn't separate immediately is gum arabic, tapped by hand from acacia trees across the Sahel. Spray on perfume and the reason the scent is still there at dinner is frankincense, a resin cut from Boswellia trees on the dry escarpments of the Horn of Africa. The fat that gives a chocolate bar its snap may well be shea, gathered and pressed by women in the parkland belt of West Africa. The cashmere jumper came from goats that can only be raised on cold, dry rangelands.

These are drylands. They cover 44 per cent of the planet's land, hold 44 per cent of the world's cropland and half its livestock, and two billion people live in them. We have spent decades describing them as empty or unproductive. For a long list of things most of us use without thinking, they are the only places on earth that produce them at all.

It is no secret that our world is becoming hotter and drier. Three quarters of the planet's land experienced drier conditions in the last 30 years than the previous 30. This year's El Niño is intensifying fast, compelling the world to look back at what dryland systems already know. Nearly every model now points to a record-strength event: the US Climate Prediction Center puts the odds of a "very strong" El Niño at over 90 per cent for this fall and winter, and a 69 per cent chance it exceeds anything on record since 1950.

Drylands have been living through exactly this kind of shock-and-recovery cycle for generations, and their playbook offers real lessons. Farmers in places that have always been able to count on rain are beginning to face a question that dryland farmers answered generations ago: what do you grow, and how, when the water is not guaranteed?



Dryland systems are the longest-running operating record anywhere of producing value under conditions of scarcity, volatility and shock. These landscapes are home to generations of knowledge on how to thrive with limited water and high variability. This includes practices such as spreading risk across several crops and animals rather than betting the season on one, understanding land closely enough to move livestock before the pressure is too much, and building income that arrives at different times of the year so a bad month is not a ruined one. These are powerful lessons needed now.

Now is the time to listen and learn from dryland communities, practices, and regenerative production models. When this wisdom, data, and experience serve as our foundation, we can transition to sustainable business models and unlock investments to power our future world using knowledge that already exists in the places we have been calling marginal.

Mongolia, the host of the recently concluded UN's COP17 talks under the Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), is a case in point. Three quarters of Mongolia's land is already classified as degraded or at risk. However, Mongolian herders supply 40 per cent of the world's raw cashmere, increasingly innovating to shift away from an extractive model to practices that generate diverse value, from wool to grass-fed meat, examples of what a healthy landscape can offer.

In northern Ghana, the Ojoba Women's Shea Cooperative processes shea butter by hand in the arid Upper East Region, using a skill passed down through generations. They now supply international buyers including L'Occitane and Lush.

In both instances, the land already had value, and the skills already existed within the communities. What was missing was a route to the market willing to pay for them. These initiatives demonstrate what is possible when investment is designed around the realities and value in drylands.

Investment can take many forms: from financing cooperatives through the shift to new practices; insurance that pays out on rainfall; water and energy infrastructure that keeps a harvest sellable in extreme heat. There is growth potential beyond raw commodities too; processing into oils, powders, waxes compounds the returns. And payments for ecosystem services, from stored carbon, biodiversity and watershed protection, sit alongside that.

Donors like the European Union have already recognised the value of drylands with the €20 million Thrivelands initiative, led by Landscape Alliance, to build the coalitions and action this work needs; including innovations needed to protect and restore land. These innovations range from the tools to monitor and restore soil health accurately to the Land Degradation Surveillance Framework and the Regreening Africa app, which brings this data into the hands of farmers.

But public funding alone cannot unlock the drylands opportunities. Adapting to a drier world means restoring a broken nature finance system and closing the $700 billion finance gap to apply proven expertise across a growing area.

Many companies already depend on drylands through what they source, without having assessed how much of their supply comes from them. For those in the agrifood, textiles, and cosmetics sectors, investing in restoring and protecting these landscapes is a way to stabilise their supply chains, manage growing levels of risk and meet climate goals.

Close 

There is also the question of what inaction costs. Investing in drylands agriculture could avert a 12 per cent reduction in global food production over the next 25 years and prevent the release of about 60 per cent of stored carbon.

COP17 is a reminder of how little time is left. The UNCCD finance framework closes in 2030, with 82 per cent of the cumulative need for finance unmet. Time is running out to leverage the lessons from drylands to protect future food security. The gap between what is needed and what is being invested remains enormous.

The landscapes on which our future depends may be getting drier, but they are not devoid of opportunity. With science and innovation that enhances traditional knowledge, they are saturated with opportunities to bolster food security and climate resilience.

Dr Éliane Ubalijoro, chief executive officer of Landscape Alliance; Salina Abraham, Head of Thrivelands, Landscape Alliance

World.title: Uganda: Tooro Kingdom At Crossroads Over Succession
World.content:
Fort Portal, Uganda — The Tooro Kingdom is at a crossroads as some questions arise over the choice of the heir to King Oyo Kabamab Iguru Rukiidi IV, who passed away last Thursday in the United States where he was undergoing medical treatment.

The death has sparked a debate about the future of the kingdom's leadership amid conflicting information about the existence of a successor.

In an official statement, the Prime Minister of Tooro, Calvin Armstrong Rwomire, announced that the late King Oyo left behind a son who could potentially inherit the throne.

President Yoweri Museveni also echoed this claim, stating that the Queen Mother had informed him of the child's existence.



However, this revelation has been met with skepticism by some royal insiders.

Charles Kamurasi, the Omusunga or head of the Tooro Royal Clan, expressed doubts about the story of the heir. Having known King Oyo since childhood, Kamurasi says he was surprised by the announcement of a son and questioned its authenticity.

He says the claim might be fabricated and emphasized that if no clear heir emerges, the succession should follow traditional lineage, specifically reserving the throne now for the lineage Rukidi III.

In an effort to manage the transition, a 21-member committee comprising elders from the Babiito clan has been established to oversee the traditional succession process. Led by Musuga Charles Kamurasi, the committee includes prominent Babiito elders such as Dr. Isaac Mayombo, Fr Dr. Charles Oyo, Dr. Kagoro Kaijamurubi, Job Karamagi, and Gilbert Mujogya.

The committee is tasked with planning and executting the kingdom's next steps to find a new ruler.

Kasaija Ernest Kusemerera, who is in charge of the Omukama's local security (Omukumirizi), says that as the kingdom awaits clarity, the focus remains on ensuring that the succession process respects tradition and maintains stability within the Tooro monarchy.

David Baguma, one of the ritualists at the Tooro Kingdom, states that if King Oyo's son indeed exists, his grandfather on the mother's side must first present him to the Babiito clan elders. Following this, the clan heads would conduct specific traditional rituals to prepare the heir for his future role before any formal procedures for his succession are undertaken.

Baguma emphasized the importance of maintaining calm during this uncertain period. He reassured the public that even if no clear heir emerges, the kingdom remains a well-established institution with clear protocols and structures to determine the next ruler.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 1, 2026
World.content:
Kenya Aviation Workers Call Off Strike, Resume Duties

Kenya's aviation workers have called off their strike and resumed normal duties after reaching a return-to-work agreement with employers. The deal provides for the immediate remittance of agency fees owed to the Kenya Aviation Workers Union and clears the way for fresh negotiations with the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority over a new collective bargaining agreement. The union has raised concerns about new pay guidelines issued by the Salaries and Remuneration Commission but will seek to address them through the negotiations. The agreement also covers a long-running recognition dispute between KAWU and Jambojet, which will be resolved through the courts. Workers who took part in the strike will be protected from victimisation, intimidation or disciplinary action. Both sides have committed to resolving future disputes through negotiations and established mechanisms.

Namibia Rejects US Health Data-Sharing Proposal



Namibia has rejected a United States proposal involving the sharing of health data and biological specimens, citing concerns that the agreement could undermine the country's sovereignty, privacy laws and control over its biological resources. The dispute has complicated negotiations over more than N$730 million in potential funding for the country's HIV and tuberculosis programmes. The US said that the proposed agreement would only involve aggregate rather than personally identifiable data. Namibia is exploring alternative funding options to ensure the continued delivery of essential HIV services if a mutually acceptable agreement cannot be reached.

Gabon Victims Demand Accountability a Decade After Post-Election Violence

A decade after violence erupted following former president Ali Bongo's disputed re-election in Gabon, survivors and relatives of those killed are still demanding the truth and accountability. The unrest began after Bongo was declared the winner of the 2016 election. Security forces launched an assault on opposition leader Jean Ping's headquarters, marking the beginning of several days of unrest, looting and violent repression. The true death toll remains unknown. Survivors are now calling for a full investigation. Questions persist over the possible involvement of French nationals and whether French authorities fully cooperated with investigations into allegations of crimes against humanity.

South African Airline Defends Low Flypast Over Cape Town Stadium

South African airline Airlink has defended a dramatic low-altitude flypast involving two aircraft over Cape Town's packed DHL Stadium before the Springboks' rugby match against New Zealand. Flight tracking analysis suggested the lead aircraft passed less than 50 feet above the top of the stadium, prompting criticism and concerns about the risks of the manoeuvre. However, Airlink said the stunt was carefully planned and approved by aviation authorities, with highly experienced crews after rehearsing safety and speed limits. Many South Africans have praised the pilots' precision and skill.

Close 

Niger Uprising Exposes Cracks in Military, Russia Ties

Niger's failed military uprising has exposed deepening frustration within the armed forces, where many soldiers face poor pay, inadequate equipment and dangerous conditions while battling persistent Islamist insurgencies. The unrest has also raised questions about the stability of President Abdourahamane Tchiani's military government and its reliance on Russia's Africa Corps, which reportedly helped suppress the uprising. Analysts said that the events highlight underlying structural problems within Niger's military. They said that Russian support may help stabilise the junta in the short term without addressing the grievances and security challenges threatening its long-term survival.

World.title: Zimbabwe: Zimbabweans Abroad Raise Alarm Over Political, Economic and Human Rights Crisis
World.content:
Zimbabweans living abroad have raised fresh concerns over worsening political, economic and human rights conditions in the country, warning that mounting pressures are increasingly forcing citizens to seek opportunities and sanctuary outside Zimbabwe.

The civic movement Citizens Watch Zimbabwe, based in South Africa, has called for urgent action on issues ranging from constitutional changes and the rule of law to the high cost of passports and the decline in public services.

The movement held a media briefing in Johannesburg on Saturday.

Key issues on the agenda included human rights, the rule of law, governance, economic hardship, public service delivery and challenges facing Zimbabweans in the diaspora.



Speaking on the sidelines of a delayed press conference, the movement's president, Patience Chard, said Zimbabweans were increasingly feeling that their rights were being eroded and that Government needed to listen to their concerns.

"The reason why we've gathered here is because the Zimbabweans are going through a lot of difficulties here and back home. So, we're here to speak about all these things. Maybe the government can hear us when we gather together in our numbers. We've got issues of passports. Our passports, their prices are ridiculous.

"And we also got a challenge of our constitution that was recently amended. And that was the main reason why we formed our organisation because of the constitution, we are against the president. Because our rights have been violated as citizens. So that means we no longer Zimbabweans. If we cannot vote, what is the reason for us being Zimbabweans if we can't vote."

The movement has also criticised Zimbabwe's 2030 Agenda, describing it as unconstitutional and arguing that it does not reflect the views and concerns of ordinary Zimbabweans on the ground.

Channel Africa

World.title: Kenya: Aviation Workers Call Off Strike After Deal On Pay, Union Dues
World.content:
Nairobi — Aviation workers have called off their industrial action and resumed normal duties after reaching a return-to-work agreement with their employers, ending a standoff that threatened to disrupt operations in the aviation sector.

The agreement provides for the immediate remittance of agency fees owed to the Kenya Aviation Workers Union (KAWU) and currently held by the Kenya Airports Authority (KAA).

The deal also clears the way for fresh negotiations between KAWU and the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA) over a new Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA), after the Salaries and Remuneration Commission (SRC) withdrew its earlier guidance on the negotiations.

Under the agreement, KAWU and KCAA will proceed with CBA negotiations immediately, with the authority committing to honour and implement the outcome of the talks.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The SRC had withdrawn its initial guidance contained in a July 28, 2026 letter and issued new parameters on September 1 to guide the negotiations.

KAWU, however, said it had reservations about the new SRC parameters and would seek to address what it considers shortcomings during the CBA negotiations.

The agreement marks a significant shift in the dispute, with the union opting to end the strike in exchange for commitments on the outstanding issues.

"While the union has reservations on the SRC guidelines issued on the 1st September, 2026 ... and seeks to remedy the shortcomings arising from the said advisory during the CBA negotiations," the agreement states.

The parties also reached an understanding on the long-running recognition dispute between KAWU and Jambojet.

The matter is currently before the courts, and the parties agreed to await the court's determination and abide by the eventual decision.

Jambojet also committed to complying with all applicable legal and procedural requirements relating to trade union recognition.

With the agreement executed, KAWU formally called off the industrial action and directed affected workers to resume their normal duties immediately.

The workers are expected to cooperate with management to restore and maintain normal operations.

The agreement also contains a non-victimisation clause, shielding employees who participated in the industrial action from reprisals.

Under the clause, no employee shall be victimised, intimidated, discriminated against or subjected to disciplinary action because of their participation in the strike.

The parties further committed themselves to maintaining industrial peace and resolving any outstanding disputes through consultation, negotiations and established dispute-resolution mechanisms.

Close 

The agreement effectively shifts the battle from industrial action to the negotiating table, particularly over the terms of the KAWU-KCAA CBA.

The outcome of those negotiations could determine whether the concessions secured by the union translate into improved terms for aviation workers, amid continued scrutiny of how public-sector remuneration is guided by SRC parameters.

World.title: South Africa: Limpopo Village Cut Off as Bridge Collapses - South African News Briefs - September 1, 2026
World.content:
Limpopo Village Cut Off After Makeshift Bridge Collapses

The community of Mafarafara village in Limpopo has once again been cut off from a nearby clinic after a makeshift bridge across the Tubatse River collapsed following recent heavy rains, reports EWN. The bridge, built from wooden logs, sticks and corrugated iron sheets, provided a vital but unsafe link between remote villages. Residents must now either swim across the swollen river or pay more than R100 for transport to and from the clinic.

Hawks Officer Questioned Over R3 Million Cash Deposits

The Madlanga Commission has questioned KwaZulu-Natal Hawks Lieutenant-Colonel Deenadayalan Govender over more than R3 million in cash deposits made into his bank accounts between August 2022 and December 2023, reports SABC News. The commission said that the deposits far exceeded his monthly take-home salary. He is being investigated to determine whether the movement of the funds could indicate possible money laundering. Govender has also faced questions about his relationships with tow-truck businessman Clive Naicker and convicted drug dealer Timmy Marimuthu.

Cape Town Signs Cheaper Solar Power Deals

Cape Town has signed two solar power purchase agreements that will add 70 megawatts of electricity from plants in Atlantis and Philippi to the city's grid at prices below Eskom's tariffs, reports EWN. The city said that the future price increases will be linked to inflation rather than Eskom's tariff hikes. This might potentially help to limit electricity costs for residents. Mayor Geordin Hill-Lewis said the 20-year contracts are expected to provide R8 billion worth of electricity and reduce the city's reliance on Eskom.

World.title: Rosie O’Donnell rants that Trump-era ICE facilities are concentration camps where inmates are raped

Actress Rosie O’Donnell compared ICE facilities to concentration camps in Nazi Germany, in a video she posted on TikTok on Friday.

In a TikTok titled, "Friday Ramble," O'Donnell discussed a variety of topics, including the recent death of country music legend Dolly Parton, before launching into criticism of the Trump administration.

"We all vowed ‘Never Again,’ remember?" she said in the TikTok video, referencing the Holocaust. She noted that people even today are shocked at how Germans allowed fascism to take over before claiming fascism is in full swing in the United States.

"We’re making concentration camps… We’re rounding up people without a warrant. We’re raping children in detention, in ICE detention, they’re all getting pregnant," she said. "And they’re separated, males and females. Who has access to those girls? What happens to their babies? What do they do with them? There are big questions."

DEMOCRAT COMPARES ICE TO 'DOMESTIC TERRORISTS' AS 111 HOUSE DEMS DEMAND TEXAS DETENTION CENTER CLOSE

The fierce anti-Trump critic then launched into an attack on the president, saying his supporters were in denial.

"He doesn't care about you one bit. This is not a president for all people, this is a president for people like him," she said of Trump in the same video. "White powerful men, where women are disregarded in that equation usually. It’s the White men, it’s patriarchy running the world, and it’s deadly."

"We need people like Dolly Parton to run the world," she suggested. "People with a heart."

ROSIE O'DONNELL HAMMERS TRUMP REPEATEDLY IN KIMMEL GUEST-HOST GIG AS WHITE HOUSE FIRES BACK

World.title: Arte Moreno era officially over as Angels sell to Rams owner Stan Kroenke for $4B
World.content:
Calling all Angels fans: The Arte Moreno era is officially over. After two decades of blown leads, wasted talent, and front-office chaos, Moreno has finally done what Halos fans have begged him to do for years:

Arte finally agreed to sell the team.

Billionaire Stan Kroenke, owner of the Rams, Nuggets and Avalanche, swooped in Tuesday to rescue the Angels from baseball’s purgatory. Kroenke Sports & Entertainment is buying the franchise for $4 billion — making it the most expensive sale in Major League Baseball history.

PADRES STRIKE DEAL TO SELL TO INVESTOR GROUP LED BY PRIVATE EQUITY BILLIONAIRE, VOWS WORLD SERIES CHAMPIONSHIP

"The Angels are a storied franchise anchored in a great market," Kroenke announced in a statement.

"We look forward to an exciting future with the Angels organization."

The price tag eclipses the Padres’ $3.9 billion record and crushes Steve Cohen’s $2.4 billion purchase of the Mets.

MLB ALL-STAR MIKE TROUT SHUTS DOWN IDEA OF LEAVING LA, SAYS DOUBTERS FUEL PUSH TO GET ANGELS BACK TO PLAYOFFS

Across American sports, it matches Mat Ishbia’s $4 billion Phoenix Suns takeover, trailing only the Denver Broncos ($4.65 billion) and Washington Commanders ($6.05 billion).

Moreno bought the club in 2003 for $184 million, right after its lone World Series title. He released a statement on the sale:

"The Moreno Family has been honored to steward the Angels for 23 years, and we believe with KSE’s experience and success they are the best next owner for the franchise.

"The Angels organization looks forward to continuing its commitment to the fans, our employees, the players and our business partners."

KHOSLA FAMILY REACHES DEAL TO BUY SUPER BOWL CHAMPION SEAHAWKS FOR NFL-RECORD PRICE: REPORT

The Halos haven't made the playoffs since 2014, the longest active postseason drought in baseball.

Around baseball, the Halos became an absolute punchline for squandering the prime years of Mike Trout and Shohei Ohtani on the exact same roster. Ohtani eventually left, crossing town to win a World Series with the Dodgers, while Trout stayed behind, loyal to a fault.

Under Moreno, the organization handed out disastrous contracts to aging stars like Albert Pujols, Josh Hamilton and Anthony Rendon, let the farm system rot, and constantly burned through leadership, most recently firing GM Perry Minasian in June.

Then came the cruelest tease of all: Moreno’s 2023 decision to explore a sale, only to abruptly yank the team off the market citing "unfinished business."

Through every bad contract and lost season, Halos fans kept packing Angel Stadium, proving how deeply beloved this team remains.

That loyalty is why Tuesday turned into an impromptu party outside Angel Stadium.

Hours before first pitch against the Yankees, fans gathered to celebrate Arte’s exit, like they’d just won a World Series.

The Angels enter a new era under Kroenke, whose championship empire spans the Super Bowl-winning Rams, NBA champion Nuggets and Stanley Cup champion Avalanche.

The deal won't officially close until early 2027, pending MLB approval, but the Moreno era is finished.

World.title: Tiger Woods set for plea change hearing after DUI arrest following Florida rollover crash
World.content:
Five-time Masters champion Tiger Woods is expected to arrive at a Florida court Wednesday for a hearing on a possible plea change in his DUI case, court records show. The case stems from a rollover crash on Jupiter Island, Florida, in March more than five months ago.

A photo from WPTV at the time showed what was reportedly an SUV registered to Woods lying on its driver’s side. Authorities found Woods at the crash scene in Martin County, Florida, roughly 40 miles outside West Palm Beach. An arrest affidavit said Woods did not pass a field sobriety test and had prescription painkillers in his pocket.

In the aftermath of the crash, Woods announced he would take some time away from the public eye and explore personal recovery treatment options.

Woods initially entered not guilty pleas to misdemeanor counts of driving under the influence and refusing to submit to testing.

He also received a citation for careless driving and had been scheduled to make an appearance in court on Sept. 8. However, a court notice filed Tuesday moved Woods’ appearance up to Wednesday morning.

JUDGE APPROVES TIGER WOODS' HOSPITAL RECORDS RELEASE TO PROSECUTORS AFTER FLORIDA CAR CRASH

The 15-time major champion’s plea conference is scheduled to begin at 8:30 a.m. Wednesday at the Martin County Courthouse. It remains unclear whether Woods plans to change his plea or whether his attorneys have reached a plea agreement with prosecutors.

Fox News Digital attempted to contact Woods’ legal team about the latest development, but did not immediately receive a response.

The rollover added to a series of crashes involving Woods and created another obstacle in his latest comeback bid after years of injuries.

TIGER WOODS MAKES FIRST PUBLIC APPEARANCE SINCE DUI, REHAB STINT AS PGA TOUR ANNOUNCES SWEEPING CHANGES

Woods was seriously injured in a February 2021 single-vehicle crash outside Los Angeles. His SUV rolled several times, leaving him trapped inside the vehicle.

Emergency surgery treated "open fractures" in Woods’ lower right leg. Doctors placed a rod in his tibia and inserted screws and pins in his foot and ankle. He remains hospitalized for several weeks following the procedure.

Though Woods remains away from competition, he has continued to follow the game closely. On Sunday, he congratulated Scottie Scheffler on social media after the current world No. 1 won the Tour Championship, secured his second FedEx Cup title and passed Woods atop the PGA Tour’s career earnings list.

World.title: Van Jones calls out El-Sayed for ‘insane’ belief that he’s ‘smarter than Barack Obama’ on Israel policy
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

CNN host and former advisor to President Barack Obama Van Jones questioned if Michigan Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed thought he was "smarter than Barack Obama" on foreign policy in fiery comments discussing the "dangerous" beliefs held by many progressive figures in the Democratic Party.

El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel and former CNN commentator, has been embroiled in political controversies regarding his stance toward Israel and his relationship with a famous left-wing livestreamer, Hasan Piker.

In late August, Jones appeared on the "Ask Haviv Anything" podcast, where he addressed how the long and historic alliance between Black and Jewish Americans has recently fractured. He went on to criticize El-Sayed over his stance on Israel, saying, "his positions on Israel and foreign policy are insane."

"Look, some Democrats are going to say that we should condition military aid. That, you know, 'Israel's gone too far in Gaza and in the West Bank and in Lebanon. We're going to put some conditions on you.' I think that's a defensible position if you're a Democrat," he said. "That's not Abdul's position."

VAN JONES WARNS FAR-LEFT SOCIALIST AGENDA IS 'REGRESSIVE' THREAT TO DEMOCRATIC PARTY

"I can get why you would say, ‘No more aid, they got to pay their own way.' That’s not Abdul’s position. Abdul’s position is a total and complete arms embargo against the state of Israel, including defensive weapons. That’s an insane position," Jones continued. "That says, if Israel wants to pay for interceptors to stop a rocket coming from Iran or coming from Hezbollah or coming from Hamas, an interceptor, we should deny them the right to buy the interceptors to knock down rockets going at Israeli children, women, men, babies. That’s an insane position."

Jones went on to question if El-Sayed believed he was wiser than Obama on U.S. policy toward Israel.

"And by the way, it offends me because that’s — you know, Barack Obama was a part of creating that Iron Dome. Barack Obama was a part of creating those interceptors. Barack Obama thought that the Israeli people were in such a tough neighborhood, they needed to be able to knock down rockets," Jones recalled. "So you’re telling me you’re smarter than Barack Obama? You have better ideas about foreign policy than Barack Obama? And you want to de-plug and defund and take away Israel’s — half the world’s Jews'— ability to defend themselves? That's an insane position."

"The fact that people are having a hard time figuring out what to do about it, I find alarming," he continued. "This is not acceptable."

MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE CONFRONTED REPEATEDLY OVER ISRAEL’S RIGHT TO EXIST, DEFUNDING THE POLICE

Julian Epstein, a Democratic consultant and former chief counsel to the House Judiciary Committee, argued that El-Sayed has a long pattern of concerning positions and statements.

"Bless Van Jones' heart, I agree with him," Epstein said in comments to Fox News Digital. "To my mind, El Sayed is clearly aligned with the Muslim Brotherhood propaganda machine that gives a pass to the butchering of millions of Arabs by extremist Islamist overlords in the Middle East while slandering Israel with lies like a 'apartheid' and 'genocide' to justify the exterminationist and racist ideology that has always driven this conflict."

Theo Wold, former assistant attorney general and former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy under President Donald Trump warned that El-Sayed is part of a generational phenomenon of migrant populations taking up radical positions as they gain political power.

"Abdul El-Sayed is not a one-off. He’s the avatar of the rising generation of Third World immigrants who were resettled in the United States over the last thirty years," Wold said. "Visit a high school classroom in Anaheim or Queens, and you’re likely to encounter similar radical claptrap. El-Sayed’s foreign policy is more ‘global south’ than it is American. His messaging is so radically foreign to American ears because it’s just that: radical and foreign. And increasingly, that’s what the post-American, pro-Antifa Democrat Party has become, as well."

"Jones’s frustration reflects a larger struggle within the Democratic Party. Reasonable liberals like him — especially those rooted in the African American community —recognize that they are losing control of a party they helped build. As the Democratic coalition becomes Whiter, richer, and more ideologically extreme, the preferences of most Black voters are increasingly subordinated to those of the party’s new activist base," he added further. World.title: Chiefs heiress Gracie Hunt wrestles the franchise's attention back from Taylor Swift with engagement party
World.content:
Move over Taylor Swift, Kansas City Chiefs heiress Gracie Hunt has some headlines of her own to make. The attention surrounding the singer's wedding to Travis Kelce this offseason was nice, but it's back to business.

The offseason is over, the NFL regular season kicks off next week and the face of the front office has engagement party content to share. This is about love. This is about football. And this is about the future of the franchise.

The engagement party debrief at the place they met tells the story for Gracie and her fiancé, Derek, son of former Chiefs quarterback Trent Green, who popped the question back in April.

TRAVIS KELCE CALLS MARRYING TAYLOR SWIFT AT MADISON SQUARE GARDEN 'THE BEST NIGHT OF MY LIFE'

The Chief's heiress wrote, "Of all the places, all the moments—God wrote our story to begin right here. So grateful to have come back to this stadium engaged, surrounded by the people we love. 🤍"

Exactly. Their story had to start at Arrowhead Stadium. She has a franchise to lead one day and whoever she marries has to be prepared for what that takes.

I don't mean to suggest that there's some rift between Tay Tay and Gracie. For all I know, they get along fine. This isn't personal. This is about making sure the Chiefs Kingdom knows who will be there long term.

CHIEFS HEIRESS GRACIE HUNT DUMPS OUT WORLD CUP CONTENT, SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM LOVES HER FINGER POINT & FAST FOOD

When Travis Kelce calls it quits, the Taylor Swift sightings at Chiefs games will become rare at best. She'll show up for the Ring of Honor ceremony and whenever else the tight end is honored, but not much else.

The same can't be said for Gracie Hunt. She's been there for everything and, in one way or another, will be going forward. She doesn't have the luxury of just showing up on Sunday.

CHIEFS COACH ANDY REID HAS A BLUNT RESPONSE TO EVERYONE FREAKING OUT OVER TRAVIS KELCE'S DAD BOD

World.title: Colin Kaepernick is done with the NFL. He isn’t done fighting.
World.content:
The same league that let Michael Vick play again after he went to prison for dogfighting, and allowed Deshaun Watson to sign a contract for $230 million following accusations of sexual misconduct by more than 20 women (Watson has maintained his innocence), was keeping Kaepernick out.

“There’s not a definitive moment that I would point to,” Kaepernick says about when he realized what was happening.

Instead, it was more of a culmination.

“Coming on the back of going to a Super Bowl, going to an NFC Championship, setting records, and not a single team would bring me in, even for a workout?” Kaepernick says.

In August 2017, the Miami Dolphins — whose owner Stephen Ross previously launched a nonprofit to fight systemic racism — signed quarterback Jay Cutler after an injury to starter Ryan Tannehill, even though Cutler had already retired. NFL team executives, meanwhile, used the media to try to throw water on the idea that Kaepernick was blackballed.

Some coaches and GMs did reach out, Kaepernick says, and explicitly told him, “Yeah, we want to bring you in, but it’s getting shut down above us.”

One of those coaches, Kaepernick writes in his book, was John Harbaugh, the then-head coach of the Baltimore Ravens. Kaepernick spoke extensively with Harbaugh during the summer of 2017. Harbaugh’s brother Jim was Kaepernick’s coach during the 49ers’ run to the Super Bowl.

Kaepernick writes that Harbaugh was “pushing” to sign him, but was “shut down from above.”

In October 2017, Kaepernick filed a grievance against the NFL under the terms of the league’s and players’ collective bargaining agreement, alleging that owners were colluding against signing him due to his protest.

“Everybody believes that he was blackballed,” says one former player who was in the league during 2016. “Players knew that this would happen. That was a firm belief around the league.”

Goodell pushed back on the notion of organized collusion to keep Kaepernick out of the NFL.

“Those are decisions that each individual owner has to make and their clubs, coaches, GMs,” Goodell told NBC in 2020. “And I’ve talked to a lot of our clubs about it and I’ve encouraged them. I’d love to see him play again.”

Jesse Dittmar for NBC News

In November 2019 — months after the NFL settled Kaepernick’s lawsuit — the league tried to arrange a midseason workout for him in front of all 32 teams. The details of this day are now infamous, as Kaepernick ultimately called off the NFL’s workout the morning of due to an extensive waiver he refused to sign — a waiver Kaepernick believed would sign away his employment rights and potential future claims — and instead managed to organize a workout of his own.

The dissolution of the workout drew another round of skepticism, with many claiming Kaepernick was pulling a media stunt or was not serious about wanting to play again.

While Kaepernick was out of the league, the NFL went about trying to turn the temperature down on his protest, battling the aftermath of an especially divisive election and a ratings slide some attributed to the player demonstrations.

The league partnered in 2017 with the Players Coalition, a group founded to address systemic racism, and has since committed more than half a billion dollars to various social justice causes. Kaepernick wasn’t part of the group. (Reid said in 2017 that Kaepernick was kicked out of communications with the group by co-founder Malcolm Jenkins, which Jenkins denied.)

The NFL did whatever it could to stop the kneeling, the former player says, believing the league wanted to weed out players who kneeled: “What happened was the league and the Players Coalition came to a deal, and then the league did what they were going to do … They wanted their games to go back to normal.”

Kaepernick’s protest likely cost him tens of millions of dollars, even accounting for whatever he got from the NFL in the settlement.

But as his career was sacked, as television pundits continued to make personal attacks, and as 986 people were killed by police in 2017, Kaepernick stayed largely quiet.

He says that was by design.

“No individual should be speaking for everyone across the country. I don’t think that’s a responsible way to approach things,” Kaepernick says. “It’s also being able to enable other people to step into leadership positions, because that’s what movements actually are. It’s not one person just driving things.”

Months after his workout snafu, events unrelated to Kaepernick raised the volume on his protest once more.

On May 25, 2020, 46-year-old George Floyd was killed by police officer Derek Chauvin in Minnesota.

Video revealed Chauvin kneeled on Floyd’s neck for over nine minutes, killing him. Chauvin was convicted on multiple murder charges in 2021.

Nearly four years after Kaepernick kneeled in response to police brutality, worldwide protests emerged in the wake of Floyd’s killing. Kaepernick says seeing the protests around the world made him hopeful in the moment, especially as people in some cases risked their own well-being to be heard in the middle of the pandemic.

Nike included Kaepernick in its 30th anniversary "Just Do It" campaign in 2018. Supporters gathered outside NFL headquarters in New York City after Kaepernick filed a grievance against the league alleging that owners were colluding against signing him because of his protest. Getty Images file

“There was a significant portion of the population that previously was disconnected from these realities,” Kaepernick says. “It was like, oh, actually I have to sit with this now and I have to grapple with this. And am I OK with this? And what is my role within this? Am I complicit?”

Corporations also scrambled to meet the moment, including the NFL. In June 2020, several NFL players coordinated social media posts asking for the league to condemn racism and “admit wrong in silencing our players from peacefully protesting.”

The next day, Goodell responded in a video message.

“We, the National Football League, condemn racism and the systematic oppression of Black people,” Goodell said in the video, echoing the words players demanded from him. “We, the National Football League, admit we were wrong for not listening to NFL players earlier and encourage all to speak out and peacefully protest. We, the National Football League, believe Black lives matter.”

Kaepernick wasn’t impressed.

“His response through that video was only because of pressure from players, not because it was altruistic,” Kaepernick says.

The idea that the league should have listened to protesting players “is so laughable in my mind, and so disingenuous,” Kaepernick says. “We had been trying to address the issue that the NFL created with blackballing me for years. To come out and say we should have listened on the back of that — while I’m still actively trying to play in the NFL — it’s so performative.”

World.title: Alaska finalizes Senate race for November: 3 Republicans, including 2 named Dan Sullivan, and 1 Democrat
World.content:
The Alaska Division of Elections on Tuesday named the four Senate candidates who will be on the ballot this fall in a closely watched race that will be decided by ranked-choice voting.

Voters will make their selections among two Republicans named Dan Sullivan, another named Gerald Heikes, and Democrat Mary Peltola, who finished first during the all-party primary in which the top four advance to the general election.

Democrat David Leslie had finished fourth, but he withdrew from the race Monday. His withdrawal means fifth-place candidate Gerald Heikes, a Republican, will appear on the ballot.

Dan J. Sullivan and Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, R-Alaska. AP; Getty Images

The race is considered one of the most competitive in the 2026 cycle, and a potential pickup for Democrats, who are hoping to gain control of the Senate. It’s made headlines due to the novelty of having two candidates with the same first and last name.

Dan J. Sullivan, a former schoolteacher who came in third in the primary, is seeking to unseat Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. But his candidacy has faced legal challenges from the senator and other Republicans who allege he is working with Peltola, a former congresswoman, and entered the race as a potential spoiler. He and Peltola have denied any coordination with each other, as have their campaigns.

Although the Alaska Supreme Court allowed Sullivan to stay on the ballot after originally being disqualified by the Division of Elections, state and federal authorities are conducting their own investigation into his campaign.

The Division of Elections on Tuesday also named general election candidates for the governor’s contest, including Republicans Dave Bronson and Bernadette Wilson and Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the top finisher in the primary.

They are running to replace term-limited GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy.

Tom Begich, a Democrat who had finished second in the primary, withdrew from the race before Tuesday.

World.title: Whistleblower says USPS system Trump ordered for mail ballots is flawed and untested
World.content:
An anonymous federal official warned in a whistleblower complaint this week that the technical system the U.S. Postal Service built for mail voting is flawed, untested and likely to cause major disruptions in this fall’s midterm elections if it is implemented.

President Donald Trump signed an executive order in March that directed his administration to create federal lists of citizens and asked the Postal Service to transmit mail ballots to only those people. A federal judge has blocked the order from going into effect amid ongoing litigation over its constitutionality; the whistleblower complaint highlights potential issues that could arise if the courts ultimately declare it lawful.

The USPS typically is responsible only for transporting mail ballots between election officials and voters, and the federal government has never kept a central list of all American citizens. Trump ordered the agency to take on an unprecedented and complex role in the process this year amid a broader attempt to exert greater control over the country’s elections and his continued unfounded claims of widespread voter fraud.

The technical system the USPS assembled to vet voters was developed in a “rushed, chaotic, and fundamentally flawed process,” according to a whistleblower complaint sent to the office of Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., a member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. Blumenthal sent the complaint to Postmaster General David Steiner on Monday, asking for more information.

“This administration seems hell-bent on changing the framework of casting ballots in this country, clearly for political reasons,” Blumenthal said on a call with reporters Monday. “It is unconstitutional, as is argued in the courts by the litigation that is ongoing, but this disclosure indicates that it is also blatantly incompetent and incapable of actually delivering ballots that are lawful in this midterm election.”

In a statement Tuesday, the White House disputed the whistleblower’s allegations.

“The process of building software to carry out this new verification check is neither complex nor unique for USPS since the Postal Service regularly uses bulk mailing and intelligent mail barcodes for a wide variety of large customers,” said Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson.

The USPS didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The whistleblower is identified as an anonymous federal official who is being represented by Whistleblower Aid, a nonprofit group that represents public- and private-sector employees making such complaints. They allege that the USPS didn’t begin building its portal for verifying ballots “in earnest” until June, giving itself less than three months to complete a system that would ordinarily take at least nine to 12 months to build.

The agency last month finalized the rule for how it would implement the changes, which would create a massive new workload for election officials and put up hurdles for millions of voters to cast ballots by mail.

Large batches of ballots would be rejected by the portal if even a single ballot couldn’t be verified, the whistleblower said.

“As presently designed, if even one bar code on one single ballot in a bulk-mailing of 10,000 ballots fails to properly scan during the verification process, the entire batch is rejected and sent back to the state — effectively stopping the ballots from being mailed to voters,” the complaint reads. “Even under ordinary circumstances this would be problematic because of predictable errors in any barcode scanning process.”

The whistleblower said workers involved in developing the USPS system feared it would crash and described the process just days before the project was originally scheduled to be released to the public Tuesday as a “s--- show,” according to the complaint.

The whistleblower also said the USPS had ordered workers to continue developing its system, despite court orders blocking implementation of the project.

A federal court order Monday said the government could continue building its portal as long as the states aren’t required to participate.

World.title: No plans for ICE to be at polls for midterms, DHS says
World.content:
ICE officers have not received guidance telling them they need to do anything in addition to their regular duties on the day of November’s midterm elections, a senior Homeland Security official told NBC News.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said at a news conference Tuesday in New York that ICE officers will be at a polling place only if “there is a threat to that polling place” or if officers are serving a warrant on someone “that we have been actively tracking down.”

“ICE isn’t there to patrol the polling places,” Mullin said.

Asked whether ICE officers would enter polling places, Mullin said they would if they had warrants.

“If we’re serving a warrant, we will be where we need to be,” Mullin said.

President Donald Trump and Mullin have claimed without offering any evidence that there are over 250,000 noncitizens on voter rolls across several states. Mullin recently threatened state election officials with possible prison time if they didn’t comply with the administration’s methods to determine whether noncitizens were on their voter rolls. Several state officials have pushed back against sharing private state voter roll data that includes personal information, such as Social Security numbers.

World.title: Key Texas county votes to cut polling sites ahead of the midterms
World.content:
Officials in Texas’ third-largest county voted Tuesday to significantly reduce the number of polling sites for this fall’s midterm elections, drawing protests from Democrats and voting rights advocates.

Commissioners in Tarrant County, a fast-growing and politically competitive area that includes Fort Worth, approved a plan that results in 92 fewer Election Day polling locations compared with the 2022 midterms. The roughly 30% reduction leaves the county with 224 polling sites to serve 1.3 million voters. Voters in the county are able to cast ballots at any of those polling sites.

The three Republicans on the Tarrant County Commissioners Court voted for their plan, while the two Democrats voted against it.

Research has found that each additional minute of travel time to a polling location can affect voter participation. The NAACP, the American Civil Liberties Union of Texas and other groups said in a letter that the changes would hit voters of color hardest because many of the reductions are in majority-minority areas in Fort Worth and Arlington.

Supporters of the plan say that it will save money and that there are more than enough options for people to vote.

The move comes amid a critical Senate contest in Texas, with Democratic state Rep. James Talarico taking on state Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican.

Talarico urged the county to reject the plan ahead of Tuesday’s vote.

“The most powerful people in this county, the most powerful people in this country, don’t want us to be able to vote easily,” Talarico told reporters Sunday, according to The Associated Press.

Tarrant County has emerged as a key political battleground in Texas. President Donald Trump won it in the 2024 presidential race after Joe Biden flipped it four years prior. And Democrats Beto O’Rourke and Colin Allred narrowly carried the county in the 2018 and 2024 Senate races, respectively, even as they both went on to lose.

Texas law gives counties the power to decide how many polling sites they use. And some counties have begun using fewer sites as they have moved to countywide voting in recent years.

Dozens of voters urged the commissioners to vote against the cuts. Some criticized the elimination of specific polling places — like one at the University of Texas at Arlington — while others noted that the county has experienced significant population growth and voter participation in recent years.

“The right to vote is the bedrock of our democracy,” said a woman named Linda Northern. “This will make it harder for brown, Black and low-income voters to have the same right to vote as you do. This is wrong.”

Tarrant County Commissioner Roderick Miles Jr., a Democrat, added ahead of the vote, “This is about ensuring that the rights that people bled and died for are accessible to everybody.”

Tarrant County Judge Tim O’Hare, a Republican on the commissioner court, argued that Miles wanted more polling sites in his area.

“There’s no argument to that that you can come up with other than you want to be able to have more in your precinct,” O’Hare said.

A handful of speakers supported the plan, noting that some sites were used by few voters and required a significant number of poll workers and financial resources.

“I support the proposition that’s in front of us as far as reducing the number of voting sites. I’ve been a poll watcher, a poll worker, a precinct chair and all those things, and when you vote, when you go to a poll place that had 34 people all day long, you think this is kind of a waste of resources,” said one speaker, who did not identify herself.

World.title: House passes short-term funding bill to prevent a shutdown before the election
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The House voted Tuesday to pass a short-term funding bill and avert a government shutdown at the end of September, keeping money flowing at current levels until Dec. 11.

The legislation, which has already passed the Senate, sailed through the chamber by a vote of 370-48. It now goes to President Donald Trump, who is expected to sign it.

That would take the biggest legislative item off the to-do list for Congress ahead of the elections Nov. 3, punting stalled negotiations over a full-year funding deal until after the midterms.

The two parties have clashed over the scope of federal spending as Democrats reject Trump’s call for a massive $1.5 trillion military budget, a spike from the already record-breaking $1 trillion that Congress gave the military this year.

Funding the government requires 60 Senate votes to defeat a filibuster, meaning it must have bipartisan support even though Republicans control both chambers and the White House.

House Appropriations Committee Chair Tom Cole, R-Okla., accused Democrats of blocking a deal to weaken politically vulnerable Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee.

“I do want to finish all the bills before the end of the year. Now, whether we can do that or not is another matter,” Cole said, referring to the 12 appropriations bills that fund the government. “We won’t know if we’ll be doing that till after the election.”

The winners of the midterm elections will feel empowered to press their demands in the lame-duck negotiations, knowing that they’ll have more power in the upcoming year.

The election “has a tremendous impact,” Cole said. “We will act like we can come back and things will be exactly the way they were when we left. They won’t be. Everybody’s calculations will change. Everybody’s point of view will change. It’ll have an enormous impact about what happens for the balance of the year.”

Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., said she hopes to become chair of the Appropriations Committee again if Democrats win the House.

But she said her only priority now is to finalize a full government funding deal for the new fiscal year before 2027 begins.

“The midterm election will have an effect, but the goal is that we need to pass appropriations bills before the end of the year. That is a bipartisan view of where we need to go with the committee, and so that’s what we are going to press for,” DeLauro said. “Let’s get to the finish line.”

World.title: Tropical Storm Edouard makes landfall along Gulf Coast
World.content:
Tropical Storm Edouard made landfall on Louisiana's coast Tuesday afternoon, the National Hurricane Center said.

Edouard had maximum sustained winds of about 60 mph when it made landfall near Johnson Bayou, Louisiana, close to the border with Texas, at 2:20 p.m. Central Time, the hurricane center said. Those winds dropped to 50 mph by 5 p.m. ET. It was moving northwest with a predicted path over Texas.

Earlier, forecasters warned that the storm could bring near-hurricane conditions to some areas along the U.S. Gulf Coast.

Maps show storm's path and forecast

A tropical storm warning is in effect for Texas's Port Bolivar, while the same alert for Louisiana's Vermilion/Cameron Parish Line has been discontinued, the hurricane center said in its 5 p.m. ET update.

Strong thunderstorms were expected to bring powerful wind gusts and dump heavy rain, with 3 to 6 inches possible along the Texas coast and inland, and some areas could get up to 9 inches.

Map shows the path of Tropical Storm Edouard, which is forecast to hit the Gulf Coast of Texas and Louisiana on Tuesday. CBS News

A hurricane watch that had been issued earlier was also discontinued Tuesday. A storm surge watch was also discontinued for parts of Texas and southwest Louisiana, but the hurricane center still warned that coastlines could see rising water levels and possible flooding.

Forecasters warned heavy rain in both states "could produce flash flooding, especially in low-lying and urban areas."

After making landfall, Edouard moved inland along the northwestern Gulf Coast, bringing gusty winds and heavy rainfall across southeastern Texas on Tuesday night. The storm is forecast to rapidly weaken and dissipate by Wednesday night.

Map shows the rain forecast for Tropical Storm Edouard along the Gulf Coast of Texas and Louisiana. CBS News

The storm was moving at about 7 mph on a northwest path on Tuesday afternoon.

Edouard is the fifth tropical storm so far during the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season.

World.title: Judge sends Lindsay Clancy jury back for deliberations after they could not reach a verdict
World.content: Judge sends Lindsay Clancy jury back for deliberations after they could not reach a verdict The chance of a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy case grew on Tuesday after the jury said they were unable to reach a unanimous verdict and the judge sent them back to continue deliberating. Clancy is on trial for the killing of her three children. Shanelle Kaul reports from the Massachusetts courthouse and Caroline Polisi has more.

World.title: House censures Rep. Chuck Edwards over "inappropriate conduct" toward aides
World.content:
Washington — The House censured Rep. Chuck Edwards on Tuesday after a House Ethics Committee investigation found the North Carolina Republican engaged in "persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct" toward two young women who worked for him.

The House approved Edwards' punishment — standing in the chamber as the resolution condemning his conduct was read aloud — in a 413 to 2 vote. Censure requires a simple majority.

The bipartisan Ethics Committee released a report in early August detailing Edwards' conduct toward the two women, who previously worked for him when he was a state senator before joining his congressional office. While the committee found no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with the women or explicitly propositioned them, his behavior toward them created "rumors and innuendo" and violated House rules related to sexual harassment and toxic workplaces.

House rules prohibit lawmakers from having a sexual relationship with a subordinate and from engaging in "unwelcome sexual advances or conduct" toward a House employee.

"Both women were uncomfortable with his behavior (which they attempted to communicate) but were put in an untenable position by virtue of his status as their boss and a Member of Congress," the report said. "Representative Edwards was at minimum blind to that reality, and at worst, dismissive of the impact his inappropriate conduct had on the careers and wellbeing of two women on his staff."

In a speech on the House floor ahead of the vote, Edwards admitted to "poor judgment," but said "regret is not an admission of sexual harassment." He also apologized to the two women and his wife.

"I want to say something directly and publicly to the two women who have been at the center of all of this. I am sorry. I'm sorry that my actions, my judgment or the way that I expressed a friendship ever put either of you in an uncomfortable position," he said. "My intentions were only grounded in what I understood our friendship to be, and in genuine admiration and respect that I had for each of you, not only as professionals but as people."

Edwards said on social media after the vote: "I respect the House vote. I do not accept the conclusion that it produced." He insisted his conduct was not sexual harassment.

According to the report, Edwards provided the women with lavish gifts, including jewelry, designer purses, guns, flowers, a KitchenAid mixer and a robotic vacuum, among other things. He also commented on their appearance, invited them to one-on-one dinners and vacations and sent notes "regarding his effusive affection."

The conduct detailed in the report included Edwards arranging for a singer to attend one woman's birthday party and sing Ed Sheeran's "Hills of Aberfeldy" and say that it was "from a special someone." He wrote poems for the woman, including one that he read at her going-away party in front of her colleagues. Edwards also booked and paid for massages and other spa treatments for the woman, skipped House votes to decorate her Christmas tree and took her on a casino trip in which he bought her drinks and paid for her to gamble.

Edwards brought the other woman on political trips, planning personal activities for them, such as a helicopter ride, dinner and a Broadway show. He brought her flowers before picking her up for a holiday event at the White House. The report also said Edwards left early from an event, later telling the woman that he did so because she brought a date. About the episode, the committee said Edwards testified that he told the woman that he did not want to be "in the way or something to that effect."

The committee called Edwards' actions "at minimum inappropriate."

"A Member of Congress should not single out a staffer and isolate them from other staff, make frequent comments regarding that person's appearance and weight, send messages in the middle of the night, text staff deeply personal and seemingly romantic thoughts, intrude on personal occasions without invitation, pay for personal vacations, and spend thousands of dollars on gifts for staffers," the report said.

"In his interview with the Committee, the Congressman repeatedly asserted that he knows well what constitutes 'sexual harassment,' and seemed to believe that by avoiding inappropriate physical touch, explicitly sexual comments, and occasionally telling the staffers that they were free to put up boundaries with him, he had immunized himself from such a charge. That is not the case," it said. "Despite the absence of an explicit proposition, a reasonable person could interpret Representative Edwards' intimate and effusive attentions, where he prioritized the personal over the professional, as thinly veiled advances."

According to the report, Edwards "knew or had reason to know" as early as May 2025 that his conduct made the women uncomfortable when a senior staffer spoke to the congressman on their behalf.

Though Edwards argued the committee's findings "completely exonerate" him under House rules, the North Carolina Republican ended his reelection bid days later.

In a letter sent to his colleagues last week, Edwards made a last-ditch effort to save himself from censure. He asserted that the evidence does not support the committee's conclusions and that the behavior was reciprocated.

"An affectionate friendship is not a sexual proposition. A gift is not sexual misconduct. A compliment is not sexual misconduct. Poetry is not sexual misconduct. Socializing with a colleague is not sexual misconduct. Caring deeply about someone with whom you have worked and come to know for years is not sexual misconduct," he said in the letter obtained by CBS News.

Edwards said he sent the letter because his colleagues "deserved to hear directly from me and have the opportunity to review the facts for themselves."
