World.title: Months before ICC trial, Duterte wants prosecution to refile cases vs him
World.content:
Former president Rodrigo Duterte wants the prosecution to refile a document that 'frames the charges in terms of counts with a defined scope, being crimes under the ICC Statute'

MANILA, Philippines – Just a few months before his scheduled historic trial, former president Rodrigo Duterte asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to order the prosecution to refile the cases against him.

“The [defense] accordingly requests the Trial Chamber to order the prosecution to re-file a document before the Pre-Trial Chamber that frames the charges in terms of counts with a defined scope, being crimes under the ICC Statute, and with an exhaustive list of underpinning acts, which represent the entirety of the charges against the accused,” said the Duterte camp’s motion dated August 31.

In the motion, Duterte’s lead counsel Peter Haynes argued that the prosecution’s document containing the charges or DCC “is not fit for [its] purpose” and should be struck out.

This is the Duterte camp’s latest bid to challenge his case before the ICC after recent legal defeats.

Just last April, the ICC pre-trial chamber confirmed all three counts of Duterte’s crimes against humanity case, thus sending him to trial that will start in November.

Even on the issue of jurisdiction or whether the ICC was the right platform for the cases, Duterte did not score a win. The ICC Appeals Chamber junked his jurisdiction challenge and cleared the way for the trial.

The latest defeat was in May, when the pre-trial chamber denied Duterte’s request to appeal the ruling that confirmed his ICC cases.

In their August 31 motion, the Duterte camp said the prosecution’s DCC was framed around “illustrative non-exhaustive incidents.” They argued that the way the charges were framed violated Duterte’s right to be informed in detail of the nature, cause, and content of the charges against him under 67(1)(a) of the Rome Statute.

They said the only effective remedy to this is for the prosecution to refile the charges that properly inform Duterte about his case.

According to the defense, the prosecution’s decision to frame the charges that way makes it impossible for Duterte to know what case he has to meet at the upcoming trial.

“The Prosecution’s desire and intention to add further incidents is noteworthy as it plainly indicates that the Prosecution, at least, does not believe that it needs to prove all or most of the incidents. However, with a trial due to start in three months, the [defense] has no idea what is regarded as necessary proof of a ‘count’ on this DCC,” said the motion.

Duterte’s camp further argued that the prosecution’s charge document — which has broad topical headings rather than charged crimes — would allegedly be unacceptable in any criminal jurisdiction.

“The accused cannot even begin to make strategic decisions about how to approach this case, because he does not know what case he has to meet. The Duterte charges are a literal moving target; a non-exhaustive, illustrative list of events whose proof beyond reasonable doubt may or may not trigger liability for thousands of others, and whose evidential value remains entirely unclear,” the camp added. – Rappler.com

World.title: Michael Poa as witness: Good or bad idea for the prosecution?
World.content:
POA. Defense team spokesperson Atty. Michael Poa speaks to the media before the start of the fourth day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on July 13, 2026.

Poa's wealth of legal experience is evident every time he does cross-examination for the defense. He is calm and collected, but extracts the information needed by the defense.

People know him as the spokesperson of Vice President Sara Duterte, apart from being part of the defense team for her impeachment trial.

But Michael Wesley Poa will take on a different role on Wednesday, September 2 — as the prosecution’s witness for the trial. The court is hearing the prosecution’s evidence of Duterte’s alleged misuse of confidential funds of both the Office of the Vice President and the Department of Education.

This makes sense in a way, considering that Poa was chief of staff and spokesperson when Duterte was the DepEd chief. So, sure.

But is this a good idea for the prosecution?

Let’s not forget, Poa himself is no ordinary lawye; he’s a litigator. He knows how court proceedings work and understands the law. He knows how to argue before a court.

Poa’s wealth of legal experience is evident every time he does cross-examination for the defense. He is calm and collected, but manages to extract the information needed by the defense.

He even held his own when he faced House prosecutor Chel Diokno during oral arguments on the request to subpoena Duterte’s financial records last month.

Additionally, Poa would also be somehow freer in expressing his thoughts because he will not be acting as counsel, but as a witness.

Poa said he will answer whatever question is thrown at him, as long as it’s within his personal knowledge about DepEd’s confidential funds.

“If the questions cover or will be about DepEd and my participation [in] the audit observation memorandum (AOM), the reply to the AOM, I will answer them just like what I did in the House,” the defense spokesperson said on August 26.

Also, Poa really had familiarity with the issue. Under him, COA cleared DepEd over questions on the P75-million confidential funds.

So putting the defense lawyer on the witness stand might be a gamble for the prosecution. A challenge, definitely, but if the prosecutors are successful in getting the information they need from Poa, then it would be a plus to their case against Duterte.

Another challenge, of course, is Poa’s obvious inclination toward the defense.

To dispel any claim, any allegation of witness tampering, Poa stayed inside the holding area for the witnesses on Tuesday. This was according to defense deputy spokesperson Justin Nicol Gular.

Poa also did not sit beside defense lawyers inside the Senate plenary hall as would be usual; nor did he enter the defense lawyers’ holding area.

At this point, only Poa knows how his responses will go. For Gular, the public should just wait for the Wednesday trial.

“Let’s just wait for his testimony,” said the deputy spokesperson. – Rappler.com

World.title: What prompted Escudero’s reminder on digital devices ban at impeachment trial?
World.content:
Over the weekend, some netizens spotted what seemed like an earpiece purportedly worn by Office of Vice President (OVP) Assistant Chief of Staff Lemuel Ortonio as he testified at the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte earlier in the week.

The photos went viral, with some social media users speculating he was being coached, some even linking the appearance of OVP Chief of Staff Zuleika Lopez at the Senate with his testimonies.

But was Ortonio indeed being assisted in his testimony?

On Day 20 of the impeachment trial, presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero put the matter to rest as he debunked the social media posts. He said that upon verification, the viral photos were confirmed to be generated through artificial intelligence (AI).

“Hindi totoo ‘yung mga lumalabas na litrato na diumano mayroong earpiece si Mr. Ortonio, ‘yun po ay AI. What he had was an ear piercing in the front fold helix of his ear, not an earpiece,” said Escudero.

(The photos circulating online that Mr. Ortonio was purportedly wearing an earpiece was false. It was AI-generated. What he had was an ear piercing in the front fold helix of his ear, not an earpiece.)

Escudero said the controversy underscored the “need for a uniform safeguard,” prompting him to remind witnesses about the ban on the use of any hearing, listening, or electronic device during their testimonies. He also said they must testify “solely from his or her knowledge free from coaching or influence from counsel or any other person.”

He then directed the clerk of court to inform the witnesses about the ban, secure their electronic devices before taking the stand, and obtain their express consent vowing they would testify based only on their own will and without assistance from any device.

“Accordingly, no witness while testifying shall possess, have access to, or use any earpiece, headsets, cellphones, smart watch, smart glasses or any other similar device capable of transmitting or receiving information or communication,” Escudero said.

“Witnesses are also prohibited from receiving or attempting to receive any communications, suggestion, answer signal, message or prompt for any person whether inside or outside of this court, regardless of the means employed. The prohibition shall remain enforced during recesses and until the witness is formally discharged by the court,” he added.

Legitimate alias vs fake name

During the trial, Senator-judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III also made a manifestation, this time clarifying the difference between the use of alias and fictitious names.

Sotto cited Republic Act (RA) No. 6085 or the Anti-Alias Law, saying the use of pseudonyms is “permitted only for literary, cinema, television, radio, athletic, or other entertainment purposes, provided an actual living person is behind the name.”

“If there is a person behind the alias, then it is an alias. If there is no person behind the name, it is a fictitious name or a fake name,” he said.

Sotto, in raising the manifestation, rejected news reports that House private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia was not given the chance to answer Senator-judge Robin Padilla during his interjection over the use of aliases in the documents tied to the OVP’s confidential funds.

“We confirm that indeed, Atty. Mae was able to give an answer to the query of Senator-judge Padilla, also she was not able to give that much detail that the good senator-judge made,” Escudero said.

There were 16 senator-judges at the impeachment trial on Tuesday, September 1. Among those absent was Senator-judge Loren Legarda, who remains under extended medical leave until Wednesday, September 2. – Rappler.com

World.title: Haze and air quality index: Things to know
World.content:
AIR QUALITY. Haze blankets the Metro Manila sky on September 1, 2026, due to smoke from forest fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia. The Manila local government advises residents to take precautions and wear face masks when going outdoors.

Here's what you should know about air quality indexes and how they help identify the health risks brought by haze

MANILA, Philippines – It may look like a harmless fog blanketing the skies, but haze carries small particles in the air that can lead to serious health risks.

Here’s everything you need to know about haze, how to protect yourself from its effects, and how air quality indexes help in measuring risks.

What is haze?

Haze is smoke, dust, moisture, and vapor in the air that affects visibility. It originates from large-scale forest or land fires.

These fires create very fine particles with a diameter of 2.5 micrometers (PM2.5) or smaller that go into the air.

Unlike coarse particles that dissolve in the atmosphere within hours, fine particles can stay in the atmosphere for up to weeks and can travel for hundreds to thousands of kilometers.

These often grow in size as humidity increases and affect air quality by filling the atmosphere with high concentrations of fine particles.

This poses health risks, especially for those with respiratory diseases.

How does haze affect health?

Haze is a form of air pollution that leads to health risks when particles are inhaled.

According to the Department of Health, it could lead to the following:

difficulty breathing

coughing

chest pains

watery eyes or excessive tearing

itchy nose

worsening of respiratory disease

The health department advises people experiencing these symptoms to proceed to the nearest health center for treatment.

What are air quality indexes?

The Department of Environment and Natural Resources-Environmental Management Bureau (DENR-EMB) reviewed air quality indexes in compliance with the Philippine Clean Air Act of 1999.

In 2020, it formulated the PM2.5 air quality index breakpoints, which are divided into six levels from cleanest to most polluted.

It is used to inform the public about potential health risks.

Below are the air quality indexes, their corresponding colors, and cautions to follow:

Good (Green) – air quality is clean and safe

Fair (Yellow) – safe but with a presence of pollution

Unhealthy for sensitive groups (Orange) – people with respiratory disease should limit outdoor exposure

Very Unhealthy (Red) – avoid traffic-heavy areas, and people with respiratory disease should stay indoors and rest as much as possible; trips are encouraged to be postponed, and the use of vehicles is restricted

Acutely Unhealthy (Purple) – people should limit outdoor exposure, and those with respiratory disease should stay indoors and rest as much as possible; unnecessary trips should be postponed, motor vehicle use may be restricted, and industrial activities are limited

Emergency (Maroon) – everyone must stay indoors with windows and doors closed unless heat stress is possible; motor vehicles are only allowed for emergencies, and industrial activities (except those vital for public safety and health) are limited

How to protect yourself from the haze

Here are some tips from the health department to avoid the risks brought by haze:

Stay indoors as much as possible.

Wear a KN95 face mask if going outside.

Close all doors and windows and use a wet cloth to cover their crevices.

Use headlights or fog lights when traveling, especially during nighttime.

Stay away from low-lying areas where smoke and suspended particles may settle.

Public events in open areas may continue but must observe air quality before deciding whether to push through or cancel.

Using masks is also encouraged in classrooms, with teachers keeping a close eye on sick students or those with existing heart and lung conditions.

When the haze worsens, vulnerable people (elderly, pregnant, with health conditions) should be stopped from doing long outdoor work. – Rappler.com

World.title: Comelec seeks bigger budget for 2027 as it prepares for 2028 elections
World.content:
ELECTIONS. Voters cast their vote at polling precincts of Guadalupe Elementary School in Cebu City, in the midterm elections, on May 12, 2025.

Speaking at a House budget hearing, Comelec Chairman George Garcia says P9.12 billion was cut from the poll body's budget for preparation for the national and local elections

MANILA, Philippines – The Commission on Elections (Comelec) on Tuesday, September 1, appealed to the House of Representatives to restore its proposed P52.66-billion budget request for 2027.

The Comelec requested a higher budget in preparation for the national and local elections in 2028. The Department of Budget and Management (DBM), however, only recommended a P44.7-billion budget for the poll body in 2027.

Speaking at a House budget hearing, Comelec Chairman George Garcia said P9.12 billion was cut from the Comelec’s budget for preparation for the national and local elections.

He warned that the cuts could compromise the poll body’s preparations if the budget proves insufficient.

The Comelec estimated that there would be around 74 million voters by 2028, which would also increase the demand for a higher number of voting precincts.

The DBM also slashed P5.75 billion from the Comelec’s proposed budget for regular operations and P345 million from its other locally funded projects.

If the budget cuts were not restored by Congress, the Comelec said there would be a shortage of 9,310 election counting machines. This could increase the number of voters assigned to each polling precinct, resulting in longer lines and voting times on election day.

Garcia said the cuts would also affect the printing of ballots, forms, and voter information sheets, as well as the deployment of machines and supplies to polling places. Other affected expenses include ballot packaging, consultancy for an international certification entity, and overtime pay.

The DBM also removed the P118-million budget proposal of the Comelec for the lease of warehouses and venues. Without this, Garcia said they will not have a venue for the filing of certificates of candidacy in September 2027.

The filing of certificates of candidacy is typically held in October, but the Comelec wants to set the filing period from September 20 to 27, 2027.

The Comelec said an earlier filing of certificates of candidacy will allow the poll body to print ballots earlier.

The 2027 budget proposal also contains no allocation for the Comelec’s capital outlay, which covers physical assets such as buildings. Garcia said the commission’s lack of adequate office space has long been a problem. – Rappler.com

World.title: Purple harvest: Safeguarding the future of the ube industry
World.content:
VISCA UBE-2. One of the nationally recommended variants of ube from the Philippine Root Crops Research and Training Center.

As demand for ube surges worldwide, Leyte farmers call for laws that may help stop raw ube from being sold abroad

BAYBAY CITY, Philippines — “Hulog ng Langit.” (Unexpected blessing.)

This is how Olegario Paredes Jr., a root crop farmer from Eastern Visayas, describes the rise of ube (purple yam) in global food trends.

Ube has been steadily finding its place in the global market in recent months, earning comparisons to Japan’s matcha as a distinctly Filipino product with growing international appeal.

Transparency Market Research values the global ube market at roughly US$455 million in 2024, with projections climbing to $943 million by 2035. For farmers like Paredes, it is a chance to turn a once-ordinary crop into a reliable source of income.

One of the founders of Organikong Magsasaka at Mangingisda ng Rehiyon Otso (OMMRO), Paredes previously cultivated sweet potato and cassava at the Juanito Eco Farm School for Practical Agriculture (JEFSPA) in Kananga, Leyte.

But ube changed farming for him.

“Labing pamatuod lang, ang ube ang maoy naghatag ug maayong kita sa akoa, sa JEFSPA, ug sa uban pa nga mga farmers,” Paredes says.

(More than anything, ube has provided a good source of income for me, JEFSPA, and other farmers.)

Global demand

Paredes started planting ube in 2023.

The crop that once seemed ordinary was beginning to attract an extraordinary amount of attention. Soon, the surge reached Eastern Visayas directly.

As international interest in ube spiked in 2024, the Fatima Multi-Purpose Cooperative, a cooperative that uplifts local farmers, fisherfolk, and low-income groups, began venturing into ube processing.

They reached out to Paredes for an organic supply agreement.

Soon, foreigners began visiting the region in search of ube suppliers, Paredes tells Rappler.

“Niabot sa farm, niari sa region para pagkita sa amo production area ug ang processing sa Fatima,” Paredes recalls.

(They visited the farm and came to the region to see our production area and the processing facility in Fatima.)

FOREIGN INTEREST. Moroccan nationals visit Paredes’ farm to get ube supply deals. Photo Courtesy of Olegario Paredes Jr.

In March 2026, a Moroccan buyer who was looking for a steady source of ube powder visited Paredes. The buyer wanted 1,000 kilograms of ube every month for distribution across four countries.

That single order alone works out to roughly 80 tons of raw ube a month.

And that Moroccan buyer wasn’t an outlier.

Purple gold

Since he started planting ube, Paredes’ farm has fielded over 10 separate foreign inquiries.

That demand pushed him to convert more of his farmland to ube production.

As a general rule, 50 tons of ube, sold at P50 per kilo, brings in P2.5 million. However, that kind of sales, he says, is only possible with consistent monitoring and cooperative weather.

But ube farming can also be challenging.

Ube’s full production cycle—from land propagation to harvest—takes about a year, Paredes explains.

In the early days, Paredes’ crops were vulnerable to pathogens, waterlogging, and mistimed planting. All the risks are concentrated in the plant’s fragile first few months.

Starting an ube farm isn’t cheap, either. Testing and planting materials come at a cost, with each seedling running P30 to P40 which can potentially rise proportionally to the demand.

While ube is a resilient crop—which means it can handle intense weather conditions—Leyte’s frequent exposure to disruptive storms could still affect yield, particularly given that harvest season is from September to November.

Support system

To meet the demand in the long run, farmers need more than planting materials: they need proper ube production training, processing tools, and adequate funding support.

RESILIENT CROP. Ube can handle intense weather conditions, but ube farmers need support to protect ube varieties and meet global demand. Photo Courtesy of JEFSPA

For instance, right now, farmers are having difficulties sourcing seedlings, Paredes says. To help close that gap, he started supplying planting materials beyond his own region, with buyers often offering advance payment just to reserve stock.

The Department of Agriculture’s high-value crops division also distributed over 50,000 ube seedlings to OMMRO members and other farmers in the first quarter of 2026.

Paredes and OMMRO work with various institutions, including the Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Training Institute, and other local and international agencies to address these challenges.

Among these agencies is the Philippine Root Crops Research and Training Center (PhilRootCrops), which is based at Visayas State University (VSU) in Baybay City.

Established in 1977, PhilRootCrops is the country’s national research and training center for root crops and tubers. It conducts regular cultivation workshops and crop monitoring.

The center’s director, Professor Marlon Tambis, calls ube one of the most resilient crops in the Philippines. Ube is a perennial crop with strong economic upside, he notes, yet many farmers still lack the training to make the most of it.

Tambis says the crop’s potential is outpacing the resources needed to develop it. PhilRootCrops is currently developing new cultivation technologies but the funding hasn’t kept pace.

“While we are provided by VSU of P500,000 every year, it’s still very small,” Tambis says.

“Of course, that is not enough because we are a national center. We have a national mandate. We have clients from everywhere in the Philippines. That’s just one month’s expenses,” he says.

It’s been this way for years, Tambis says. Through PhilRootCrops’ long and continued efforts, the center has managed to acquire multiple partnerships that continue to fund its operations and development, a lifeline that has kept its research going even as government funding stays thin.

Safeguard ube

Ube’s rise is an opportunity too important to let slip away, Paredes points out. Securing that opportunity starts with protecting the crop itself.

SUPPORT SYSTEM. PhilRootCrops conducts regular cultivation workshops and crop monitoring to support ube farmers.

First, Paredes wants ube formally declared a priority crop by law, a status he believes would unlock more structured, long-term government support. He also calls for safeguarding the country’s ube varieties, beginning with a stop to raw ube from being sold abroad.

“Unta, ang gobyerno, dili nila i-allow na ibaligya sa gawas ang raw ube. Kung pwede, powder or processed product lang para maprotect nato ato mga gipananom na mga ube varieties,” says Paredes.

(Hopefully, the government will not allow raw ube to be sold abroad. If possible, only powdered or processed products should be exported so we can protect the ube varieties that we have cultivated.)

On August 22, Leyte 4th District Representative Richard Gomez filed House Bill No. 10225, known as the Philippine Ube Industry Development Act, to declare purple yam a national priority crop and boost production and exports.

Then there’s the matter of people.

Small farmer groups need to be organized and backed with real support so that big companies don’t end up monopolizing the industry and dictating prices at farmers’ expense.

Paredes says there should be a dedicated agency to help farmers navigate exports and move faster.

For years, farmers struggled with low demand for their crops. With ube, for the first time in a long while, that’s no longer the problem.

Whether Eastern Visayas farmers will be able to take full advantage of this demand depends on the support they get. – Rappler.com

Jennifer Jezreel Kaye Pading is an economics student at Visayas State University in Baybay City in Leyte. An Aries Rufo Journalism Fellow for 2026, she is also the executive editor of Amaranth and community officer of AYEJ-Leyte Panaad Ha Sinirangan.

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

World.title: Tokayev Calls for Stronger SCO Cooperation as Experts See SCO Emerging as Key Multipolar Platform
World.content:
ALMATY – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has called for stronger cooperation within the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) on security, trade, transport, investment and water, as the organization marks 25 years of development, while experts say its expanding agenda is positioning the SCO as an increasingly important platform in the emerging multipolar international order.

Speaking at the Sept. 1 SCO summit in Bishkek, the Kazakh President described the organization’s evolution from the Shanghai Five into a major international organization spanning much of Eurasia and representing almost half of the world’s population.

“The SCO operates outside the logic of military-political blocs and is not directed against any state. It is based on a completely different political philosophy – the ‘Shanghai Spirit,’ whose foundation is the idea of joint work for the sake of progress,” Tokayev said.

According to Prof. Dr. Zijad Bećirović, director of the International Institute for Middle Eastern and Balkan Studies (IFIMES) in Ljubljana, the organization’s transformation reflects broader changes in the international system.

“The transformation of the organisation reflects the wider transformation of the international system. The SCO has evolved from a regional security mechanism into a broader platform addressing security, trade, energy, investment, connectivity and economic cooperation,” he told the Astana Times.

“Its importance is not simply a matter of size. The organisation brings together major political, economic and demographic centers, making it one of the most significant institutional expressions of the emerging multipolar order,” he added.

From regional security to wider cooperation

Tokayev also called for stronger mutual trust and security cooperation, noting that the SCO brings together major Eurasian powers whose positions influence the emerging international order. He proposed holding an SCO ministerial conference on strategic stability and confidence-building measures in Eurasia, with discussions potentially covering reducing military risks, preventing a new arms race, and avoiding dangerous incidents.

“Of particular concern is the fact that the consequences of armed conflicts are already extending beyond the immediate zones of hostilities, affecting international markets, commercial shipping, and the sustainability of energy and transport links. This has significantly increased the risk of the cross-border spread of crisis phenomena,” Tokayev said.

Connectivity as a practical area of cooperation

Economic and transport cooperation was another major theme of Tokayev’s address. President Tokayev proposed establishing SCO cross-border trade zones based on existing border cooperation centers. Such zones, he said, could test simplified trade procedures, digital processes and modern payment mechanisms.

He also supported creating an SCO Development Bank and proposed directing its resources primarily toward infrastructure, technological and industrial projects.

Bećirović sees connectivity as one area where the SCO can translate its broad political ambitions into practical cooperation.

“The diversity of the SCO is both a challenge and an opportunity. Its members have different strategic priorities and, in some cases, serious bilateral disagreements. But economic cooperation does not require political uniformity. It requires identifiable interests that can be pursued together,” he said.

The strongest potential, in his view, lies in Eurasian transport connectivity.

“The geography of trade is changing rapidly, with new transport corridors, railways, ports, logistics centres, energy infrastructure and digital networks reshaping commercial links across the continent,” Bećirović added.

Kazakhstan links SCO agenda to global governance

Tokayev also used the SCO+ format to present Kazakhstan’s broader vision of the international system. Speaking during the extended meeting, he noted that the world needs an order in which confrontation and the “cult of force” give way to mutual responsibility, joint development and long-term cooperation.

President Tokayev proposed that the key principles of the SCO be reflected in a special UN General Assembly resolution dedicated to the International Day of Multilateralism and Diplomacy for Peace.

“The UN should remain the core of the international system, and its Charter – the universal foundation of international law,” Tokayev said.

Manarbek Kabaziyev, deputy chairman of the Foreign Policy Research Institute under Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry, also stressed that the SCO should not be regarded as a replacement for other international organizations, in a conversation with the Astana Times.

“The SCO occupies a somewhat different niche. It is primarily a platform for broad political dialogue and practical cooperation among Eurasian states, bringing together countries with different political systems, economic models, civilizational and cultural characteristics,” Kabaziyev said.

According to Tokayev, strengthening preventive diplomacy should be an important part of reforming global governance.

The Kazakh President also called for SCO support for Kazakhstan’s proposals to establish an International Water Organization under the UN and an SCO Water Issues Analysis Center.

Cooperation without political uniformity

The ability to pursue common economic interests despite political differences may ultimately determine how effective the SCO can become. The organization brings together China, Russia, India, Iran, Pakistan and the Central Asian states, among others, with different foreign policy priorities and economic models. Bećirović does not see this diversity as necessarily preventing cooperation.

“Its strategic value lies in its ability to bring together states with different interests and political systems and provide a framework for dialogue and cooperation,” he said.

Kabaziyev similarly notes that the emerging Eurasian approach should not be understood as a model based on uniformity.

“I would speak not so much of a ready-made ‘Eurasian model’ as of the formation of its individual principles and mechanisms,” he said.

He described the approach as based on “pluralism of development paths,” where countries can maintain their own political and economic systems while developing practical cooperation.

“Therefore, I would call it integration through connectivity, rather than integration through unification,” Kabaziyev said.

The test of the next years

The Bishkek summit therefore comes at a point when the SCO’s main challenge is no longer simply defining its areas of cooperation. Its agenda has already expanded considerably. The question is how effectively its members can turn that broad agenda into mechanisms and projects.

At the global level, Tokayev’s emphasis on multilateralism and the UN reflects Kazakhstan’s effort to position the SCO not as a replacement for existing international institutions, but as a regional platform contributing to a more multipolar system.

Bećirović believes the organization’s ability to maintain dialogue among states with divergent interests may itself become one of its most important functions.

“In an increasingly fragmented international environment this function is becoming more important,” he said.

Twenty-five years after its establishment, the SCO has grown far beyond its original security-focused mandate. Its next stage will depend on whether its members can use that diversity not as an obstacle, but as a basis for practical cooperation across the increasingly interconnected Eurasian space.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyz Republic Meet US Fiscal Transparency Requirements, Report Finds
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan and the Kyrgyz Republic are the only Central Asian countries to meet the United States Department of State’s minimum fiscal transparency requirements, while Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan did not meet the criteria, according to the 2026 Fiscal Transparency Report released by the U.S. Department of State.

The report assesses whether governments receiving U.S. assistance meet minimum standards for the public disclosure of budget and financial information. The latest review covered the period from Jan. 1 to Dec. 31, 2025 and evaluated 139 governments.

Overall, the department found that 73 governments met the minimum fiscal transparency requirements, while 67 did not. Of the governments that fell short, 14 were assessed as having made significant progress toward meeting the requirements.

Kazakhstan and the Kyrgyz Republic were included among the 73 governments that met the standards. The three other Central Asian states – Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan – were included among the 67 governments that did not meet the minimum requirements. None of the three was identified as having made significant progress during the review period.

What the U.S. fiscal transparency assessment measures

The assessment focuses on whether governments make key public financial information available and whether citizens and other stakeholders can meaningfully examine how public resources are managed. The criteria include the public availability of national budget documents, including revenues and expenditures by ministry, as well as information on sovereign debt and the terms and conditions of sovereign loans made to foreign borrowers.

The department also examines the independence and effectiveness of supreme audit institutions, public disclosure of government audits, and transparency surrounding natural resource extraction and public procurement.

For the 2026 assessment, the U.S. strengthened the criteria by specifically requiring governments to make the terms and conditions of sovereign loans to foreign borrowers publicly accessible, including information on liabilities and collateralized assets.

The report said fiscal transparency contributes to effective public financial management, market confidence and economic sustainability. It can also reduce risks associated with corruption, financial crimes and unfair practices in international markets. At the same time, the State Department stressed that the assessment does not constitute an assessment of corruption. A country failing to meet the minimum fiscal transparency requirements does not necessarily mean that significant corruption exists, while meeting the requirements does not necessarily indicate a low level of corruption.

A broader concern for Central Asia

The contrasting assessments highlight differences in the region’s approach to fiscal disclosure. For Central Asian economies seeking to attract investment, the issue extends beyond compliance with a particular U.S. assessment. Greater transparency over government budgets, public debt, state-owned enterprises, natural-resource contracts and public procurement can affect how investors assess fiscal risks and the predictability of the business environment.

The State Department noted that fiscal transparency helps build market confidence and supports economic sustainability by giving citizens and markets greater visibility into government finances.

The 2026 report also warns that assessments can change from year to year because the U.S. government is required to update and strengthen its minimum criteria, while governments’ performance and available information can also change.

World.title: Tokayev Joins World Nomad Games Opening in Bishkek
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev attended the official opening ceremony of the sixth World Nomad Games in Bishkek and greeted Kazakhstan’s national team, which consists of 152 athletes competing across all 43 disciplines at this year’s games, reported Akorda.

The WNG officially opened at Bishkek Arena, drawing more than 50,000 spectators. Presidents of 17 countries also attended the ceremony.

Turganbek Kurmanbek, world champion in kokpar and captain of Kazakhstan’s national team, carried the Kazakh flag during the opening ceremony.

Opening the games, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov said sporting competition could help strengthen friendship among peoples.

He noted that the idea was consistent with the philosophy of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization.

“The simultaneous hosting of the meeting of heads of state in the Kyrgyz Republic and the WNG also carries deep symbolic significance. At one event, the leaders of states seek ways toward peace and cooperation through dialogue, while at the other, people from around the world come closer together through sport and culture,” Japarov said.

According to Japarov, the games represent a rich cultural heritage inherited from ancient nomadic peoples who inhabited the Eurasian region, including the Huns, Kyrgyz, Turks, Turgesh and other nomadic peoples.

“This spiritual and cultural heritage is being revived today in a new form through the World Nomad Games,” he said.

The cultural program featured performances by several Kyrgyz artists, as well as American singer Nicole Scherzinger.

The WNG will continue through Sept. 6. Most competitions will be held at the Kyrchyn Gorge and the hippodrome in the resort town of Cholpon-Ata in the Issyk-Kul Region.

The previous WNG were held in Astana in 2024, when Kazakhstan topped the overall medal standings.

The seventh WNG will be held in Tatarstan in 2028.

World.title: UN Declares April 22 International Day of Planet Greening at Kazakhstan’s Initiative
World.content:
ASTANA – The United Nations General Assembly has adopted a Kazakhstan-initiated resolution proclaiming April 22 as the International Day of Greening the Planet, marking another step in Kazakhstan’s efforts to promote global environmental cooperation.

The resolution was adopted in New York on Aug. 31. The initiative was first proposed by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev during the General Debate of the 80th session of the UN General Assembly in September 2025.

April 22 was chosen for the International Day of Greening the Planet as the date also marks Earth Day, an international environmental observance traditionally associated, among other activities, with mass tree planting. The new UN observance therefore builds on an existing global tradition of environmental awareness and action.

Thirty-two countries from different regions of the world joined the resolution as co-sponsors, reflecting broad international support for the initiative. The new international day is intended to raise global awareness of the importance of greening and restoring natural ecosystems and encourage governments, the UN system, international and regional organizations, civil society and other stakeholders to undertake related initiatives and activities.

The resolution focuses on strengthening efforts to protect the environment, restore ecosystems, expand green spaces and promote environmental awareness and culture.

The initiative is also aligned with Kazakhstan’s national environmental campaign, Taza Kazakhstan, which promotes responsible attitudes toward the environment, improvement of public spaces and greater environmental awareness among citizens.

The adoption of the resolution represents the practical implementation of another international initiative put forward by President Tokayev and underscores Kazakhstan’s efforts to advance environmental issues through multilateral cooperation.

By establishing a dedicated international day, Kazakhstan is seeking to place ecosystem restoration and greening higher on the international agenda and encourage countries to translate environmental commitments into practical action.

World.title: Experts: Kazakhstan’s New Security Council Apparatus Signals Shift Toward Preventive Security
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is strengthening the institutional role of its Security Council, a move experts say could mark a shift toward more systematic strategic analysis and preventive risk management as the country’s understanding of national security expands beyond traditional defense and law enforcement.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a decree on Aug. 28 establishing the Security Council Apparatus as a state body directly subordinate to and accountable to the President. The move was accompanied by changes to the council’s leadership: Aida Balayeva was appointed Deputy Chair of the Security Council, while Gizat Nurdauletov was relieved of his position as Secretary.

The changes raise a question about the direction of Kazakhstan’s security architecture: whether the new structure primarily strengthens the administrative capacity of an existing institution or signals a more substantive expansion of the Security Council’s role in strategic governance.

On Aug. 31, Tokayev met with Balayeva in her new capacity and outlined several priority tasks, including those related to establishing the Security Council Apparatus. The new state body will deal with issues related to national security, legality and law and order.

A more defined institutional role

The Security Council is a constitutional collegial body chaired by the President and responsible for coordinating a unified state policy in national security, defense capability and the protection of sovereignty.

Political science expert Gaziz Abishev said the change could increase the council’s analytical and coordinating capacity. According to him, creating a separate apparatus gives the council a more clearly defined institutional structure.

“The Security Council of Kazakhstan is acquiring more specific institutional contours. President Tokayev signed a decree on establishing the Security Council Apparatus as a state body directly subordinate to the head of state. This, it should be understood, anticipates strengthening the Security Council with personnel, technical and other resources,” Abishev wrote on his Telegram channel.

Manarbek Kabaziyev, deputy chairman of the Board of the Foreign Policy Research Institute under Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry, sees the change primarily as an effort to improve strategic governance.

“The creation of the Security Council Apparatus should, first of all, be considered in the context of further improving the system of strategic governance of the state. Under modern conditions, the concept of national security has expanded significantly: it is no longer only defense and the law-enforcement sphere, but also information, technological, economic, energy, environmental and other components,” Kabaziyev told the Astana Times.

Why the security agenda is changing

The broader definition of national security reflects the increasingly interconnected nature of modern risks. For Kazakhstan, this is particularly relevant given its geographic and economic position at the intersection of major Eurasian political, trade and transport routes. Kabaziyev said the main objective of strengthening the Security Council should be to improve the state’s ability to identify risks before they develop into crises.

“In my view, the main task is to ensure more systematic and professional analysis of internal and external risks, their early identification and the timely development of government decisions,” he said.

According to Kabaziyev, legislation already provides the Security Council Apparatus with functions related to information and analytical support, organizational support, coordination and monitoring the implementation of Security Council decisions.

The current reform therefore represents, in his assessment, not the creation of an entirely new institution but its organizational and substantive strengthening in response to changing security requirements.

From reaction to prevention

One of the reform’s most important potential consequences is a greater emphasis on preventive rather than reactive approaches to national security.

“The long-term effect, in my view, is a transition from a predominantly reactive approach to security to a more preventive model,” Kabaziyev said.

Such a model requires the state to identify connections between risks that traditionally might have been considered separately. Kabaziyev said the apparatus should have strong analytical capabilities, engage with the expert community and use modern forecasting and scenario-analysis tools.

“Then its role will consist not only in responding to threats that have already emerged, but also in identifying potential risks in advance and proposing options for their neutralization,” he said.

Appointments’ role

The creation of the apparatus coincided with Balayeva’s appointment as Deputy Chair of the Security Council, adding an important personnel dimension to the institutional reform. Political analyst Talgat Kaliyev noted that Balayeva’s new position significantly expands her responsibilities.

“The election of Yerlan Karin as Vice President and the appointment of Balayeva as Deputy Chair of the Security Council are events of the same order. Essentially, President Tokayev now has two deputies, and separating the Security Council Apparatus into a separate body allows us to discuss the delineation of powers,” Kaliyev wrote on his Telegram channel.

He described Balayeva as effectively becoming a “vice president for security,” suggesting that her responsibilities could extend to oversight of law-enforcement bodies and the implementation of the Law and Order policy in everyday governance.

The precise distribution of responsibilities within the new structure will become clearer as the apparatus is organized and its institutional framework develops.

Security and international reputation

The Security Council’s institutional strengthening could also affect how Kazakhstan is perceived internationally. Kabaziyev said the development should not automatically be interpreted as a move toward greater state isolation or excessive centralization.

“On the contrary, if the new format ensures professional decision-making, interagency coordination, strategic forecasting and the rule of law, this could strengthen Kazakhstan’s international reputation as a state capable of effectively managing complex risks,” he said.

The creation of a dedicated Security Council Apparatus provides the institutional foundation for a potentially stronger role, but its ultimate significance will depend on how effectively the new structure operates. Kabaziyev emphasized that the reform’s effectiveness should ultimately be measured by its results rather than by the expansion of the institutional structure itself.

“Ultimately, the effectiveness of the Security Council will be assessed not by the number of structural divisions, but by the state’s ability to foresee challenges, make balanced decisions and ensure their consistent implementation,” he said.

World.title: Teachers at Heart of President’s Vision: NU Researchers on Kazakhstan’s Education Future
World.content:
Kazakhstan has backed its education ambitions with substantial investment in new schools, higher teacher salaries and measures to strengthen the profession. Speaking at a Republic Day event in October 2025, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said education funding had tripled over the previous five years and teachers’ salaries had doubled.

Yet investment alone cannot transform learning. As Tokayev emphasized in 2024, even the best programs and modern schools cannot succeed without good teachers. In July 2026, he described artificial intelligence as a tool that should empower teachers rather than replace them. Against this national backdrop, Nazarbayev University’s Science Café examined a timely question: what do teachers need to turn Kazakhstan’s education investment into better learning?

Three Graduate School of Education (GSE) researchers Assel Sharimova, Duishon Shamatov and Askhat Makhmetov examined teacher preparation, professional status, well-being and technology. Their research suggests that physical and digital modernization must be matched by investment in teachers’ capacity, autonomy and working conditions.

A teacher’s first year tests the system

For Shamatov, an associate professor specializing in teacher preparation and professional development, the decisive test begins after graduation. Young teachers often enter schools with limited classroom experience and little structured support. When they struggle or leave, the problem may lie less in their ability than in the conditions in which they begin. Preparation should therefore extend beyond a diploma through practical experience, systematic mentoring and opportunities to learn from experienced colleagues. Shamatov also serves on a working group of Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Science and Higher Education that is improving accreditation standards for teacher education. He cautioned against treating PISA as an exam for teachers or a competition between schools. It indicates how well an education system enables students to reason, solve problems and apply knowledge in real-life situations. Improving Kazakhstan’s performance requires investment not only in assessment, but in teachers’ preparation, continuing development and ability to create meaningful learning experiences.

Professional status, he added, cannot be reduced to salary or public recognition. Although Kazakhstan’s Law on the Status of a Teacher marked important progress, status is ultimately experienced through working conditions, professional trust, autonomy and respect for teachers’ judgment.

When high performance leads to exhaustion

Makhmetov, a postdoctoral researcher specializing in teacher well-being and educational equity, presented findings from Kazakhstan’s first study focused on teacher well-being. His analysis identified six profiles, challenging the simple division of teachers into “good” and “bad” performers. One vulnerable group consists of highly effective yet exhausted teachers, representing almost a quarter of the workforce. These educators often lead innovation, accept additional responsibilities and support school improvement. The commitment that makes them valuable can also expose them to chronic overwork and burnout.

This shifts the leadership question from how to demand more to how to retain those already driving change. Makhmetov highlighted workload monitoring, burnout prevention and conditions that keep professional motivation sustainable.

His study also revealed a “master’s degree paradox.” Holding a master’s degree was associated with lower subjective well-being, while the proportion of such teachers has risen from approximately 3.5% to 11%. Schools could respond by offering them greater autonomy and roles as mentors, curriculum developers and leaders of professional initiatives.

Support must continue inside schools

Sharimova, an assistant professor specializing in teacher preparation and professional development, emphasized that teachers’ early years are critical. New teachers learn through relationships with experienced teachers, subject colleagues and school leaders, while managing lesson preparation, assessment, reporting and class-teacher responsibilities.

Meaningful mentoring should include opportunities to observe lessons, receive constructive feedback and approach a trusted colleague when difficulties arise. Practical assistance and openness from school leaders are equally important.

The speakers also viewed digital technologies and AI as useful resources. They can support lesson planning, assessment and feedback, student engagement and the visualization of complex STEM concepts. Yet technology cannot compensate for weak preparation, excessive workloads or a lack of professional trust.

Kazakhstan’s education modernization will ultimately be judged not only by the schools it builds or technologies it introduces, but by what happens inside classrooms. The Science Café discussions point to the next stage of reform ensuring that teachers are well prepared, professionally trusted, protected from burnout and supported throughout their careers. Strong schools require strong teachers and national ambition depends on giving them the conditions to succeed.

The author is Saqib Raza, a PhD scholar in education and an MSc graduate in Educational Leadership in Higher Education from Nazarbayev University Graduate School of Education, Kazakhstan.
