World.title: Historic KMG Dim Sum Bond Issue Sets New Benchmark for Yuan Financing in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – KazMunayGas’ (KMG) historic issuance of 3.5 billion yuan (US$520.3 million) in Dim Sum bonds could mark a new stage in Kazakhstan’s access to yuan-denominated financing, financial analyst Andrei Chebotaryov said.

The transaction, which includes the first 10-year Dim Sum bonds issued by a company from Kazakhstan and Central Asia, attracted more than 25 billion yuan (US$3.7 billion) in orders.

KMG closed the order book on Aug. 26, with proceeds earmarked for its investment program. The bonds are scheduled to be placed on Sept. 2.

A new benchmark in yuan financing

The issue consists of two tranches. The five-year bonds, worth 1.5 billion yuan (US$223 million), carry a 2.3% annual coupon and a 2.45% yield. The 10-year tranche totals 2 billion yuan (US$297.3 million), with a 2.8% coupon and a 2.98% yield.

According to Chebotaryov, KMG became the first company in Kazakhstan and Central Asia to issue 10-year Dim Sum bonds, creating a long-term benchmark for yuan-denominated borrowing in the region.

“KMG became the first company in Kazakhstan and Central Asia to issue 10-year Dim Sum bonds. In the region, a 10-year benchmark was formed for the first time – in other words, a long-term yuan borrowing market has opened, which we did not have before,” Chebotaryov wrote on his Telegram channel on Aug. 28.

Dim Sum bonds are yuan-denominated securities issued outside mainland China, typically in Hong Kong. For Kazakhstan, access to this market provides an alternative international financing channel.

Moody’s assigned the bonds a Baa1 credit rating, matching KMG’s rating.

Investor demand is the stronger signal

The most striking indicator was the scale of demand. Investor orders exceeded 25 billion yuan (US$3.7 billion) at the peak – more than seven times the announced issue size. According to KMG, this was the largest order book in the history of Dim Sum issues by issuers outside mainland China and Hong Kong.

Investors included banks, insurance companies, hedge funds and sovereign investment funds. A two-day roadshow in Hong Kong preceded the issue.

Chebotaryov said the combination of borrowing costs, maturity and demand points to strong investor confidence.

“Low funding costs, a long maturity and sevenfold oversubscription together say one thing: investors trust KazMunayGas and see the company as financially stable,” he wrote.

He added that the signal extends beyond KMG itself.

“Asian investors were buying Kazakhstan’s credit risk for 10 years ahead – and they were buying it willingly,” he said.

Why the deal matters for Kazakhstan

The transaction could have implications beyond KMG. According to Chebotaryov, it provides a reference point for other Kazakh issuers considering yuan financing.

The deal also broadens access to Asian capital markets and could reduce reliance on dollar financing, according to Energy Monitor.

Whether other Kazakh companies can replicate KMG’s terms will depend on investor demand. The key indicator will be whether other domestic issuers follow KMG into the Dim Sum market.

What to watch next

The immediate milestone is settlement on Sept. 2. The longer-term test will be whether other Kazakh issuers follow KMG into the Dim Sum market.

“KMG has set a trend for other domestic companies. This deal is now a natural reference point for any Kazakh issuer looking toward yuan financing: there is a price, there is a maturity, and there is confirmed demand,” Chebotaryov said.

The deal builds on Kazakhstan’s recent expansion into yuan-denominated capital markets, following KMG’s 2025 plan for a Dim Sum program of up to 15 billion yuan (nearly US$2 billion) and Samruk Kazyna’s 3 billion yuan Panda bond issued in April.

If other issuers follow, the transaction could establish a benchmark for future yuan borrowing in Kazakhstan.

World.title: Kazakhstan Has Begun Structural Shift Toward Non-Resource Economy, Expert Says
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has entered a new investment cycle that is beginning to change not only the volume but also the structure of capital entering the economy, according to the country’s leading financial analyst Rassul Rysmambetov.

While the country remains dependent on extractive industries, growing investment in manufacturing, processing and high-technology production suggests that the long-discussed shift toward a more diversified economy is beginning to take shape.

“We can already confidently speak about the beginning of a structural shift. It is still too early to say that we are moving away from the resource-based model, but the figures show that the state is now moving toward a non-resource model not just in words, but in practice,” Rysmambetov said in a comment to The Astana Times.

From investment growth to structural change

The change is visible in investment data. Between 2019 and 2025, investment in fixed capital in Kazakhstan increased from 12.6 trillion tenge (US$27.3 billion) to 23.5 trillion tenge (US$51 billion), while investment in manufacturing tripled from 1 trillion (US$2.2 billion) to 3 trillion tenge (US$6.5 billion). The sector’s share of total investment rose from 8.1% to 12.7%, reported the Prime Minister’s press service on Aug. 31.

Foreign investment is also diversifying. Gross foreign direct investment reached $20.5 billion in 2025, up 14.4%. Investment in manufacturing increased by 47.4%, or $1.4 billion, while investment in mining fell by 47%, or $3 billion. The changing composition suggests Kazakhstan is attracting more capital into activities beyond raw-material extraction.

This trend is supported by the growing pipeline of industrial projects. The Kazakh Invest portfolio currently includes 215 projects worth $78.6 billion, with more than 88,000 jobs expected to be created. Of these, 93 projects worth $32.2 billion are already being implemented, while 122 projects worth $46.4 billion remain under development.

A new system for turning capital into projects

The government is seeking to reinforce this shift through a new investment-support system. Since 2025, a three-level investment attraction model has been operating, with regions identifying priority projects and targeting investors. Fast Track mechanisms, investment headquarters and a “prosecutorial filter” are intended to reduce administrative barriers, while the National Digital Investment Platform provides monitoring and coordination.

Investment agreements are another part of the framework. Since the mechanism was introduced in 2021, 66 agreements worth more than 17.8 trillion tenge (US$38.6 billion) have been concluded. In 2025 alone, 30 agreements worth nearly 11.2 trillion tenge (US$24.3 billion) were signed. By August, another 25 agreements worth approximately 4.4 trillion tenge (US$9.5 billion) had been concluded.

The approach reflects a broader shift in investment policy: attracting capital is increasingly being linked to specific economic needs, including import substitution, exports, localization and the development of domestic supply chains.

The real test is what happens after investment

The quality of this investment, however, will ultimately matter more than the headline figures, Rysmambetov said. In his view, the next test is whether new factories generate exports, domestic value added, higher productivity and better-paid jobs.

“Investments should not simply increase gross output, but also increase labour productivity and real wages,” he said.

This distinction matters as Kazakhstan expands projects in pharmaceuticals, agricultural processing, food production and digital infrastructure. New pharmaceutical plants are expected to localize production of hundreds of medicines, while projects by international companies in agriculture and food processing are designed to create demand for domestic suppliers.

Large-scale projects such as Dalian Hesheng Holdings’ $739 million wheat-processing complex, Fufeng Group’s $340 million corn-processing plant and Tiryaki Agro’s approximately $320 million agro-industrial complex illustrate the move toward deeper processing. Rather than exporting agricultural commodities with limited processing, these projects aim to produce starches, gluten, amino acids, protein isolates and other higher-value products.

Beyond factories: building domestic technological capacity

A similar logic is emerging in digital infrastructure. The planned Data Center Valley near Ekibastuz is being developed as a major computing and artificial intelligence hub, with investment potentially reaching $30 billion and energy capacity expanding from 300 megawatts to 1 gigawatt. In June, Kazakhstan signed a $10 billion package of agreements with Firebird and NVIDIA covering AI and digital infrastructure.

For Rysmambetov, however, industrial diversification must be accompanied by stronger domestic technological capacity. He pointed to limited spending on research and development and underused laboratories at universities and enterprises as areas requiring greater attention.

“Industry often relies on ready-made engineering solutions from abroad instead of developing them internally,” he said, arguing that Kazakhstan needs greater investment in R&D, industrial analytics and applied research.

From foreign capital to domestic value

The international dimension is equally important. Kazakhstan’s ability to attract capital from the UAE, Qatar, Singapore, China, the United States and European countries gives the country access not only to financing but also to technology, markets and supply chains. The challenge is to ensure that foreign investment creates lasting links with domestic businesses rather than operating as isolated production facilities.

The emerging investment cycle therefore represents a transition rather than a completed transformation. Manufacturing’s growing share, rising non-resource investment, and the expansion of processing industries provide evidence that Kazakhstan’s economic structure is changing.

The decisive indicators over the next several years will be whether these projects reach operation, increase exports, deepen domestic value chains, raise productivity and stimulate innovation.

“The transformation has begun. But to replace the economic model, we still need some time – three to five years,” Rysmambetov said.

World.title: What Pashinyan and Putin agreed in Bishkek amid peak tensions in relations
World.content:
Pashinyan-Putin meeting in Bishkek

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Russian President Vladimir Putin met in Bishkek, where an SCO+ meeting was held as part of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit. Their talks took place late in the evening.

There was no shortage of issues to discuss as bilateral relations have recently become increasingly strained. The previous meeting between Pashinyan and Putin took place on 1 April. Since then, Armenia held parliamentary elections in June, in which Pashinyan’s party won a majority and formed a government. However, the Russian president has yet to congratulate Pashinyan on his victory.

Judging by statements from Moscow, the main issue concerning the Russian authorities is Armenia’s ambition to join the European Union.

In the opening minutes of the Bishkek meeting, Putin said Armenia’s aspiration to join the EU was the country’s legitimate right. However, he said this “creates difficulties” for Armenia’s membership of the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU).

“The sooner Armenia decides on the issue of joining the EU, the better. Moscow needs to understand how to develop relations further. The adoption of a law launching the process of Armenia joining another organisation amounts to a declaration of withdrawal from ours,” Putin said.

Pashinyan responded by reiterating that Armenia had no intention of leaving the EAEU.

The Armenian prime minister also recalled that, under the EAEU’s charter, there was no procedure for expelling a member state unless the country itself decided to leave.

“We greatly value our relations with the Russian Federation. We hope these relations are important to Russia as well. I think that Armenia and Russia, and we personally, should treat these relations with great care. I want to confirm that I personally and our government treat them with great care. I am sure that you also treat these relations with great care, and I want to thank you for that,” Pashinyan said.

He stressed that the issue of EU membership had not yet reached the stage at which a referendum could be held. He explained that Armenia did not currently have the alternative of actual EU membership to put before the public. In other words, the issue would be decided once the Armenian authorities had a concrete alternative to offer voters.

Putin, however, stood his ground: “The people should indeed always have a choice. So give them one, and we will close the matter. That’s all. The simplest thing is to ask people: what do you want — this or that?”

After the meeting, the Armenian prime minister posted a video on social media summarising the outcome of the talks.

Pashinyan described the meeting as “very good” and said he and Putin had agreed to continue their “sincere and constructive dialogue” during his visit to Moscow, which is apparently expected to take place in the near future.

“It should be noted that bilateral relations between Armenia and Russia are extremely important for both countries. […]However, it should also be noted that, in the new environment and under the new circumstances, there is a need to rethink these relations. I am convinced that, as a result of this reassessment, relations will become better, more constructive, more mutually beneficial and warmer,” he said.

Context: other issues on agenda

In Armenia, the meeting had been expected to involve difficult discussions on several critical issues. Armenian analysts had also warned that the meeting was unlikely to produce any positive developments on any of them.

In Armenia, there were expectations that the two leaders would discuss holding a referendum on whether the country should remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership.

Russia and other EAEU member states have recently been pressing for such a referendum. The Armenian authorities have responded that there is little point in holding one at this stage, as the country has not yet formally applied for EU membership.

The EAEU comprises Russia, Belarus, Armenia, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.

Meanwhile, there has already been talk within the EAEU of discussing Armenia’s status in the bloc. However, under the union’s charter, only Armenia itself can decide to withdraw. As Pashinyan has repeatedly pointed out, there is no other procedure for ending its membership.

At the same time, on 24 August, the Armenian prime minister raised the possibility of submitting a formal application for EU membership. This prompted a fresh wave of criticism and an even sharper reaction in Russia. Commentators there said that “EU membership is a marathon lasting decades”, while Yerevan would feel “the costs of breaking with Russia and the EAEU here and now”.

Russian experts even predicted a “fatal outcome” for Armenia. According to them, the country faces a choice between “Turkification” and a “Ukrainian scenario”.

The two leaders had also been expected to discuss Russian restrictions on imports of Armenian food and other goods, which were introduced in May and remain in place.

Russia has traditionally been a key export market for Armenia. However, since the restrictions were introduced — which Russia has attributed to concerns over product quality — Armenian goods have increasingly been exported to EU countries, where higher standards apply.

Armenian analysts had also expected the two leaders to discuss Armenia’s membership of the Russian-led CSTO military alliance.

The Collective Security Treaty Organisation comprises Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Armenia.

Armenia has effectively frozen its participation in the organisation for the past two years in response to what Yerevan sees as inaction by its allies.

When Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s sovereign territory in 2021-22, its CSTO allies neither intervened nor condemned Baku’s actions. They argued that the Armenian-Azerbaijani border had not been delimited. Pashinyan responded:

“To say that there is no border between Armenia and Azerbaijan is to say that the CSTO has no defined area of responsibility. And if there is no area of responsibility, then there is no organisation.”

While Pashinyan had previously said he was not concerned about the possibility of Armenia being expelled from the military bloc, just a week before his meeting with Putin he went further, saying he would welcome such a move:

“At least it would relieve us of the dilemma of whether or not to leave [the CSTO].”

In addition, ahead of the leaders’ meeting, Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said the talks would take place at a time “when opposition leaders are being arrested en masse in Armenia”.

He was referring, among others, to the arrest of former Armenian President Robert Kocharyan. Kocharyan is accused of abuse of office, accepting a particularly large bribe and money laundering. A court ordered him to be held for two months. It is the former president’s fourth arrest.

In Armenia, there was speculation that Putin, who has close ties with Kocharyan, might once again ask for his release.

During his previous meeting with Pashinyan in April, Putin expressed hope that Russia’s “friends” and pro-Russian political forces would be able to take part in Armenia’s elections.

He was believed to have been referring to the party of Russian businessman Samvel Karapetyan, who is currently under house arrest on charges of making calls to seize power, as well as a bloc led by former President Robert Kocharyan. Both contested the elections but failed to secure a parliamentary majority.

Representatives of Armenia’s ruling party believe that these pro-Russian forces are encouraging the Russian authorities to take steps that could fuel public discontent. Pashinyan’s team believes the opposition hopes to use such discontent as a means of coming to power.

World.title: Azerbaijan versus Western media: Why were different reports labelled a single ‘information campaign’?
World.content:
Azerbaijan and foreign media

Four separate reports about Azerbaijan have appeared in international media: a TVP World programme by Poland’s public broadcaster on political repression, an Independent report on the conditions in which Ali Karimli is being held, a BBC analysis of political prisoners, and a Guardian review of a documentary about Karabakh.

Baku responded with two official statements. Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry summoned Poland’s ambassador over the TVP World programme and handed him a protest note. In a separate statement, the Media Development Agency described the other three publications as possible elements of a single “targeted information campaign”.

However, when examined individually, the reports clearly differ in their subject matter, format and main sources.

TVP: international success and domestic repression

The central question of the TVP World programme “Peace in Azerbaijan comes with repression”, broadcast on 26 August, is why Azerbaijan’s political space continues to shrink despite Baku’s growing international influence.

The programme discusses the arrests of journalists from AbzasMedia, Meydan TV and Toplum TV, as well as criminal cases against opposition figures, activists and researchers. Presenter Benjamin Lee and İPEK Centre deputy director Türkan Bozkurt discuss oil revenues, the transfer of power within one family, the legitimacy Ilham Aliyev gained from victory in Karabakh, relations with the West and the position of national minorities.

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry described the programme as biased and the presenter’s conduct as provocative. Since TVP receives state funding from Poland’s budget, the Azerbaijani side linked the programme’s content to the Polish government’s position and described its broadcast as an “unfriendly act”.

The Independent: conditions of Ali Karimli’s detention

The British newspaper’s 30 August report focuses on a narrower issue. The family and lawyers of Ali Karimli, the detained chairman of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party, say he has no access to safe drinking water, ventilation, adequate sleep, outdoor exercise or reading materials. A Human Rights Watch representative says the authorities have not presented convincing evidence to the public in his case. The UK Foreign Office confirms that it has raised the issue with Azerbaijani authorities.

The article’s emotive headline highlights the family’s claim that authorities are trying to “break” Karimli. The report also describes the charge against him as “treason”. Officially, however, prosecutors have charged him under an article concerning actions aimed at the violent seizure of power and the forcible alteration of the constitutional order. This is a specific point on which Baku could request a correction.

The newspaper also says it contacted Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry for comment but received no response.

BBC: figures and the case of Igbal Abilov

The Russian Service of the BBC’s article “Why is Ilham Aliyev stepping up repression?”, published on 31 August, focuses not on Ali Karimli but on Talysh researcher Igbal Abilov, who received an 18-year prison sentence.

The BBC analysed lists compiled by the Institute for Peace and Democracy from 2021 to May 2026. It concluded that the number of political prisoners had more than tripled, while the average prison sentence in politically motivated cases reached about 12 years in 2026. The article also examines the cases involving AbzasMedia, Radio Azadliq and Toplum TV, as well as the trials of researchers Bahruz Samadov and Igbal Abilov.

The fact that the calculations rely on lists compiled by a single human rights organisation may be open to debate. However, the BBC explains its methodology in detail, includes Ilham Aliyev’s position that he denies political persecution, and says it contacted the Penitentiary Service for comment but received no response.

Who is restricting access to the official position?

The MEDİA Agency accuses foreign news organisations of failing to seek Azerbaijan’s official position. However, in February 2025, the BBC closed its Baku bureau on the Foreign Ministry’s instructions. The bureau had operated in the country since 1994.

The Foreign Ministry cited the principle of reciprocity and the lack of a legal basis for the bureau’s operation. When authorities restrict the work of local bureaus and government agencies leave journalists’ requests unanswered, foreign news organisations have to rely more heavily on lawyers, relatives and experts based outside the country.

The information landscape that Baku describes as one-sided may therefore partly result from the authorities’ own media policies.

The Guardian: a review of a film about Karabakh

The Guardian article is not a political investigation. It is a short review of The Black Garden, a documentary by director Alexis Pazoumian. The film explores the wartime experience of Karabakh Armenians through the stories of two children and a young soldier who lost a leg.

The review’s introduction says Karabakh Armenians fought against “countless military campaigns” by the Azerbaijani army. However, it does not mention the First Karabakh War, the occupation of Azerbaijani territories, Azerbaijani internally displaced people or other aspects of the conflict. The reviewer also acknowledges that the film lacks a broader political and historical context.

Baku can reasonably criticise this one-sided presentation. However, expecting a film critic to seek comment from the Azerbaijani government would mean applying standards associated with news journalism to a piece about culture.

What do the different reports have in common?

What the four publications have in common is not any proven coordination between them, but the fact that the picture of Azerbaijan they present differs from the government’s official narratives.

TVP and the BBC question the authorities’ arguments about domestic stability and the legitimacy of criminal prosecutions. The Independent raises concerns about the conditions in which a particular detainee is being held. The Guardian, meanwhile, presents the Karabakh war primarily through the experience of the Armenian side.

The reports therefore cover different subjects, but within a single week they touch on three sensitive areas for the Azerbaijani state: domestic political control, relations with international partners and the historical narrative surrounding Karabakh. Baku sees them as part of a single attack not because their content is similar, but because all four diverge from the international image that the Azerbaijani authorities seek to project.

Is the “information campaign” proven?

The MEDİA Agency statement does not specify which facts in the reports are incorrect, nor does it provide evidence that could indicate coordination between the news organisations. At the same time, it claims that the authors did not attempt to establish Azerbaijan’s official position.

However, The Independent says it sent a request for comment to Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry. The BBC quotes the president’s position and says it also sought comment from the Penitentiary Service.

A separate response to each report would have been more convincing. In the case of the Guardian, the authorities could have pointed out factual inaccuracies in its account of the historical context. For The Independent, they could have provided a documented response to the claims about the charges against Karimli and his conditions of detention. The BBC could have received alternative data on the criteria for including people on political prisoner lists and on sentencing statistics. TVP could also have been asked to give the Azerbaijani side a right of reply on air.

Grouping all the reports together in a single statement and presenting them as a politically motivated campaign erases the differences between them. Moreover, the absence of specific rebuttals does not end the debate. Instead, it creates the conditions for further reporting.

The confrontation here is not simply a conflict between “Baku and Western media”. The main problem is that the state places verifiable factual errors, editorial assessments, statements by human rights groups and even a film review in the same political category. This approach does not weaken the criticism. On the contrary, it creates the impression that different news organisations really are acting as a united front.

Although the agency said it intended to take “necessary measures”, it did not specify whether this meant seeking corrections and a right of reply, filing an official complaint or taking other steps.

Azerbaijan and foreign media

World.title: Georgia’s central bank explains how new transfer restrictions for people over 60 will work
World.content:
Georgia’s central bank on new rules for older customers

Georgia‘s central bank has clarified that new restrictions on electronic transfers for people over 60 will not apply to regular payments and transactions.

The new rule applies only when a bank or other payment service provider suspects that a customer may be the victim of fraud.

Under the National Bank’s new regulation, if a person over 60 makes an electronic transfer of more than 500 lari and the bank suspects that the transaction may be linked to fraud, it will suspend the transfer for 48 hours.

When does the rule apply?

According to the National Bank, all four conditions must be met for a transaction to be suspended:

The user must be over 60;

The transfer must exceed 500 lari;

The bank or payment organisation must detect unusual spending or behaviour by the customer;

The payment must involve activity that carries a high risk of fraud.

In other words, being over 60 and making a transfer of more than 500 lari are not, by themselves, enough to trigger a suspension.

For example, if a 65-year-old regularly pays 700 lari in utility bills each month or transfers money to a family member, the transaction will not be automatically suspended.

The situation changes if, for example, the same person is suddenly asked to transfer a large sum to an unknown account and their behaviour within the banking system appears suspicious. In that case, the new protection mechanism may be triggered.

What can the bank do?

If all four of the above conditions are met, the bank or relevant payment service provider will suspend the electronic transaction for 48 hours.

During this period, the bank must contact the customer and explain in simple terms why it considers the transaction suspicious and what risks it may involve.

The final decision then rests with the customer.

If the customer decides they still want to transfer the funds, they must confirm this to the bank, and the transaction will go through.

Why did the central bank introduce the rule?

The National Bank of Georgia says the measure aims to protect vulnerable customers, particularly older people, from fraud.

The idea is simple: if a fraudster convinces someone to make an urgent transfer, the 48-hour pause gives them additional time to consider whether they really want to go ahead with the transaction.

According to the National Bank, a similar approach is used in other countries, including the US, Canada, Brazil, the UK and EU member states.

The new rule therefore does not ban people over 60 from making bank transfers. Instead, it temporarily suspends transactions that appear suspicious based on a number of indicators. This gives customers another opportunity to reconsider their decision before falling victim to fraud or losing their money.

Georgia’s central bank on new rules for older customers

World.title: ‘In Kramatorsk, we look to the sky’: Life in Ukrainian city under Russian air strikes
World.content:
Kramatorsk, Ukraine war

This report comes from Kramatorsk, a city in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region. It is now one of the region’s largest frontline cities, and the Russian army attacks it almost daily.

In the latest attacks, two Russian drones struck a trauma clinic on 29 August, and Russian forces attacked the hospital again on 30 August.

Many residents have left the city or have been evacuated. But many others remain despite the constant threat.

A hunt on the streets

In Kramatorsk, people have to watch their step, keep an eye on their surroundings and look up at the sky. Long, transparent strands are scattered across the streets – fibre-optic cables from Russian FPV drones. In some places, there is so much cable that it gets tangled around people’s feet.

Shards of glass and metal and burned-out cars are everywhere. At times, traces of blood can still be seen on the asphalt.

Fibre-optic cable from a Russian drone. Kramatorsk. August 2026. Yulia Kalaban for JAMnews.

Blood at the site of a Russian guided aerial bomb strike. Kramatorsk, August 2026. Yulia Kalaban for JAMnews.

The facade of a damaged building hit by a guided aerial bomb. Kramatorsk, August 2026. Yulia Kalaban for JAMnews.

Anti-drone netting stretched over the roads. Kramatorsk, August 2026. Yulia Kalaban for JAMnews.

Russian FPV drones attack people and vehicles every day. They can follow a car along the road while the operator chooses when to strike.

A car burned out by a Russian drone. Kramatorsk, August 2026. Yulia Kalaban for JAMnews.

There are also so-called “loitering drones” – Russian unmanned aircraft that can hover and wait for a target to appear. This means it is dangerous not only to drive but simply to walk outside. People have to watch the sky, listen for sounds and constantly look over their shoulders.

Anyone who comes within an operator’s line of sight is at risk.

A man walks his dog in front of a school destroyed by a Russian guided aerial bomb. Kramatorsk, August 2026. Yulia Kalaban for JAMnews.

Almost no homes left undamaged

There are now almost no homes in the city that have escaped damage from Russian attacks. Facades bear the marks of strikes, while many buildings have shattered windows and destroyed roofs.

Some homes have been completely destroyed.

Shrapnel mark from a Russian bomb. Kramatorsk, August 2026. Yulia Kalaban for JAMnews.

A residential building destroyed by a Russian FAB-250 aerial bomb on 13 August. Kramatorsk, August 2026. Yulia Kalaban for JAMnews.

Russian attacks are forcing shops and cafés to close, businesses to relocate and families with children to evacuate. Rail services to the city have been suspended.

Staying here is becoming increasingly difficult. Yet many people still remain, often because they simply have nowhere to go. They have no relatives or homes in safer regions, and not enough savings to start a new life elsewhere.

Older residents say they are not ready to start again from scratch. For them, Kramatorsk means home, memories and the graves of loved ones.

A house destroyed by a Russian aerial bomb. The inscription on the facade reads: “I will never forgive Russian scum for what they did to Krama (the city’s slang name).” Kramatorsk, August 2026. Yulia Kalaban for JAMnews.

Why Russia needs Kramatorsk

Kramatorsk, together with neighbouring Sloviansk, plays a key role in the defence of northern Donetsk region. Capturing the two cities would be an important step for Russia towards establishing control over the remaining Ukrainian-held parts of Donetsk region.

Russian forces view the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk urban area as a strategic target. Taking control of it would allow them to push their offensive further west.

For local residents, this means a scenario they have already seen in Bakhmut and Avdiivka: the city first becomes a battlefield and may then face near-total destruction.

Kramatorsk, August 2026. Yulia Kalaban for JAMnews.

Kramatorsk, Ukraine war

World.title: ‘Kocharyan’s arrest is driven by geopolitical motives’: Former Armenian president’s team speaks out
World.content:
Former president Robert Kocharyan’s team on his arrest

“President Kocharyan should be released because his detention is illegal, not at the request of President Putin,” opposition Armenia faction leader Anna Grigoryan said. In Armenia, people have spent recent days discussing whether the Russian president will ask for the release of Armenia’s former president, with whom he has friendly ties. Today, on Robert Kocharyan’s birthday, his allies and lawyer held a news conference. They said there were no legal grounds for his detention. Putin also congratulated Kocharyan, wishing him “strength in the face of adversity”.

Meanwhile, Russian officials have announced that Putin will meet Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan in Bishkek on 1 September. Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said the meeting would take place at a time “when opposition leaders are being arrested en masse in Armenia”.

Anna Grigoryan, who represents the faction led by Armenia’s former president, does not believe that Kocharyan’s detention should dominate the Pashinyan-Putin talks. She says the two sides should first resolve the crisis in bilateral relations to “avoid an economic collapse”. She hopes Russia will lift its restrictions on imports on Armenian food and goods, or at least refrain from introducing new restrictions.

At the same time, the opposition MP considers it natural and logical for Russia to discuss Kocharyan’s detention alongside other issues on the bilateral agenda. She notes that he is a “rational politician who supports maintaining good-neighbourly relations with Moscow”.

Former president’s lawyer Aram Orbelyan said both the criminal case against Kocharyan and the detention order were illegal.

“We have not yet received the detention order. As soon as we receive it, we will begin the appeal process,” he said.

Prosecutors have charged Kocharyan with abuse of office, accepting a particularly large bribe and money laundering. A court ordered the former president to spend two months in detention.

The lawyer argues that the alleged actions do not fall under the Criminal Code article cited in the detention order. He says the charges concern Kocharyan’s approval of certain government decisions while he served as president. According to Kocharyan’s defence, he had no choice but to approve them. The lawyer says the president’s office had no “tools, procedures or powers” to act otherwise.

Police detained Robert Kocharyan on 25 August. On the same day, law-enforcement officers searched companies belonging to the Kocharyan family and carried out other investigative measures. On 27 August, the Anti-Corruption Court granted the investigator’s request to detain Kocharyan. On 26 August, authorities also detained his eldest son, Sedrak Kocharyan, in the same case.

“Pashinyan is trying to minimise resistance”

Anna Grigoryan, head of the Armenia faction, believes that the case against Robert Kocharyan is not economic but political and even geopolitical. She says the fact that the issue will also come up at the Pashinyan-Putin meeting during the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit supports this view:

“If Kocharyan’s arrest were purely an economic and domestic issue for our country, would it be discussed at such an important forum? We are indeed facing a serious political and geopolitical arrest.”

She does not believe Robert Kocharyan’s “neutralisation” is accidental. She has put forward her own explanation for what prompted his arrest. In particular, she believes the Armenian authorities are preparing to amend Armenia’s Constitution and intend to “hand over territories to Azerbaijan”. She believes Pashinyan is trying to achieve “minimal resistance” in this context.

The MP says the case should also be viewed in a broader context. She believes Armenia will eventually find itself at the centre of a “clash of interests between geopolitical centres”. She says a similar process in Ukraine led to territorial losses and a mass exodus:

“But in the end, Ukraine achieved nothing. The country is still neither an EU nor a NATO member. And it remains unclear whether it will join the EU in the future. The Armenian authorities talk about diversification and reducing dependence on Russia, but they are leading the country towards Turkish domination and hostile relations with Russia.”

Lawyer says there are no grounds for arrest

Lawyer Aram Orbelyan says neither the former president nor his son committed any unlawful acts:

“They cannot fully understand what they are being accused of or what role specific individuals played in the whole process. All the processes were lawful. There were no fictitious processes carried out in the names of other people.”

According to him, the actions described in the indictment relate to the former president only through the phrase “persons associated with him”.

The lawyer stresses that the law prohibits accusing one person of another person’s actions, especially restricting someone’s freedom when “the other person’s actions are lawful in themselves”.

Orbelyan also announced that the statute of limitations for the charges had expired. In such cases, he explained, a court does not order detention, except in exceptional circumstances.

“If they saw a need to detain him, why could they not impose house arrest? It is unclear who the former president could have influenced, and what influence he could have had, if he had remained free,” he said.

Details of the case presented by the Anti-Corruption Committee

According to the Anti-Corruption Committee, Kocharyan, while serving as president, acquired several valuable public assets together with a group of people linked to him. They bought the assets at prices significantly below market value. Investigators also found that he received large bribes in some of the deals.

“According to evidence gathered during the preliminary investigation, the property was registered in the names of affiliated companies to conceal the actual ownership and the criminal origin of the assets. The acquired property was later transferred through development and sales, transfers to third parties, and the transfer of company shares, including as gifts,” the Anti-Corruption Committee said.

Investigators are also examining transactions made in the former president’s son’s name between 2001 and 2019. The investigation covers money transfers totalling around 144 billion drams (more than $397 million at the current exchange rate), $309 million, €77 million and 18 million Russian roubles during that period. It also covers the acquisition of more than three dozen properties in Armenia and abroad.

The same investigation has also opened criminal cases against nine other people. They include former Defence Minister Serzh Sargsyan, former Prime Minister Andranik Margaryan and former Yerevan Mayor Gagik Beglaryan.

In addition, the Prosecutor General’s Office has brought criminal cases against current and former directors of several local companies linked to Kocharyan. Authorities accuse them of failing to pay taxes on a particularly large scale. The total unpaid tax bill amounts to around 2.567 billion drams (more than $7 million).

Context

Opposition figures say Kocharyan’s arrest was politically motivated. They argue that the law-enforcement system is acting at the whim of a single person – the prime minister.

They also point to the heated parliamentary exchange between Nikol Pashinyan and Kocharyan’s son, Levon Kocharyan, an MP from the Armenia faction, which preceded Robert Kocharyan’s arrest.

“If the country’s prime minister says that this or that person should be sent to prison, or that this or that person should have their property confiscated, that is a political order. It is abnormal and goes against European standards, democracy and everything you fought for,” Kocharyan told Pashinyan.

The prime minister replied:

“Explain why you are a millionaire. Where did you get this property? And are you saying that you should remain a millionaire in Armenia? Are you saying that your millions should pass to your children and then from your children to their children? I’m sorry, but I’m telling you directly: that will not happen. For me, this is not a personal issue but a political one.”

Pashinyan said he had pledged to return to the people, “piece by piece”, all property that had been illegally plundered.

“In a democratic country, the court, not the country’s leader, should decide what should be returned to whom,” Levon Kocharyan replied.

Later, speaking to journalists, Pashinyan returned to the issue. He said that if Armenian citizens considered the government’s actions unlawful, they could stage a revolution.

“Let them remove us from power through a revolution. Let them bring their beloved and most honourable Robert Kocharyan, [former president] Serzh Sargsyan, [Russian businessman under house arrest on charges of calling for the seizure of power] Samvel Karapetyan, [major businessman arrested on charges of fraud, money laundering and extortion] Gagik Tsarukyan into government buildings. Let them take us to Republic Square and hang us. I’m fine with that scenario. If that is what they want, the people’s decision is not open to discussion for me,” the prime minister said.

Former president Robert Kocharyan’s team on his arrest

World.title: 1,795 applicants in Georgia to get second chance to enrol
World.content:
University admissions in Georgia in 2026

A total of 1,795 applicants in Georgia who passed the minimum threshold in the Unified National Examinations but failed to secure a place at a university will be given a second chance to enrol.

This year, the number of applicants who passed the minimum threshold but were unable to gain admission to a university increased 2.5 times compared with the previous year.

Education Minister Givi Mikanadze announced the decision, saying it had been made as a one-off exception this year because it is the first year of the higher education reform introduced by the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Mikanadze said that registration for vacant places at public and private higher and vocational education institutions would open in the first half of September for applicants who had not previously secured a university place.

“As we have embarked on nationwide higher education reform, and this year is something of a transitional period, we are making an exception. Only this year, at the initiative of Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, we are giving 1,795 applicants who passed the minimum competency threshold in the Unified National Examinations the opportunity for so-called second-round admission,” Mikanadze said.

The Georgian government has radically changed the higher education system. Under the new reform, admission to public universities is organised around strict specialisation, with specific academic fields assigned to individual cities and universities.

The authorities say the measures are aimed at aligning the education system with labour market needs and concentrating resources. However, the changes have already raised questions about academic freedom, regional development and university autonomy.

More on the higher education reform can be found here.

World.title: Salaries rise 7% while house prices climb 12.4%: Is it worth buying home in Azerbaijan?
World.content:
Buying a home in Azerbaijan

The average price of a 65-square-metre flat in Baku is now around 178,000 manats (about $105,000). Someone earning the country’s average monthly salary of 1,174 manats (about $690) would have to save their entire income for 12 and a half years to afford it. But once the cost of food, rent, transport and other everyday expenses is taken into account, this calculation is purely theoretical.

According to an August review by the Central Bank, house prices rose by 8.6% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026. Prices for newly built homes increased by 12.4%, while those on the secondary market rose by 8.6%. Rents increased by 7.4%. Over the same period, average nominal wages rose by 7%.

Wage growth is failing to keep pace with house prices

In Azerbaijan, the average nominal wage rose by 7% over the year, or about 77 manats (around $45), reaching 1,174.4 manats. At the same time, prices for newly built homes increased by 12.4%. This means new homes became 5.4 percentage points more expensive than the rate at which average wages increased.

The gap shows that housing affordability for potential buyers has not improved. The rise in wages increased a worker’s annual pre-tax income by around 920 manats (about $541). Meanwhile, a 12.4% increase in house prices means that a flat costing 170,000–180,000 manats would have become roughly 19,000–20,000 manats (about $11,200–11,700) more expensive over the year.

It should also be noted that 1,174 manats is the average nominal wage across the economy as a whole. The figure is calculated before taxes and social contributions and does not reflect the actual income of most workers.

How many years would it take to buy a 65-square-metre flat?

The m2map platform, which analysed more than 82,000 active listings in August, estimated the median asking price in Baku at 2,735 manats (about $1,609) per square metre. At that price, a 65-square-metre flat would cost 177,775 manats.

According to July data from the Azerbaijan Chamber of Appraisers, the median price per square metre for newly built homes was 2,812.5 manats (about $1,655), compared with 2,616.7 manats (about $1,540) on the secondary market. This puts the price of a flat of this size at roughly 170,000 to 183,000 manats (about $100,000–108,000), depending on the segment.

At the national average monthly wage of 1,174.4 manats, 177,775 manats is slightly more than 12 and a half years of a worker’s total earnings. Using Baku’s average wage of 1,487 manats (about $875), the period falls to around 10 years. But this is only a theoretical calculation, assuming a person spends none of their salary on anything else. In reality, someone on an average income would need considerably longer to save the full price of a flat.

If a buyer can save 20% of their salary, it would take around 50 years to accumulate the full cost of the property. To save the down payment required under a standard mortgage, which in this case would be around 28,000 manats (about $16,500), would take almost eight years.

The average wage also does not reflect the incomes of all workers. According to data from the State Statistics Committee, during the first five months of the year, average monthly wages were 763 manats (about $449) in retail, 825 manats (about $485) in education, and 800 manats (about $470.50) in tourism and catering. For workers in these sectors, a mid-range flat in Baku is equivalent to around 18–19 years of their combined earnings.

Does a mortgage make housing more affordable – or more expensive?

The maximum amount available under a standard mortgage from the Mortgage and Credit Guarantee Fund is 150,000 manats (about $88,235), with a loan term of up to 25 years, an annual interest rate of 8% and a minimum down payment of 15%. However, 85% of the 177,775-manat price of the flat exceeds the loan limit, meaning the buyer would have to provide at least 27,775 manats from their own funds.

If the remaining 150,000 manats were borrowed for 25 years at 8% interest, the monthly payment would be around 1,158 manats (about $681.20). Over the full term, the borrower would repay more than 347,000 manats (about $204,000) to the bank. Including the down payment, the total cost would exceed 375,000 manats (about $220,600). Insurance, property valuation, notary fees and other associated costs are not included.

A monthly payment of 1,158 manats is almost equal to the average salary across the country and represents 78% of the average salary in Baku. Under the Fund’s rules, mortgage payments must not exceed 70% of borrowers’ combined income after tax. This means that a Baku resident earning a single average salary would find it practically impossible to service such a mortgage alone.

In a household where two people earn the average Baku salary, the monthly mortgage payment would account for 39% of their combined nominal income. After tax, the share would exceed 40%. According to OECD and Eurostat methodology, housing costs exceeding 40% of disposable income are considered an excessive housing burden.

Under the subsidised mortgage scheme, the annual interest rate is 4%, the loan term can be up to 30 years, and the maximum loan amount is 100,000 manats (about $58,820). Although the monthly payment would be around 477 manats (about $280.60), buying a 65-square-metre flat at Baku’s average price would require around 78,000 manats (about $45,882) in the buyer’s own funds. The lower interest rate therefore does not solve the main problem for families without substantial savings.

Is renting cheaper?

The median advertised rent in Baku is 11 manats (about $6.50) per square metre per month. Renting a 65-square-metre flat would therefore cost around 715 manats (about $420.60) a month – 443 manats (about $260.60) less than the monthly payment on a standard mortgage. However, this still amounts to around 48% of the average salary in Baku, excluding utility bills.

If an investor bought such a flat for 178,000 manats and rented it out for 715 manats a month, the gross annual rental yield would be around 4.8%. After accounting for maintenance, periods when the property is vacant and other associated costs, the actual return would be even lower. Buying a flat with a mortgage and then renting it out therefore generally does not allow the owner to cover the full cost through rental income alone. The model may make sense primarily for investors with substantial capital who are betting on further increases in property prices.

What is driving prices higher?

The Chamber of Appraisers attributes the rise in new-build prices to strong demand in the mid-to-upper and premium segments, the availability of mortgage financing and the perception of housing as an investment asset. The Chamber’s land price index also points to rising prices and limited supply in premium areas. This may put additional pressure on the cost of newly built homes.

At the same time, according to the State Statistics Committee, investment in residential construction fell by 2.7% in real terms in the first half of the year. These figures strengthen the suggestion that demand, growing faster than household incomes, is running up against limited supply.

State-backed mortgages make housing more affordable for some families: in the first half of the year, 2,242 families received mortgage loans worth a total of 226.3 million manats (about $133.1 million). Since 2019, just over 10,000 families have used the rent-to-own scheme. However, it remains unclear whether these programmes are large enough to curb the overall rise in property prices.

Buying a home in Baku today is therefore more affordable for a household with two stable official incomes, substantial savings for a down payment or another property that can be sold than for someone living on a single average salary. Those who qualify for subsidised mortgages and have tens of thousands of manats in savings are also in a stronger position.

For everyone else, the choice is essentially between increasingly expensive rent and taking on long-term, substantial debt.

Buying a home in Azerbaijan

World.title: ‘Occupation is off’: Russian state media RIA Novosti on Georgian PM Kobakhidze’s remarks
World.content:
RIA Novosti on Russia-Georgia relations

Russia’s state-run news agency RIA Novosti has responded to remarks by Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, saying that Tbilisi had decided to reassess the history of its relations with Moscow.

The article, published on 24 August 2026 under the headline “Occupation is off”: Another country refuses to consider Russia an enemy, focused on Kobakhidze’s remarks about the Treaty of Georgievsk.

Background

On 18 August 2026, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said that Georgia’s decision to sign the Treaty of Georgievsk had been a “civilisational choice”.

His main argument was that King Erekle II’s decision ultimately ensured the physical and political survival of the Georgian nation. According to Kobakhidze, Christian Georgia, surrounded by Muslim states, chose to align itself with Orthodox Russia.

Kobakhidze argued that the decision was not only justified but also “the only correct and only possible” choice at the time. He said Russia honoured the terms of the treaty during Erekle II’s lifetime:

“While Erekle II was alive, he ensured that the agreement was upheld to the end, and almost 20 years passed between the signing of the Treaty of Georgievsk and the annexation of Georgia. For two decades, our country effectively survived.”

The Treaty of Georgievsk was an agreement between the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and the Russian Empire, signed on 24 July 1783. Under the treaty, King Erekle II accepted the protection of Russian Empress Catherine II, while Russia pledged to defend the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and preserve its territorial integrity. The treaty formally preserved the internal independence of the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and did not declare it part of the Russian Empire. However, in 1801, the Russian Empire abolished the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti and incorporated it into its territory.

What RIA Novosti says in its article

The Russian state-run news agency says Kobakhidze presented Georgia’s decision to accept the Russian Empire’s protection as the only way for the Georgian people to survive Ottoman and Persian aggression.

The article quotes the views of several political experts, including Nino Skvortsova, whom the agency describes as a “Tbilisi-based political analyst”.

According to Skvortsova, Kobakhidze’s focus on the reign of Erekle II serves not only to reinterpret history but also to justify the government’s current policies.

“Kobakhidze is trying to place Erekle II back in his historical context. For him, the king is important as a ruler forced to choose between major powers while his country’s existence was under threat,” the expert says.

In her view, this approach allows parallels to be drawn with the current policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party:

“Modern Georgia is also caught in competition between major powers, while the authorities justify their actions by the need to preserve peace, sovereignty, traditional identity and freedom of foreign policy manoeuvre.”

RIA Novosti also quotes another expert, Artur Ataev, who says that Georgian Dream is trying to raise a new generation free from old stereotypes. Ataev argues that the opposition, in turn, wants Georgia to follow the example of Ukraine, the Baltic states and other former Soviet republics.

“Today, this is one of the main topics of debate in Georgian society. There are even calls to recognise the independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia,” Ataev says.

He argues that Georgian society and the political elite are gradually changing, but that the restoration of diplomatic relations with Russia is unlikely in the near future.

“After all, most Georgians still see Russia as an occupier,” the expert concludes.

World.title: Kyrgyz, Russian presidents discuss strategic partnership and bilateral ties
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 1. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, who arrived in Kyrgyzstan on a working visit.

This was reported in a statement by the Kyrgyz Presidential Administration.

The parties reportedly discussed current issues of Kyrgyz-Russian cooperation in the political, trade, economic, energy, and humanitarian spheres.

At the beginning of the meeting, President Sadyr Japarov noted the strategic nature of Kyrgyz-Russian relations and the high level of cooperation between the two countries.

"Our bilateral relations have a solid foundation and are strategic in nature. We attach great importance to the high level of cooperation achieved with the Russian Federation and are committed to further strengthening and expanding practical cooperation," the Head of State said.

Sadyr Japarov thanked President Vladimir Putin for his participation in the Bishkek SCO Summit and his support for Kyrgyzstan's priorities during its chairmanship of the Organization.

In turn, Vladimir Putin noted Kyrgyzstan's extensive work in preparing and hosting the SCO summit, emphasizing the achievements of the country's chairmanship.

"During Kyrgyzstan's chairmanship, with your direct participation, important decisions were reached on the further development and strengthening of the Organization. Following the summit, a number of key documents were approved, including the Bishkek Declaration and the Protocol to the SCO Charter," the Russian President noted.

During the meeting, the parties also discussed a wide range of bilateral cooperation issues, noting the positive dynamics of interaction in trade, economics, investment, energy, humanitarian affairs, and other areas.

Particular attention was paid to the further development of interregional ties, the implementation of joint economic projects, as well as cooperation in education and support of the Russian language.

Vladimir Putin emphasized that the Kyrgyz-Russian strategic partnership and alliance are successfully developing based on traditions of friendship, mutual respect, and consideration of each other's interests.

"We are personally monitoring the key issues of bilateral cooperation and are committed to further consistently developing our collaboration," the Russian President said.

At the end of the meeting, President Sadyr Japarov presented Alexey Likhachev, Director General of the Rosatom State Corporation, with the Order of Dostuk, a state award of the Kyrgyz Republic, for his significant contribution to the development of Kyrgyz-Russian cooperation.
