World.title: Ferrari's Schumacher-inspired livery, F1 leader to cop penalty in Italy
World.content:
Ferrari will be celebrating the legacy of Michael Schumacher this weekend at its home race, with a special livery dedicated to the seven-time Formula 1 world champion.

This year marks 30 years since Schumacher joined the Scuderia, and 20 years since his final F1 victory in the 2006 Chinese Grand Prix.

Piastri searching for answers as teammate re-enters F1 title picture Oscar Piastri's "disappointing" end to the Dutch Grand Prix leaves the Australian and his McLaren team searching for answers, while his teammate has roared back into the Formula 1 title picture.

With Schumacher at the wheel, Ferrari rose to the top of F1 after years spent without championships.

Ferrari's constructors' championship win in 1999 ended a 16-year wait in the teams' competition, while Schumacher's drivers' championship triumph in 2000 made him the first Ferrari race to become world champion since Jody Scheckter in 1979.

Schumacher won five of his seven drivers' championships with Ferrari, from 2000-2004.

This weekend at the Italian Grand Prix in Monza, a race Schumacher won five times with Ferrari, the Scuderia has a one-off livery which pays tribute to the F1 champion.

Among the features are seven stars on the nose of the car, representing Schumacher's world titles, and drivers Lewis Hamilton — the sport's other seven-time world champion — and Charles Leclerc will wear racing suits that also feature the seven stars and Schumacher's logo.

F1 championship leader to take grid penalty at Monza

Kimi Antonelli has celebrated his 20th birthday as the Formula 1 drivers' championship leader, and heads into his home grand prix with a significant 59-point advantage over his two nearest rivals.

F1 drivers' championship leader Kimi Antonelli is set to start the Italian Grand Prix from the back of the grid. (Reiters: Benoit Tessier)

But the youngest-ever leader of the F1 championship heads into this weekend's race at Monza knowing he has work to do to be near the front of the grid.

Mercedes announced during the previous race weekend in the Netherlands that Antonelli will take an engine penalty this weekend.

F1 teams have an allocation of power unit components they can use in a season. When a driver is fitted with a power unit component that exceeds the allocation, they are handed a penalty at the first event that new part is used.

Mercedes has had multiple power unit issues this year, with Antonelli failing to finish in Barcelona and teammate George Russell suffering issues in Canada and Belgium.

Despite the Italian Grand Prix being Antonelli's home race, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff said now was the right time to do it for the championship leader.

"Our calculations say that that's the best track to take it," Wolff said.

"Obviously, algorithms don't take their nationality into consideration. We're here to fight for a championship and not get the most PR. So yeah, that's what we're going to do."

Monza, known as the Temple of Speed, is expected to be a strong track for Mercedes, which is likely why it is taking the penalty now.

With long straights, there should be plenty of opportunities for Antonelli to pass with his impressive Mercedes power unit.

Monza has been the scene of impressive drives through the field in recent years.

Pierre Gasly won from 10th on the grid driving for AlphaTauri (now Racing Bulls). Max Verstappen won in 2022 after taking a five-place grid penalty, while Lewis Hamilton charged from the last row on the grid to place fifth.

Last year, Isack Hadjar started in the pit lane for Racing Bulls and was able to finish 10th.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Formula 1 Italian Grand Prix from 9pm AEST on Sunday, September 6.

World.title: 'Meteorwrongs' and murder at sea: Meet the next generation of Australian artists
World.content:
Who decides what is remembered? What happens to the objects and stories consigned to history's rubbish bin? Can we ever truly understand or recapture the past?

These are some of the questions the artists showcased in this year's Primavera exhibition, which features Australian artists aged 35 or younger, are wrestling with.

Exhibition curator Antares Wells travelled to dozens of studios and galleries in every state and territory to find the most compelling emerging artists, finding many were interested in working with archives, or records of the past.

"When you visit that many artists, five different exhibitions could come out of that," she tells ABC Arts.

"But I identified a preoccupation with what I've called traces; an interest in the relics of the past, picking them up and making something new with them.

"I think it's an eternal theme, but what [the artists in Primavera] are doing with it is distinctive."

Now in it's 34th year, dozens of Australian artists have been highlighted by Primavera. (Supplied: Jessica Maurer)

The six artists featured this year in Primavera approach the theme from different angles, but there's a through-line of the idea of value; why we discard or overlook things.

Wells says it's an exhibition for the head and the heart.

"It's not a cold, big, bad archive — there's a human heart beating in all of these works, even the ones that seem very sleek and detached," she says.

"I hope [visitors] take away a sense of the intellectual and aesthetic vitality of work in this country, the sheer range and diversity of that work, but also the richness of human stories around us."

Murder at sea and suppressed queer history

Callum McGrath's work, History Piece, examines a queer love triangle which ended in the stabbing murder of 19-year-old stoker John "Jack" Joseph Riley on naval ship HMAS Australia II in 1942. The incident sparked complex and often opaque legal proceedings.

The Naarm/Melbourne based artist has often explored queer history in his work, though this thread of the story was initially suppressed by the authorities dealing with the murder.

"The homosexual element really comes out of a confession that the victim made to the surgeon while he was being treated for stab wounds before he died," McGrath says.

"That [confession] letter was left out of the court proceedings, so that bit was a bit difficult, but I found a copy of it in the archives eventually," McGrath says.

"The fact that the letter was left out of the court hearings on the boat, I think, speaks volumes."

Callum McGrath's History Piece delves into a love story with a grisly ending. (Supplied: Callum McGrath)

McGrath recasts the story as a complex intersection of queer history, power and politics. His multimedia often uses overlapping layers of images and text to produce a work that resists easy interpretation.

"It's accumulative and exhaustive," McGrath says of History Piece.

"Rather than having something concise, the idea was to present the evidence as this accumulation of stuff."

McGrath's magpie approach includes a series of line drawings he did of the key people involved in the case. He created images from original photos using digital software, etched them onto glass with a computer-driven cutting tool and in-filled the etching marks with ink.

McGrath says he liked the allusive properties of creating portraits on glass.

"In my mind, glass is a visual storage device. The [portraits] are meant to be physical objects of history containing data and information. It's a way of engraving history on these objects that could be reused."

Weaving history and family connection together

In Linda Sok's Deities in Temples XXI, a sacred art form almost extinguished by the Khmer Rouge regime is both revived and reinvented.

When the regime seized power in 1975, they set about destroying religious or pre-revolutionary artefacts, including pidans, a traditional form of Cambodian silk weaving that people usually hung from the ceiling of a temple.

Linda Sok delves into her family history via screen printing. (Supplied: Eloise Cato)

Often, the only record of the lost pidans was archival cards stored in the National Museum of Cambodia.

Sok, now based in the USA, found recreating these lost treasures helped her reconnect her with her family and Cambodian heritage. She shared the archival card descriptions with her family, who then drew what they thought each lost pidan looked like.

"I'd moved to the US and was feeling far away from them," she says.

"I had to overcome their hesitancy, but when they began doing the drawings and sketches, they became more open to it."

Rather than using the intricate traditional weaving technique, which can take years to learn, let alone master, Sok devised her own method.

She would pull a group of threads tight, screen-print the images her family had created onto the threads, and then add painted elements.

"Screen-printing was my way of paying homage to the practice without actually replicating it, and putting my own spin on it as well," she says.

Recreating the pidans led Sok to reflect on how our record of the past is always fragmented and imperfect.

One of the images her family created featured a tree front and centre despite the official record of that pidan, created by French archivists, not mentioning any trees.

"When I went back to Cambodia, I noticed how prevalent the imagery [of trees] was throughout Buddhist iconography, so it was interesting that they chose to reintroduce it," she says.

"Maybe the archivists had thought the tree wasn't important to include, so it got left out.

"There's no way of telling what exactly the truth of the matter is, but it's an interesting question that I've been thinking about a lot."

Meteorites and 'meteorwrongs'

Sometimes, a member of the public believes they've found a meteorite, an exotic item that has travelled to Earth from outer space.

Then they send the item to their local science museum, only to be told it's just a regular rock or a lump of industrial debris.

These items are sometimes called 'meteorwrongs', and they're the focus of Meteorite Enquiries, a gently funny and melancholy work by Boorloo/Perth-based artist Jack Wansbrough.

"They're essentially waste, but there's still all this life and personality in them," Wansbrough says of the objects.

Jack Wansbrough's collection of ‘meteorwrongs’. (Supplied: Jessica Maurer)

Working from an archive cataloguing a museum's correspondence on 'meteorwrongs', Wansbrough sought to recreate (or find) substitute objects for each oddity and give these rejected items their moment in the sun.

He then displayed the objects on a low floor bed alongside the archive's yellowing letters and beneath a pair of stained-glass fixtures he made.

Wansbrough spent about six months making and sourcing the objects, combing crystal shops, industrial estates, roadsides and even the car park of a university geology department to find what he was after.

Artist's dazzling terracotta earrings celebrate Indian heritage Monica Rani Rudhar's embellished gold earrings are more than just accessories — they are cultural markers connecting her to family.

"Sometimes, I was looking at photos and a piece I literally found on the ground was almost a perfect match. That was really exciting," Wansbrough says.

"But sometimes, the descriptions are extremely brief, which can make it harder but also easier, in a way. Some letters would just say 'A rock that's been carved', so that gave me an interpretive freedom to carve anything I want."

While the rocks and debris Wansbrough's installation recreates may not be of scientific interest, each has its own idiosyncratic human story.

"With my work, I'm often pointing away from myself, towards an archive or something external. I find it's an interesting way to work in that you're always looking at this thing in front of you, but also imagining this thing that you can't see."

Primavera 2026: Young Australian Artists runs until September 28 at the Museum of Contemporary Art Australia in Sydney.

World.title: Breaking: AFP raid Melbourne home of former CFMEU official
World.content:
Australian Federal Police officers have raided the home of a former senior official of the militant construction union as part of their probe into corruption in Victoria's building industry.

At least half a dozen officers and a sniffer dog arrived at former CFMEU official John Perkovic's Keilor home in Melbourne's northern suburbs early this morning.

Police could be seen searching items in the house's backyard and under a black Range Rover SUV parked in the driveway.

Mr Perkovic left the house a short time later.

John Perkovic gestures while exiting his Melbourne home during the AFP raid. (ABC News: Jess Longbottom)

Mr Perkovic was a CFMEU organiser for more than a decade in the union's Victorian branch when it was led by John Setka.

He was promoted to second in charge after the union was placed under administration in 2024, amid accusations of widespread wrongdoing.

However, he was dismissed in October 2025 after allegations of corruption against him were exposed in the media.

Mr Perkovic’s Keilor property is at the centre of the alleged wrongdoing, which has since been detailed in a report by anti-corruption barrister Geoffrey Watson submitted to Queensland's Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU.

Home and vintage cars highlighted by CFMEU inquiry

Mr Watson alleged Perkovic netted at least $1 million from corrupt property transactions involving the block of land when he worked for the CFMEU.

His house was built by a business that was getting benefits from Mr Perkovic, Mr Watson alleged, while Mr Perkovic was unable to say how much the building cost, or how the works were financed.

Former CFMEU organiser John Perkovic. (CFMEU)

The block at the back of the home was purchased by another contractor in 2020 who was allegedly benefiting from Mr Perkovic.

The land was transferred to Mr Perkovic's daughter in 2024, free of charge, according to the Watson report.

Mr Watson alleged Mr Perkovic benefited from other companies as well — getting his home insurance paid for by a labour hire firm, and also owning three cars that had been paid for by construction companies.

One was a vintage Ford Falcon GT worth more than $100,000.

Mr Watson said Mr Perkovic was high up in the informal power structure of the CFMEU, holding a position of influence just below that of Mr Setka.

World.title: Amateur drone pilots put races and aircraft at risk, authorities say
World.content:
The galloping of camels, then the unmistakable buzzing of a drone.

Photographer Ann Britton inadvertently captured a small quadcopter filming the action up close at the Winton Camel Races in Western Queensland in July.

An unpermitted drone gets an aerial view of a camel race in Winton. (Supplied: Ann Britton)

"It actually followed the camels down the track," she said.

"The drone was basically there at the same level as the crowd. And I'm like, 'Oh, that is so cheeky.'"

Race organisers, unsure of who was at the controls, requested three times over the PA that the drone land.

Ms Britton had planned to fly her own drone from a safer distance and with permission but decided to keep it grounded during the search for the unsanctioned pilot in the grandstand, worried about the risk of collision.

Ann Britton had to take formal training to become commercially certified as a drone pilot. (Supplied )

"I've done the hard yards and I've got my commercial licence. I find it a privilege that I can fly that drone, capture these moments," she said.

"It's not a toy."

A pattern of rogue drone sightings has raised concerns about the potential for a serious accident.

The Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) has reiterated the safety risks and penalties that come with disobeying the rules.

Drone flies too close to chopper

Kate de Koning is frustrated after multiple encounters with dangerously piloted drones. (Supplied: Elite Aviation Services/Kelly Edwards)

Winton-based helicopter tour pilot Kate de Koning said she was happy to liaise with drone pilots at events, but those who did not communicate or follow the rules made her uneasy.

While she set up her gazebo at this year's Boulia Camel Races, an unidentified drone flew near her face.

But that paled in comparison to a potential catastrophe at last year's event.

Drones must not be flown when a crewed aircraft is nearby or within 5.5 kilometres of a controlled airport. (Supplied: Elite Aviation Services/Kelly Edwards)

Landing her helicopter after one tour, Ms de Koning happened to look up and see a drone a couple of metres above her spinning blades.

"I saw red instantly," she said.

"That just meant that they were definitely flying around while I was coming in to land, which made me so nervous."

Her helicopter tour takes off and lands many times each day near the racecourse.

"I was shutting down at that point in time, but they didn't know that," Ms de Koning said.

Race organiser Beck Britton said there was a zero-drone rule for patrons, but it was difficult to enforce.

"I suppose it's one of those really, really difficult situations because human nature, if you see a drone being used, most people are going to assume that, 'OK, well, they're using a drone, I can use a drone.'"

Organiser Beck Britton (right) says it can be difficult to enforce recreational drone bans across large event grounds. (Supplied: Elite Aviation Services/Kelly Edwards)

Ms Britton said organisers would consider how to more clearly communicate the policy.

"If you want to go fly a drone, head a couple of [kilometres] down the road. You've got wide open spaces everywhere," she said.

Known as the 'Melbourne Cup of camel racing', Boulia Camel Races is a popular photo opportunity. (Supplied: Boulia Camel Races/Matt Williams)

Authority issues warning to overeager pilots

All drone pilots must follow national rules, whether or not they have gone through formal training.

"If you have a recreational drone, which is several million people these days, you really cannot fly out over gatherings of people," CASA spokesperson Steve Creedy said.

" That runs from rock concerts to camel races. You shouldn't even take your drone to the event. "

Properly licensed operators are the exception.

"If you see a drone over an event, it could be a commercial drone that has an approval, so not every drone is necessarily a bad thing. But recreational drones, absolutely not," Mr Creedy said.

Recreational pilots do not need a license to fly drones recreationally but must follow CASA rules. (ABC News: Norman Hermant)

He said users needed to be aware of other aircraft, even when outside the range of controlled airports.

"If you become aware of a crewed aircraft nearby, you have to move away and land your drone as quickly as you can and as safely as you can," Mr Creedy said.

There are no age or licence requirements to use small drones, but pilots are expected to be familiar with CASA rules before flying.

Drones risk emergency responses

Acting Superintendent Cameron Herbert said the Queensland Fire Department occasionally saw drones fly into emergency-incident areas or found aerial footage uploaded to social media afterwards.

"[That] enables us to at least investigate that and try and make these operators aware that, during an emergency incident, we need clear airspace, particularly with bushfire season coming up," he said.

FBI investigates drone that collided with aircraft fighting LA wildfires The FBI is searching for the owner of an unauthorised drone that crashed into a firefighting aircraft in Los Angeles last week.

He said drones not only risked the safety of crewed aircraft but forced them to land, potentially delaying life-saving operations.

"We just would request that all amateur drone operators just stay away from emergency services incidents, whether it be a large bushfire or smaller incidents around structure fires, even road traffic crashes," he said.

World.title: Bledisloe Cup quadruple-header announced as sevens added to ticket
World.content:
Australia's sevens teams will share the stage in a scheduling first, with the Wallabies and Wallaroos creating a Bledisloe Cup quadruple-header in Sydney.

The Stadium Australia Test against the All Blacks on October 17 already had a support act secured, with the Wallaroos due to host Scotland for the first time in their WXV Global Series clash.

Kick-off times for Bledisloe Cup in Sydney Wallaroos v Scotland, 12pm

Australian sevens men v Fiji, 2:05pm

Australian sevens women v New Zealand, 2.25pm

Wallabies v New Zealand, 3:45pm All times in AEDT

Now two more fixtures will be added to the ticket, with Australia's world champion sevens women to face rivals New Zealand and the men up against two-time Olympic gold medallists Fiji.

"This is an historic moment for Australian rugby, with all four of our Teams In Gold competing on the same pitch, on the same day, on an unmissable occasion," Rugby Australia chief executive Phil Waugh told AAP.

"The day will showcase the very best of rugby with our elite male and female players across the XVs and Sevens formats taking on famous rivals from around the world in an unprecedented line-up of international rugby.

"We look forward to celebrating this extraordinary occasion with our great Australian rugby community and we thank our friends from New Zealand Rugby, Fiji Rugby Union and Scottish Rugby for helping make this day a reality."

The Wallaroos will begin the action before the men's and women's sevens outfits take the field, followed by the Wallabies, who will complete the four-course menu with a late afternoon kick-off at the venue set to host next year's World Cup final.

AAP

World.title: Search underway for NSW hiker missing at Mount Remarkable National Park
World.content:
A 66-year-old New South Wales woman is missing at Mount Remarkable National Park in South Australia.

The woman failed to return from a hike yesterday, prompting a late-night search by PolAir and local crews.

A renewed search is commencing this morning, with police patrols, Mounted Operations and about 20 SES volunteers.

The woman, who police described as an experienced hiker, was walking with her friend yesterday afternoon.

Superintendent Paul Isherwood said the friend decided to return to town about 4pm, leaving the 66-year-old to climb the summit alone.

SES North duty officer Ben Birbeck said volunteers were dealing with wet conditions.

"We've had a long wet period in the region, so there's a bit of dampness and water in the area," he said.

Mr Birbeck said crews were searching by foot, drone and on motorbikes and utility terrain vehicles (UTVs).

The popular hiking spot in South Australia's Mid North region is about 250 to 290 kilometres north of Adelaide.

More to come.

World.title: Hidden in an attic for decades, rare photos shed new light on Pilbara strike camps
World.content:
The glint in Captain Wilson's eye softens as he looks at the decades-old image.

Warning: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains images and names of people who have died.

Two men frozen in time on a sun-hardened desert landscape.

The Nyamal elder recognises the one on the left. It is him, with a solemn expression and arms set like stone for the task at hand.

But it is his companion who seizes his attention.

"He was my friend," he said.

Nyamal elder Captain Wilson (left) circa 1959 at Gorge Creek camp near Marble Bar, lifting an air compressor. (Supplied: John Wilson/UWA)

The photograph is one of dozens recently uncovered in an attic more than 1,500 kilometres away from Mr Wilson's Roebourne nursing home.

Taken around WA's Pilbara region by an anthropologist during the 1950s and 60s, they tell the story of what one professor called "a revolutionary communist movement … on the very margins of Australian society".

Two decades before the famed Wave Hill walk-offs, the 1946 Pilbara strike and ensuing struggles helped launch the Indigenous rights movement.

Forgotten chapter revealed

The snapshots are being displayed for the first time at the University of Western Australia's Lawrence Wilson Art Gallery in Perth.

The Pilbara's Aboriginal people formed communities of their own, pursuing independence after walking off pastoral stations in 1946. (Supplied: John Wilson/UWA)

In 1946, hundreds of Aboriginal stockmen and women walked off the Pilbara's pastoral stations after years of poor wages and brutally unfair working conditions.

The workers had carved sheep-grazing country from the arid expanse and did so for little more than rations of tea, tobacco, or sugar.

Nyamal co-curator and Captain's daughter Ursula Wilson says the photos show "hard-working" Indigenous people. (ABC News: Dominic Briggs)

They resolved to protest, sparked by unprecedented organisation across language groups and launching a bitter rebellion that lasted three years.

"I've heard that Indigenous people are lazy people … looking at the pictures here, it shows that they are very hard-working people," Captain's daughter and exhibition co-curator said Ursula Wilson said.

" It was a tough time … and they endured a lot. "

Small-scale mining supported the strikers, still excluded from Australian society at the time. (Supplied: John Wilson/UWA)

Many refused to return to the stations. Instead, they formed mining cooperatives and pearl shell farms under the guidance of communist organiser Don McLeod.

The operations were some of the first of their kind in the now-industry-heavy Pilbara.

"It doesn't really fit into mainstream Australian history about the government suddenly awarding Aboriginal people their land back in the 1970s," said UWA art history professor Darren Jorgensen.

"These guys were really out there on their own … they were economically independent."

The minerals would be sorted using a yandy, or shallow dish. (Supplied: John Wilson/UWA)

Dr Jorgensen said the visual record was a remarkable find.

"We have no Australian prime ministers that visited these camps. They were hated by governments, they were hated by local pastoralists," he said.

"[This was] a revolutionary communist movement taking place on the very margins of Australian society, taking place far from the cities."

On par with Wave Hill

One photo in particular stood out to Mr Jorgensen.

"We all know the story of the Gurundji walk-off simply because of that one amazing Mervyn Bishop photograph of prime minister [Gough] Whitlam pouring sand into Vincent Lingiari's hands," Mr Jorgensen said.

"There's a couple of pictures here that have the same iconic value.

" One of them is of Captain Wilson about to lift an air compressor. "

Nyamal elder Captain Wilson, some seven decades after he was photographed in a Pilbara strike camp. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

The place of honour is not lost on Mr Wilson's other daughter, Sharon Coppin, who will accompany her father for the journey south to attend the exhibition's opening.

"Just knowing what he's been through … [it makes me] very emotional and proud," she said.

"Proud that he's come a long way."

Chance rediscovery

The original film slides were captured by John Wilson, a white anthropologist and no relation to Captain Wilson, in the wake of the strike.

John Wilson (left), pictured with Patrick Tuntiyan Henry, was also an amateur painter. (Supplied: Katrin Wilson/UWA)

"He was fascinated by the way they actually organised themselves with artisanal mining and shell camps … and made very close connections with people there," John's daughter Bu Wilson told the ABC.

It was her chance discovery of the photos in a box in the attic of her parents' Fremantle home that led to the photos seeing the light of day again.

"All of a sudden, I saw boxes under a wardrobe, and I went, 'I don't know what those are,'" she said.

"It was a whole pile more of the slides."

Bu Wilson rediscovered the images in her parents' attic. (ABC News: Dominic Briggs)

Contained in the tiny translucent squares were lean figures toiling in rusty red earth, cloudless blue skies stretching out above them.

Ms Wilson recognised the scenes immediately.

"My dad died five years ago, but I still feel that he's with me," she said.

"It's fantastic being able to share that body of work with other people."

Strike Camps: The Photographs of John Wilson opens at Lawrence Wilson Art Gallery on Wednesday, September 2.

World.title: This valley was the last known location of a Sydney family. Then a wave 100 metres high hit
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dunche, Nepal: High on a remote hilltop, Pasang Tamang bore stunned witness to a tidal wave, its body dark and dragging debris. It crashed through his village, Syabrubesi, the start of the famed Langtang Valley trek. It also is the last known location of an Australian family from Cherrybrook, in Sydney’s north-west. It was not a full hit at first, Tamang says. Much of the surge that had only just taken out villages further north actually flowed into a Trishuli River tributary adjacent to Syabrubesi, allowing some enough time to run. Pasang Tamang stands where he witnessed his home, Syabrubesi, being swept away by flash flooding in Nepal. Kate Geraghty Tamang saw them. But it soon surged back, slamming into the torrent from which it had come, shooting waves “at least” 100 metres into the air. “That’s when [Syabrubesi] was wiped out,” Tamang tells this masthead from the hill where he saw it happen. He’d been down there in Syabrubesi last Wednesday morning, too, but left shortly after 8.30 for the small village of Sano Bharkhu, a kilometre away, to check on some property. Unknown to anyone as he curled up those hair pin turns, a massive avalanche of glacier and rock was hurtling toward the river system at 150 metres per second near the Nepal-Tibet border.



According to relatives, it was also about this time – 8.40am to 8.50am – Sydney’s Sreedharan Iyer, 53, his wife Lakshmi, 49, and their two gifted sons, Rishab, 23, and Rudhra, 20, were checking out from the Royal Himalaya, a hotel on Syabrubesi’s lower section. The Hindu pilgrims were on a family trip of a lifetime with 11 other Australian friends to see Mount Kailash, the earthly abode of Lord Shiva. A photo with most of the group a day before the flood shows them beaming in matching blue T-shirts with mountain print from Himalayan Glacier, the tour company. The Iyer family, from left to right: Rudhra, 20; Sreedharan, 53; Lakshmi, 49; and Rishab, 23. The Iyers appeared in a tour group photo. smiling and wearing matching shirts, a day before the floods hit. None of the 15 have been heard from since Wednesday morning. More than 1050 people were killed – and some 4500 are still missing, including 38 Australians – when the floods hit Nepal and Tibet. The smack of two raging water courses came about 9am, Tamang says, sending buildings “rolling and rolling in the flood”. “After half an hour, everything was similar to what we see now,” he says. That is a silver silt pan, where a village once stood.



The vantage point of Sano Bharkhu offers clear views of a handful of buildings still standing in the upper section of Syabrubesi, and more are obscured by a mountain. But the entire lower half is gone, including Tamang’s home. Images circulating of the village post-flood suggests the Royal Himalaya is too. Most of Syabrubesi was swept away or buried. Kate Geraghty Where the Iyer family was at the time is unclear. They may have spent time in the village after check-out getting organised or sourcing coffees before getting in their car to be driven about 15 kilometres north to their friends at the doomed Hotel Kailash, which was swept away. If they had left immediately after check-out, they would have been roughly halfway between Syabrubesi and Timure on the road running directly alongside the soon-deadly Trishuli.



Timure was destroyed, too. That’s where Tamang’s nephew, Lama Sanam Tamang, 28, a husband and father, was killed. His five-year-old girl, Sonam Dolma, is being minded in Sano Bharkhu by her grieving grandfather, Maywan Tamang. She is playing with a soft drink bottle and scratching at the road with a stick. “We haven’t told her her father is dead,” the grandfather says. “She keeps asking where he is.” Maywan Tamang says his granddaughter Sonam doesn’t yet know her father was killed in the flooding. Kate Geraghty The road the pilgrims took between Dunche, the small capital of Rasuwa district, and Syabrubesi is destroyed from the point it crosses the Trishuli River. Upstream and downstream, the river’s bridges are gone, leaving survivors and residents of undamaged villages on the other side cut off from the main towns and the capital, Kathmandu. Nepal’s private fleet of helicopters have been commandeered for the rescue, aid and salvage efforts, but it is still not enough. A staging point in Dunche for helicopter rescues and distributing aid. Kate Geraghty



A temporary morgue has been set up on the outskirts of Dunche. Kate Geraghty At Dunche, helicopters fly in and out, laden with sacks of food and other supplies, in perpetual motion. “But people keep asking for more,” a rescuer says. Nepal has declined offers from other nations for search and rescue teams, ostensibly because the devastating 2015 earthquake proved it was too unwieldy. It has walked back the initial hardline, however, and is asking for specialised technical teams in matters like DNA testing and tunnel rescues. Close to 900 hydropower station workers remain trapped in various tunnels across the impact zone with uncertain access to oxygen, food and clean drinking water. Time is running out, if it hasn’t already. Destroyed buildings in Betrawoti. Kate Geraghty Body bags lay on the roof of a destroyed building in Betrawoti. Kate Geraghty The flood barrelled on through Syabrubesi to the town Betrawoti, about 40 kilometres south. Unable to make the sharp right turn in the river bed, it smashed into a mountain.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Number of Australians missing in Nepal, Tibet revised to 38; US launches major strikes against Iran
World.content:
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has revised the number of Australians missing in Nepal and Tibet down to 38, from 43 yesterday morning, as it says five additional Australians have been accounted for.

Of the five citizens confirmed safe, one was in Nepal, one in Tibet, and three were outside of the disaster zone.

Because the Australians had not been in contact with families or next of kin since the floods struck last week, their welfare could not be confirmed initially.

World.title: WA news LIVE: Man attacked, knocked unconscious by teens outside Perth fast food chain
World.content:
A man attacked by a group of teenage boys and pelted with a rock outside a Perth fast food restaurant is recovering at home as police continue to investigate the incident.

A man was attacked by a group of teenagers outside Red Rooster in Falcon on Monday.

Footage shows a 25-year-old man being approached by a group of teens outside Red Rooster in Falcon about 4.30pm on Monday.

The man was knocked unconscious and taunted by the children, before bystanders came to his aide and he was transported to hospital. He left the emergency department before he could be treated.

WA Police claimed the teens were not known to the man, and it’s unclear what sparked the altercation.

No charges have been laid, and inquiries remain ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Crime Stoppers.

World.title: Former CFMEU boss raided in alleged multimillion-dollar bribe probe
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaBuilding Bad Former CFMEU boss raided in alleged multimillion-dollar bribe probe Nick McKenzie September 2, 2026 — 9:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Federal police are raiding the home of former CFMEU boss John Perkovic over allegations he took up to $3 million in bribes from company bosses. No charges have been laid. Former CFMEU boss John Perkovic outside his home. On Wednesday morning, neighbours told The Age they observed officers searching a Hislop Street, Keilor property – which was allegedly developed by Perkovic with the help of company bosses he was meant to oversee as one of the CFMEU’s most powerful organisers. The allegations that Perkovic received inducements from company bosses were first exposed as part of The Age’s Building Bad series last year prompting Perkovic’s sacking from the union and sparking a federal police investigation.



Police have raided the home of former CFMEU boss John Perkovic. A person outside a neighbouring property told The Age early on Wednesday morning that they had seen a number of officers scouring Perkovic’s property. Perkovic was the leader of the so-called Croation faction within the union and his sacking was a major blow to the Labor-backed CFMEU administration, which only weeks earlier had promoted Perkovic to the role of deputy leader of the Victorian union branch. The raid of Perkovic comes after Victoria Police’s Taskforce Hawk charged two former CFMEU delegates Tyrone Bell and Joel Brown with alleged financial crimes connected to a business Bell started after he was sacked from the union in July 2024. Both Bell and Brown were former senior members of the Mongols outlaw motorcycle gang. Neighbours said federal police scoured the property.



John Setka outside the lunch venue where he met with Perkovic. The Age The raid of Perkovic’s home will send fresh shockwaves through the construction industry given his former power within the CFMEU and his close relationship with disgraced former union chief John Setka. In his Rotting from the Top report tabled in the Queensland commission of inquiry, Geoffrey Watson, SC, took aim at Perkovic as one of a number of corrupt leadership figures. “The problem with this was that these men were corrupt, known to be corrupt, and were promoted and protected by Setka,” he said. The raid took place on Wednesday morning.



Editor's pick Exclusive

Building Bad Top CFMEU figure sacked over construction company ‘bribes’ Last month, this masthead revealed that Setka had been seen dining with Perkovic at an upmarket seafood and steak restaurant along with an allegedly corrupt construction industry boss. Perkovic is accused of using his union power to promote certain building companies owned by bosses who provided him with undeclared benefits including land on the Hislop Street property and luxury vehicles, as well as loans. Perkovic has previously claimed that the cars he was provided were merely loaned to him and he intended to repay the building company bosses for the benefits they provided. The raid will once again turn the spotlight on Victorian Premier Ben Carroll’s promised royal commission led by former SA chief justice Chris Kourakis.



No charges have been laid. In the fortnight since Kourakis’ appointment there has been no news from the royal commission about who will work as counsel assisting the inquiry, the director of operations, instructing solicitors, investigators or when the first hearing will be called. More to come Explore our investigation

World.title: ‘It’s time to plant some roots’: O’Connor comes full circle at the Force
World.content:
SportRugby UnionJames O'Connor ‘It’s time to plant some roots’: O’Connor comes full circle at the Force Jonathan Drennan September 2, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

James O’Connor is back where it all began nearly two decades later. The 36-year-old playmaker has signed a one-year contract at the Western Force, returning to the club that announced him to the rugby world as a 17-year-old prodigy. Like fellow veteran Bernard Foley at the Waratahs, O’Connor returns to his former club not just to mentor the next generation but also to compete for a spot in the Wallabies squad for next year’s World Cup. James O’Connor is back to where his rugby career began, after signing a one-year deal with the Western Force. Western Force O’Connor left Perth due to a contract dispute with the Force in 2011, moving to Melbourne to play for the Rebels. The move proved ill-fated, and he found the high expectations on him too much to handle. As part of his return to the Force, O’Connor will also work as an attack coach for the club’s Super AUS team. If he were mentoring his younger self, what would he say?



“There’s nothing I could have stopped,” O’Connor said. “But what I would say to that young man is just know there’s someone there, if things go badly wrong or if something doesn’t go right or if you are in trouble, you come talk to me. I’m here. I’m not going to judge you. James O’Connor training in Sydney for the Force in 2009. Steve Christo “No matter how dark it gets or whatever happens, You’ve got someone you can come to and talk to and we’ll figure it out together.” O’Connor had his first official coaches meeting on Tuesday in Perth after arriving in the city last Saturday. He is expecting his first baby with his partner Bridget and has moved to Cottesloe Beach.



Despite being away from Perth for 15 years, it still feels like home. “It was the happiest time of my career (at the Force), it really was. It was because it was all new as well; I’d just started my career, but it was a magical time,” O’Connor said. James O’Connor in action during his return for the Wallabies against the Springboks at Ellis Park last year. AP “There’s been incredible times in my career, but I think that at the Force it was the most joyful I’ve been ... “If I look back chronologically, it was the worst move I’ve made for my happiness, my rugby, for everything, but I needed to make that move for me to be able to be the man I am today.”



Another perspective Australian rugby Tahs send SOS to club rugby playmaker amid ugly contract stoush At the Rebels, O’Connor was forced to take on game management roles he wasn’t equipped to handle. As a young player, he was blessed with speed and agility, but controlling a team was too much. “No one would know that I was managing that stress; you might think watching me on the field I didn’t have a care in the world,” he said. “But I could never fully be present during the week because I was worried about things like, ‘Have I done the work?’ Because maybe I hadn’t done the work and I knew my body wasn’t in the place where it needed to be.” After a season in Melbourne, O’Connor wanted to return to the Force. But an incident at Perth airport in September 2013 saw him stood down by the Wallabies. Australian Federal Police alleged he was intoxicated and not allowed to board a flight from Perth to Indonesia. O’Connor denied being drunk but admitted to engaging in a heated argument over seating arrangements.



O’Connor left Australia for London Irish in 2013 to play under the late Brian Smith, before stints with Toulon in France and Sale in England. “I felt like everyone was out to get me. Was I treated unfairly? It wasn’t unfair, but I definitely think that I had a target on my back,” O’Connor said. James O’Connor playing for London Irish in 2014. Getty Images “When that door was finally shut on me after the airport (incident), it was time to go explore Europe. “It was the best thing I ever did because I got out of the fishbowl. I got out of my own way and had to figure out who I was as a man, and that started my journey back to where I am now.”



Last year, O’Connor made a shock Wallabies return and helped Australia beat South Africa for the first time at Ellis Park in 62 years. He is determined to grow as a coach in Perth, but also remains driven by the lure of the home World Cup. “I’m preparing myself for next season (at the Force). One, my first child’s on the way and number two, I’ve just moved halfway around the world three times now,” O’Connor said. The Wallabies celebrate after their epic win at Ellis Park in 2025. AP “I’m going to be honest, I want to play in that World Cup. I’ve seen myself playing in it and I know I can add value. “If I stick to my guns and I make sure I’m disciplined and I put the work in and everything goes as planned, then great. I can see myself playing in there and adding a lot of value … but after next year, after the World Cup, I think that’ll be me (as a player).”



On Tuesday morning, O’Connor went for a swim with an old teammate and close friend Kurtley Beale. After playing last season in Leicester, O’Connor fielded offers from France, Japan and South Africa, but with a baby on the way, O’Connor knew it was time to come home. “It’s time to plant some roots,” he said. “As soon as I found out that my wife was pregnant, it was like, okay, this all makes sense now ... everything just became irrelevant. This is where I want to be. I want to be close to family. I want to be in Australia. This feels right for us.”

World.title: 11 deals, $100m spent: Was this the Socceroos’ best-ever post-World Cup window?
World.content:
Analysis SportSoccerAustralian soccer 11 deals, $100m spent: Was this the Socceroos’ best-ever post-World Cup window? Vince Rugari September 2, 2026 — 8:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There was a time when the World Cup was considered soccer’s ultimate shop window; when a single performance or two in the global spotlight was enough for a player to catch the eye of a top club and earn an opportunity they otherwise wouldn’t have gotten. It doesn’t quite work like that any more. Too many clubs have been burnt over the years by vanity deals for players who looked good for those few weeks, but didn’t quite fit once they’d settled into their new surrounds. These days, recruitment departments have access to so much data, intel and footage that there are no longer any major surprises to discover. Loading But for Australian players who operate on the fringes of those scouting radars, there is still something to be gained from a good World Cup. It can still change their lives. And this transfer window, which closed 8am AEST on Wednesday morning, is proof. If one of the determining success factors in international soccer is the level in club soccer that a nation’s players operate at, this one could be remembered as transformative for the Socceroos. Eleven members of Tony Popovic’s squad who were knocked out in the round of 32 by Egypt have parlayed their experiences in the United States (and Canada) into contracts at new clubs – an unprecedented level of Australian movement in a post-World Cup window. Before it, only 28 such transfers in total had been made by players named in the Socceroos’ previous World Cup squads, the vast majority of them being free transfers.



And while not all the moves made in this window could be regarded as career progression – Jackson Irvine, Awer Mabil and Ajdin Hrustic are, respectfully, all on the way down – the majority of them involved younger players making positive moves. Those players have the chance to climb the ladder, exposing them to scenarios that will enhance their capabilities, and enable them to bring that growth with them when they next wear the green and gold. Three deals in particular stand out above the rest: Lucas Herrington’s much-heralded transfer to the Premier League’s Hull City, and Alessandro Circati and Nestory Irankunda’s moves to Benfica and Sporting Lisbon respectively, putting the Socceroos teammates on either side of Portugal’s biggest rivalry. If you count add-ons, they all broke the record set by Harry Souttar when he went to Leicester City for $23 million after the 2022 World Cup, becoming the most expensive Australian soccer player sold. Socceroos players celebrate their progression to the round of 32. AP Photo/Eakin Howard If we are counting those add-ons, then Herrington, Circati and Irankunda went for a combined total of $91 million. While precious little of that money will come back to Australia – aside from the 5 per cent of all transfer fees that is to be distributed proportionally to the clubs that trained and educated the player between the ages of 12 and 23, under FIFA’s “solidarity mechanism” – it was spent, at least in part, because of what those players displayed at the World Cup. It is up to them to prove they were worthy of the price tag.



Related Article Analysis

Australian soccer How an $800k A-League player’s value rose to $33m in just seven months Two other transfers – Patrick Beach to Troyes, and Paul Okon-Engstler to 1.FC Koln – are rare examples of Australian players moving directly from the A-League to a top-five European league and playing immediately upon their arrival. Popovic was roundly criticised for some of his selection and tactical decisions at the World Cup, but here, at least, he deserves some credit for the role he played in getting them there. Before it began, Beach was externally regarded as the third-choice goalkeeper for the Socceroos; some believed Sydney FC’s Harrison Devenish-Meares should have been picked ahead of him. But the 23-year-old was regarded by Popovic as Australia’s best option with the gloves, a shock decision that saw legendary skipper Maty Ryan relegated to the bench. Beach has since hit the ground running in France’s Ligue 1, and looms as the Socceroos’ long-term goalkeeper. Socceroos goalkeeper Patrick Beach became one of the breakout starts of the 2026 World Cup. Getty Images Okon-Engstler, meanwhile, was first selected for a Socceroos camp mid-last year, before he had played a minute of senior club soccer. Popovic was accused of nepotism because his assistant coach was Paul Okon snr. In retrospect, it was inspired; Popovic saw something in Okon-Engstler that few others could at the time, but everyone else eventually did at the World Cup.



Related Article Premier League ‘I wasn’t expecting it’: Zlatan’s surprise phone call to rising Socceroos star Not everyone got the moves they wanted. Despite a disappointing tournament on a personal level, there was big interest in Mohamed Toure, but $28 million was not enough to prise him out of Norwich City, where he has begun this season as he finished the last: on fire. Injuries at the World Cup to Jordan Bos and Jacob Italiano scuppered the possibility, at least in the immediate term, of transfers, with clubs in Germany’s Bundesliga interested in them. Souttar, meanwhile, is stuck in League One with Leicester City, with no bids for him that met his club’s valuation. It remains to be seen who will coach the Socceroos after January’s Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia; Popovic’s short-term contract extension expires with Australia’s last kick of the ball. Whoever is in charge for the next cycle, though, will have at their disposal the strongest, best-positioned pool of players in recent memory.
