World.title: What’s the best small talk for an introvert at a work event?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? What’s the best small talk for an introvert at a work event? Kirstin Ferguson Updated September 2, 2026 — 8:33am ,first published 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Each week Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: dreaded small talk, guilt over an unwell colleague and a disheartening mid-career job hunt. Remember that if you try to “sell” yourself or your company, no one will want to talk to you. Dionne Gain Related Article Got a Minute? My daughter wanted to be a nepo baby. I didn’t hire her, now she won’t talk to me I’ve just been promoted to a new executive level role at a small company and have to attend a two-day conference with many potential clients. I am an introvert and though I have built our company’s offering and believe it’s great, I find it difficult to break the ice and talk with people I don’t know, and find it even harder to “sell”. Do you have any good introduction lines or small talk advice? The biggest thing to remember is that if you try to “sell”, no one will want to talk to you, so stop thinking that is the aim of this specific event. You are there to learn and, by extension, meet people. The good thing to know is that meeting people at a conference is the same as you may meet people in any situation, just through being yourself.



One tip you may already realise is people enjoy talking about themselves, so I suspect you could get through two days – and make some strong connections for future business opportunities – just through asking questions. They can be simple, like, “What did you think of that session?” Or, “Could you make sense of that weird case study the presenter told us about?” Anything, really, that can start you chatting. Listen carefully, and maybe ask a follow-up question. It really won’t take long and the conversation will flow naturally. Do not, I repeat, do not think you need to do a sales pitch. Honestly, nothing will ensure the end of a conversation more quickly. If and when the time is right, that will follow the conference once you have established a rapport and trust with the person. Build the relationship first and the rest will follow. My promotion came because someone else had a breakdown. Everyone congratulated me, but all I can think about is the colleague whose job I’m now doing. She’s still on sick leave. I wanted this opportunity for years, but now I feel guilty every day. How do I get past that?

I am going to make a presumption that you didn’t cause your colleague’s breakdown and then take advantage of it. Instead, it sounds like a vacancy arose, you applied and your employer believed you were the right person for the role. If this is the case, you have nothing to feel guilty about, and should never feel the need to apologise. The best you can do by your colleague is undertaking the new role professionally, speak respectfully about them at all times, and support their return, if and when they’re ready. You clearly deserved this opportunity, regardless of how it came about. I’m a 49-year-old content and communications professional with more than two decades’ experience across marketing, communications and copywriting. Since having children, I’ve mainly freelanced and taken contract roles, so I haven’t held a management position for many years. My diminished self-confidence has left me less fluent in corporate language than most of my peers and I know I don’t sound impressive in interviews. I’ve been trying to secure a decent role for more than three years, but so far, I’ve only secured a few junior, poorly paid roles which I hate. I feel like a failure and know that, if not for my husband’s income, I would be close to the breadline. I’m open to doing something new but the idea of starting at the bottom at my age is disheartening.



What struck me most reading your letter was how hard you are on yourself. While you may feel like a failure, all I read was a description of someone who has managed to maintain a non-linear career while juggling family responsibilities. Someone who has worked across a changing industry through the advent of digital through to AI and no doubt had to pivot their skill base and adapt their thinking regularly. This experience is invaluable. Related Article Got a Minute? Everyone in my office gets free lunch, except me. How is that fair? First, please don’t try to sound more “corporate” in your interviews. It won’t be authentic and most employers are not looking for more buzzwords. Just be yourself. Show how the work you have done and explain how it will add value – share your portfolio, your results and the wise judgment you have shown over so long. Second, you might like to consider broadening your search to working on projects, change programs and even executive support. You may need to start in a short-term role which can often lead to something permanent when your employer sees the value you bring. Good luck. To submit a question about work, careers or leadership, visit kirstinferguson.com/ask. You will not be asked to provide your name or any identifying information. Letters may be edited.

World.title: US launches major strikes against Iran for first time since late July
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war US launches major strikes against Iran for first time since late July Michael Koziol Updated September 2, 2026 — 8:27am ,first published 2:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The US military launched its first major strikes against Iran in more than a month, prompting the regime to fire missiles at American assets in Jordan, as the war dramatically reignited on its six-month anniversary. US strikes began at 7.30pm Tehran time on Tuesday (2am Wednesday AEST), Central Command said, targeting Iranian air defence sites, radar systems, maritime facilities, mine laying capabilities and communications sites. The Strait of Hormuz near Bandar Abbas on Monday. AP Photo/Razieh Poudat “The strikes follow recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region,” Centcom said. Iranian state-run media reported explosions near the port city of Bandar Abbas, and other locations along the country’s coastline. Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting alleged the US attacked a fishmeal factory in Qeshm “and several non-military targets” in Hormozgan province.



Iran also said US strikes killed or injured as many as 50 civilians at a wedding in Kuhestak, a coastal city on the strait. It was not immediately clear how many were killed, but reports indicated as many as five, including at least one child. Esmaeil Baghaei, spokesman for Iran’s foreign ministry, counted it among a “catalogue of atrocities” he said had been perpetrated by the US, including the bombing of a girls’ school on the first day of the war, killing 175. The US has never officially acknowledged responsibility for that strike. Bandar Abbas, one of the cities targeted by fresh US strikes. Getty Images “More dangerous than the bomb itself is the normalisation of bombing; and more dangerous than silence is the conversion of silence into legitimacy,” Baghaei said on X. “Iran will respond to these savage crimes with firmness.” Semi-official Iranian media outlets reported the regime had launched missiles and drones at US assets in retaliation. PressTV published a statement attributed to the country’s military command vowing to inflict “crushing and devastating blows upon the vile and evil American enemy”.



A separate statement from the IRGC that appeared on Iranian television claimed a successful attack on Camp Titin, a facility in Jordan used by US and Jordanian marines. Reuters reported no casualties had been recorded so far, citing two US officials. Central Command told this masthead the IRGC’s claims were false. Meanwhile, Jordan’s armed forces said 10 of 13 ballistic missiles launched from Iran towards Jordan were intercepted and destroyed, while the other three fell outside populated areas. President Donald Trump, pictured in the Oval Office on Monday, has warned Iran a bigger attack is “waiting in the wings”. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin The last time the US military announced major strikes against Iran was on July 29, although it conducted “limited, precise actions” against Iranian rocket launchers near the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday. US President Donald Trump described the US strikes as “large and powerful” in a social media post. He said they were in retaliation for Iran’s failed attempt to add mines to the strait and its firing of eight missiles towards an American base in Jordan, which were intercepted.



“If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. Related Article Updated

Middle East at war US strikes Iranian targets in first attacks in weeks, Tehran retaliates The renewed strikes followed Iranian attacks on two large tankers carrying oil out of the strait on Monday night after a period of relative calm. Projectiles hit the Saudi Arabian-flagged crude carrier Sidr, followed minutes later by a Liberian-flagged vessel, Senegal Prosperity, which is owned by a South Korean company. The tankers each loaded 2 million barrels of ​Saudi crude at the Juaymah terminal last week, Kpler data showed. Saudi ⁠Aramco resumed oil loadings and sales from inside the strait in August.





“The security environment remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation,” the US embassy said. The price of oil spiked, with Brent crude futures trading above $US95 ($132) a barrel on Tuesday afternoon (New York time). US share markets also took a hit. With AP, Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: This valley was the last known location of a Sydney family. Then a wave 100 metres high hit
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dunche, Nepal: High on a remote hilltop, Pasang Tamang bore stunned witness to a tidal wave, its body dark and dragging debris. It crashed through his village, Syabrubesi, the start of the famed Langtang Valley trek. It also is the last known location of an Australian family from Cherrybrook, in Sydney’s north-west. It was not a full hit at first, Tamang says. Much of the surge that had only just taken out villages further north actually flowed into a Trishuli River tributary adjacent to Syabrubesi, allowing some enough time to run. Pasang Tamang stands where he witnessed his home, Syabrubesi, being swept away by flash flooding in Nepal. Kate Geraghty Tamang saw them. But it soon surged back, slamming into the torrent from which it had come, shooting waves “at least” 100 metres into the air. “That’s when [Syabrubesi] was wiped out,” Tamang tells this masthead from the hill where he saw it happen. He’d been down there in Syabrubesi last Wednesday morning, too, but left shortly after 8.30 for the small village of Sano Bharkhu, a kilometre away, to check on some property. Unknown to anyone as he curled up those hair pin turns, a massive avalanche of glacier and rock was hurtling toward the river system at 150 metres per second near the Nepal-Tibet border.



According to relatives, it was also about this time – 8.40am to 8.50am – Sydney’s Sreedharan Iyer, 53, his wife Lakshmi, 49, and their two gifted sons, Rishab, 23, and Rudhra, 20, were checking out from the Royal Himalaya, a hotel on Syabrubesi’s lower section. The Hindu pilgrims were on a family trip of a lifetime with 11 other Australian friends to see Mount Kailash, the earthly abode of Lord Shiva. A photo with most of the group a day before the flood shows them beaming in matching blue T-shirts with mountain print from Himalayan Glacier, the tour company. The Iyer family, from left to right: Rudhra, 20; Sreedharan, 53; Lakshmi, 49; and Rishab, 23. The Iyers appeared in a tour group photo. smiling and wearing matching shirts, a day before the floods hit. None of the 15 have been heard from since Wednesday morning. More than 1050 people were killed – and some 4500 are still missing, including 38 Australians – when the floods hit Nepal and Tibet. The smack of two raging water courses came about 9am, Tamang says, sending buildings “rolling and rolling in the flood”. “After half an hour, everything was similar to what we see now,” he says. That is a silver silt pan, where a village once stood.



The vantage point of Sano Bharkhu offers clear views of a handful of buildings still standing in the upper section of Syabrubesi, and more are obscured by a mountain. But the entire lower half is gone, including Tamang’s home. Images circulating of the village post-flood suggests the Royal Himalaya is too. Most of Syabrubesi was swept away or buried. Kate Geraghty Where the Iyer family was at the time is unclear. They may have spent time in the village after check-out getting organised or sourcing coffees before getting in their car to be driven about 15 kilometres north to their friends at the doomed Hotel Kailash, which was swept away. If they had left immediately after check-out, they would have been roughly halfway between Syabrubesi and Timure on the road running directly alongside the soon-deadly Trishuli.



Timure was destroyed, too. That’s where Tamang’s nephew, Lama Sanam Tamang, 28, a husband and father, was killed. His five-year-old girl, Sonam Dolma, is being minded in Sano Bharkhu by her grieving grandfather, Maywan Tamang. She is playing with a soft drink bottle and scratching at the road with a stick. “We haven’t told her her father is dead,” the grandfather says. “She keeps asking where he is.” Maywan Tamang says his granddaughter Sonam doesn’t yet know her father was killed in the flooding. Kate Geraghty The road the pilgrims took between Dunche, the small capital of Rasuwa district, and Syabrubesi is destroyed from the point it crosses the Trishuli River. Upstream and downstream, the river’s bridges are gone, leaving survivors and residents of undamaged villages on the other side cut off from the main towns and the capital, Kathmandu. Nepal’s private fleet of helicopters have been commandeered for the rescue, aid and salvage efforts, but it is still not enough. A staging point in Dunche for helicopter rescues and distributing aid. Kate Geraghty



A temporary morgue has been set up on the outskirts of Dunche. Kate Geraghty At Dunche, helicopters fly in and out, laden with sacks of food and other supplies, in perpetual motion. “But people keep asking for more,” a rescuer says. Nepal has declined offers from other nations for search and rescue teams, ostensibly because the devastating 2015 earthquake proved it was too unwieldy. It has walked back the initial hardline, however, and is asking for specialised technical teams in matters like DNA testing and tunnel rescues. Close to 900 hydropower station workers remain trapped in various tunnels across the impact zone with uncertain access to oxygen, food and clean drinking water. Time is running out, if it hasn’t already. Destroyed buildings in Betrawoti. Kate Geraghty Body bags lay on the roof of a destroyed building in Betrawoti. Kate Geraghty The flood barrelled on through Syabrubesi to the town Betrawoti, about 40 kilometres south. Unable to make the sharp right turn in the river bed, it smashed into a mountain.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Number of Australians missing in Nepal, Tibet revised to 38; US launches major strikes against Iran
World.content:
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has revised the number of Australians missing in Nepal and Tibet down to 38, from 43 yesterday morning, as it says five additional Australians have been accounted for.

Of the five citizens confirmed safe, one was in Nepal, one in Tibet, and three were outside of the disaster zone.

Because the Australians had not been in contact with families or next of kin since the floods struck last week, their welfare could not be confirmed initially.

World.title: WA news LIVE: Man attacked, knocked unconscious by teens outside Perth fast food chain
World.content:
A man attacked by a group of teenage boys and pelted with a rock outside a Perth fast food restaurant is recovering at home as police continue to investigate the incident.

A man was attacked by a group of teenagers outside Red Rooster in Falcon on Monday.

Footage shows a 25-year-old man being approached by a group of teens outside Red Rooster in Falcon about 4.30pm on Monday.

The man was knocked unconscious and taunted by the children, before bystanders came to his aide and he was transported to hospital. He left the emergency department before he could be treated.

WA Police claimed the teens were not known to the man, and it’s unclear what sparked the altercation.

No charges have been laid, and inquiries remain ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Crime Stoppers.

World.title: Former CFMEU boss raided in alleged multimillion-dollar bribe probe
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaBuilding Bad Former CFMEU boss raided in alleged multimillion-dollar bribe probe Nick McKenzie September 2, 2026 — 9:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Federal police are raiding the home of former CFMEU boss John Perkovic over allegations he took up to $3 million in bribes from company bosses. No charges have been laid. Former CFMEU boss John Perkovic outside his home. On Wednesday morning, neighbours told The Age they observed officers searching a Hislop Street, Keilor property – which was allegedly developed by Perkovic with the help of company bosses he was meant to oversee as one of the CFMEU’s most powerful organisers. The allegations that Perkovic received inducements from company bosses were first exposed as part of The Age’s Building Bad series last year prompting Perkovic’s sacking from the union and sparking a federal police investigation.



Police have raided the home of former CFMEU boss John Perkovic. A person outside a neighbouring property told The Age early on Wednesday morning that they had seen a number of officers scouring Perkovic’s property. Perkovic was the leader of the so-called Croation faction within the union and his sacking was a major blow to the Labor-backed CFMEU administration, which only weeks earlier had promoted Perkovic to the role of deputy leader of the Victorian union branch. The raid of Perkovic comes after Victoria Police’s Taskforce Hawk charged two former CFMEU delegates Tyrone Bell and Joel Brown with alleged financial crimes connected to a business Bell started after he was sacked from the union in July 2024. Both Bell and Brown were former senior members of the Mongols outlaw motorcycle gang. Neighbours said federal police scoured the property.



John Setka outside the lunch venue where he met with Perkovic. The Age The raid of Perkovic’s home will send fresh shockwaves through the construction industry given his former power within the CFMEU and his close relationship with disgraced former union chief John Setka. In his Rotting from the Top report tabled in the Queensland commission of inquiry, Geoffrey Watson, SC, took aim at Perkovic as one of a number of corrupt leadership figures. “The problem with this was that these men were corrupt, known to be corrupt, and were promoted and protected by Setka,” he said. The raid took place on Wednesday morning.



Editor's pick Exclusive

Building Bad Top CFMEU figure sacked over construction company ‘bribes’ Last month, this masthead revealed that Setka had been seen dining with Perkovic at an upmarket seafood and steak restaurant along with an allegedly corrupt construction industry boss. Perkovic is accused of using his union power to promote certain building companies owned by bosses who provided him with undeclared benefits including land on the Hislop Street property and luxury vehicles, as well as loans. Perkovic has previously claimed that the cars he was provided were merely loaned to him and he intended to repay the building company bosses for the benefits they provided. The raid will once again turn the spotlight on Victorian Premier Ben Carroll’s promised royal commission led by former SA chief justice Chris Kourakis.



No charges have been laid. In the fortnight since Kourakis’ appointment there has been no news from the royal commission about who will work as counsel assisting the inquiry, the director of operations, instructing solicitors, investigators or when the first hearing will be called. More to come Explore our investigation

World.title: ‘It’s time to plant some roots’: O’Connor comes full circle at the Force
World.content:
SportRugby UnionJames O'Connor ‘It’s time to plant some roots’: O’Connor comes full circle at the Force Jonathan Drennan September 2, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

James O’Connor is back where it all began nearly two decades later. The 36-year-old playmaker has signed a one-year contract at the Western Force, returning to the club that announced him to the rugby world as a 17-year-old prodigy. Like fellow veteran Bernard Foley at the Waratahs, O’Connor returns to his former club not just to mentor the next generation but also to compete for a spot in the Wallabies squad for next year’s World Cup. James O’Connor is back to where his rugby career began, after signing a one-year deal with the Western Force. Western Force O’Connor left Perth due to a contract dispute with the Force in 2011, moving to Melbourne to play for the Rebels. The move proved ill-fated, and he found the high expectations on him too much to handle. As part of his return to the Force, O’Connor will also work as an attack coach for the club’s Super AUS team. If he were mentoring his younger self, what would he say?



“There’s nothing I could have stopped,” O’Connor said. “But what I would say to that young man is just know there’s someone there, if things go badly wrong or if something doesn’t go right or if you are in trouble, you come talk to me. I’m here. I’m not going to judge you. James O’Connor training in Sydney for the Force in 2009. Steve Christo “No matter how dark it gets or whatever happens, You’ve got someone you can come to and talk to and we’ll figure it out together.” O’Connor had his first official coaches meeting on Tuesday in Perth after arriving in the city last Saturday. He is expecting his first baby with his partner Bridget and has moved to Cottesloe Beach.



Despite being away from Perth for 15 years, it still feels like home. “It was the happiest time of my career (at the Force), it really was. It was because it was all new as well; I’d just started my career, but it was a magical time,” O’Connor said. James O’Connor in action during his return for the Wallabies against the Springboks at Ellis Park last year. AP “There’s been incredible times in my career, but I think that at the Force it was the most joyful I’ve been ... “If I look back chronologically, it was the worst move I’ve made for my happiness, my rugby, for everything, but I needed to make that move for me to be able to be the man I am today.”



Another perspective Australian rugby Tahs send SOS to club rugby playmaker amid ugly contract stoush At the Rebels, O’Connor was forced to take on game management roles he wasn’t equipped to handle. As a young player, he was blessed with speed and agility, but controlling a team was too much. “No one would know that I was managing that stress; you might think watching me on the field I didn’t have a care in the world,” he said. “But I could never fully be present during the week because I was worried about things like, ‘Have I done the work?’ Because maybe I hadn’t done the work and I knew my body wasn’t in the place where it needed to be.” After a season in Melbourne, O’Connor wanted to return to the Force. But an incident at Perth airport in September 2013 saw him stood down by the Wallabies. Australian Federal Police alleged he was intoxicated and not allowed to board a flight from Perth to Indonesia. O’Connor denied being drunk but admitted to engaging in a heated argument over seating arrangements.



O’Connor left Australia for London Irish in 2013 to play under the late Brian Smith, before stints with Toulon in France and Sale in England. “I felt like everyone was out to get me. Was I treated unfairly? It wasn’t unfair, but I definitely think that I had a target on my back,” O’Connor said. James O’Connor playing for London Irish in 2014. Getty Images “When that door was finally shut on me after the airport (incident), it was time to go explore Europe. “It was the best thing I ever did because I got out of the fishbowl. I got out of my own way and had to figure out who I was as a man, and that started my journey back to where I am now.”



Last year, O’Connor made a shock Wallabies return and helped Australia beat South Africa for the first time at Ellis Park in 62 years. He is determined to grow as a coach in Perth, but also remains driven by the lure of the home World Cup. “I’m preparing myself for next season (at the Force). One, my first child’s on the way and number two, I’ve just moved halfway around the world three times now,” O’Connor said. The Wallabies celebrate after their epic win at Ellis Park in 2025. AP “I’m going to be honest, I want to play in that World Cup. I’ve seen myself playing in it and I know I can add value. “If I stick to my guns and I make sure I’m disciplined and I put the work in and everything goes as planned, then great. I can see myself playing in there and adding a lot of value … but after next year, after the World Cup, I think that’ll be me (as a player).”



On Tuesday morning, O’Connor went for a swim with an old teammate and close friend Kurtley Beale. After playing last season in Leicester, O’Connor fielded offers from France, Japan and South Africa, but with a baby on the way, O’Connor knew it was time to come home. “It’s time to plant some roots,” he said. “As soon as I found out that my wife was pregnant, it was like, okay, this all makes sense now ... everything just became irrelevant. This is where I want to be. I want to be close to family. I want to be in Australia. This feels right for us.”

World.title: 11 deals, $100m spent: Was this the Socceroos’ best-ever post-World Cup window?
World.content:
Analysis SportSoccerAustralian soccer 11 deals, $100m spent: Was this the Socceroos’ best-ever post-World Cup window? Vince Rugari September 2, 2026 — 8:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There was a time when the World Cup was considered soccer’s ultimate shop window; when a single performance or two in the global spotlight was enough for a player to catch the eye of a top club and earn an opportunity they otherwise wouldn’t have gotten. It doesn’t quite work like that any more. Too many clubs have been burnt over the years by vanity deals for players who looked good for those few weeks, but didn’t quite fit once they’d settled into their new surrounds. These days, recruitment departments have access to so much data, intel and footage that there are no longer any major surprises to discover. Loading But for Australian players who operate on the fringes of those scouting radars, there is still something to be gained from a good World Cup. It can still change their lives. And this transfer window, which closed 8am AEST on Wednesday morning, is proof. If one of the determining success factors in international soccer is the level in club soccer that a nation’s players operate at, this one could be remembered as transformative for the Socceroos. Eleven members of Tony Popovic’s squad who were knocked out in the round of 32 by Egypt have parlayed their experiences in the United States (and Canada) into contracts at new clubs – an unprecedented level of Australian movement in a post-World Cup window. Before it, only 28 such transfers in total had been made by players named in the Socceroos’ previous World Cup squads, the vast majority of them being free transfers.



And while not all the moves made in this window could be regarded as career progression – Jackson Irvine, Awer Mabil and Ajdin Hrustic are, respectfully, all on the way down – the majority of them involved younger players making positive moves. Those players have the chance to climb the ladder, exposing them to scenarios that will enhance their capabilities, and enable them to bring that growth with them when they next wear the green and gold. Three deals in particular stand out above the rest: Lucas Herrington’s much-heralded transfer to the Premier League’s Hull City, and Alessandro Circati and Nestory Irankunda’s moves to Benfica and Sporting Lisbon respectively, putting the Socceroos teammates on either side of Portugal’s biggest rivalry. If you count add-ons, they all broke the record set by Harry Souttar when he went to Leicester City for $23 million after the 2022 World Cup, becoming the most expensive Australian soccer player sold. Socceroos players celebrate their progression to the round of 32. AP Photo/Eakin Howard If we are counting those add-ons, then Herrington, Circati and Irankunda went for a combined total of $91 million. While precious little of that money will come back to Australia – aside from the 5 per cent of all transfer fees that is to be distributed proportionally to the clubs that trained and educated the player between the ages of 12 and 23, under FIFA’s “solidarity mechanism” – it was spent, at least in part, because of what those players displayed at the World Cup. It is up to them to prove they were worthy of the price tag.



Related Article Analysis

Australian soccer How an $800k A-League player’s value rose to $33m in just seven months Two other transfers – Patrick Beach to Troyes, and Paul Okon-Engstler to 1.FC Koln – are rare examples of Australian players moving directly from the A-League to a top-five European league and playing immediately upon their arrival. Popovic was roundly criticised for some of his selection and tactical decisions at the World Cup, but here, at least, he deserves some credit for the role he played in getting them there. Before it began, Beach was externally regarded as the third-choice goalkeeper for the Socceroos; some believed Sydney FC’s Harrison Devenish-Meares should have been picked ahead of him. But the 23-year-old was regarded by Popovic as Australia’s best option with the gloves, a shock decision that saw legendary skipper Maty Ryan relegated to the bench. Beach has since hit the ground running in France’s Ligue 1, and looms as the Socceroos’ long-term goalkeeper. Socceroos goalkeeper Patrick Beach became one of the breakout starts of the 2026 World Cup. Getty Images Okon-Engstler, meanwhile, was first selected for a Socceroos camp mid-last year, before he had played a minute of senior club soccer. Popovic was accused of nepotism because his assistant coach was Paul Okon snr. In retrospect, it was inspired; Popovic saw something in Okon-Engstler that few others could at the time, but everyone else eventually did at the World Cup.



Related Article Premier League ‘I wasn’t expecting it’: Zlatan’s surprise phone call to rising Socceroos star Not everyone got the moves they wanted. Despite a disappointing tournament on a personal level, there was big interest in Mohamed Toure, but $28 million was not enough to prise him out of Norwich City, where he has begun this season as he finished the last: on fire. Injuries at the World Cup to Jordan Bos and Jacob Italiano scuppered the possibility, at least in the immediate term, of transfers, with clubs in Germany’s Bundesliga interested in them. Souttar, meanwhile, is stuck in League One with Leicester City, with no bids for him that met his club’s valuation. It remains to be seen who will coach the Socceroos after January’s Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia; Popovic’s short-term contract extension expires with Australia’s last kick of the ball. Whoever is in charge for the next cycle, though, will have at their disposal the strongest, best-positioned pool of players in recent memory. World.title: What’s the best small talk for an introvert at a work event?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? What’s the best small talk for an introvert at a work event? Kirstin Ferguson Updated September 2, 2026 — 8:33am ,first published 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Each week Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: dreaded small talk, guilt over an unwell colleague and a disheartening mid-career job hunt. Remember that if you try to “sell” yourself or your company, no one will want to talk to you. Dionne Gain Related Article Got a Minute? My daughter wanted to be a nepo baby. I didn’t hire her, now she won’t talk to me I’ve just been promoted to a new executive level role at a small company and have to attend a two-day conference with many potential clients. I am an introvert and though I have built our company’s offering and believe it’s great, I find it difficult to break the ice and talk with people I don’t know, and find it even harder to “sell”. Do you have any good introduction lines or small talk advice? The biggest thing to remember is that if you try to “sell”, no one will want to talk to you, so stop thinking that is the aim of this specific event. You are there to learn and, by extension, meet people. The good thing to know is that meeting people at a conference is the same as you may meet people in any situation, just through being yourself.



One tip you may already realise is people enjoy talking about themselves, so I suspect you could get through two days – and make some strong connections for future business opportunities – just through asking questions. They can be simple, like, “What did you think of that session?” Or, “Could you make sense of that weird case study the presenter told us about?” Anything, really, that can start you chatting. Listen carefully, and maybe ask a follow-up question. It really won’t take long and the conversation will flow naturally. Do not, I repeat, do not think you need to do a sales pitch. Honestly, nothing will ensure the end of a conversation more quickly. If and when the time is right, that will follow the conference once you have established a rapport and trust with the person. Build the relationship first and the rest will follow. My promotion came because someone else had a breakdown. Everyone congratulated me, but all I can think about is the colleague whose job I’m now doing. She’s still on sick leave. I wanted this opportunity for years, but now I feel guilty every day. How do I get past that?

I am going to make a presumption that you didn’t cause your colleague’s breakdown and then take advantage of it. Instead, it sounds like a vacancy arose, you applied and your employer believed you were the right person for the role. If this is the case, you have nothing to feel guilty about, and should never feel the need to apologise. The best you can do by your colleague is undertaking the new role professionally, speak respectfully about them at all times, and support their return, if and when they’re ready. You clearly deserved this opportunity, regardless of how it came about. I’m a 49-year-old content and communications professional with more than two decades’ experience across marketing, communications and copywriting. Since having children, I’ve mainly freelanced and taken contract roles, so I haven’t held a management position for many years. My diminished self-confidence has left me less fluent in corporate language than most of my peers and I know I don’t sound impressive in interviews. I’ve been trying to secure a decent role for more than three years, but so far, I’ve only secured a few junior, poorly paid roles which I hate. I feel like a failure and know that, if not for my husband’s income, I would be close to the breadline. I’m open to doing something new but the idea of starting at the bottom at my age is disheartening.



What struck me most reading your letter was how hard you are on yourself. While you may feel like a failure, all I read was a description of someone who has managed to maintain a non-linear career while juggling family responsibilities. Someone who has worked across a changing industry through the advent of digital through to AI and no doubt had to pivot their skill base and adapt their thinking regularly. This experience is invaluable. Related Article Got a Minute? Everyone in my office gets free lunch, except me. How is that fair? First, please don’t try to sound more “corporate” in your interviews. It won’t be authentic and most employers are not looking for more buzzwords. Just be yourself. Show how the work you have done and explain how it will add value – share your portfolio, your results and the wise judgment you have shown over so long. Second, you might like to consider broadening your search to working on projects, change programs and even executive support. You may need to start in a short-term role which can often lead to something permanent when your employer sees the value you bring. Good luck. To submit a question about work, careers or leadership, visit kirstinferguson.com/ask. You will not be asked to provide your name or any identifying information. Letters may be edited.

World.title: US launches major strikes against Iran for first time since late July
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war US launches major strikes against Iran for first time since late July Michael Koziol Updated September 2, 2026 — 8:27am ,first published 2:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The US military launched its first major strikes against Iran in more than a month, prompting the regime to fire missiles at American assets in Jordan, as the war dramatically reignited on its six-month anniversary. US strikes began at 7.30pm Tehran time on Tuesday (2am Wednesday AEST), Central Command said, targeting Iranian air defence sites, radar systems, maritime facilities, mine laying capabilities and communications sites. The Strait of Hormuz near Bandar Abbas on Monday. AP Photo/Razieh Poudat “The strikes follow recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region,” Centcom said. Iranian state-run media reported explosions near the port city of Bandar Abbas, and other locations along the country’s coastline. Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting alleged the US attacked a fishmeal factory in Qeshm “and several non-military targets” in Hormozgan province.



Iran also said US strikes killed or injured as many as 50 civilians at a wedding in Kuhestak, a coastal city on the strait. It was not immediately clear how many were killed, but reports indicated as many as five, including at least one child. Esmaeil Baghaei, spokesman for Iran’s foreign ministry, counted it among a “catalogue of atrocities” he said had been perpetrated by the US, including the bombing of a girls’ school on the first day of the war, killing 175. The US has never officially acknowledged responsibility for that strike. Bandar Abbas, one of the cities targeted by fresh US strikes. Getty Images “More dangerous than the bomb itself is the normalisation of bombing; and more dangerous than silence is the conversion of silence into legitimacy,” Baghaei said on X. “Iran will respond to these savage crimes with firmness.” Semi-official Iranian media outlets reported the regime had launched missiles and drones at US assets in retaliation. PressTV published a statement attributed to the country’s military command vowing to inflict “crushing and devastating blows upon the vile and evil American enemy”.



A separate statement from the IRGC that appeared on Iranian television claimed a successful attack on Camp Titin, a facility in Jordan used by US and Jordanian marines. Reuters reported no casualties had been recorded so far, citing two US officials. Central Command told this masthead the IRGC’s claims were false. Meanwhile, Jordan’s armed forces said 10 of 13 ballistic missiles launched from Iran towards Jordan were intercepted and destroyed, while the other three fell outside populated areas. President Donald Trump, pictured in the Oval Office on Monday, has warned Iran a bigger attack is “waiting in the wings”. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin The last time the US military announced major strikes against Iran was on July 29, although it conducted “limited, precise actions” against Iranian rocket launchers near the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday. US President Donald Trump described the US strikes as “large and powerful” in a social media post. He said they were in retaliation for Iran’s failed attempt to add mines to the strait and its firing of eight missiles towards an American base in Jordan, which were intercepted.



“If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. Related Article Updated

Middle East at war US strikes Iranian targets in first attacks in weeks, Tehran retaliates The renewed strikes followed Iranian attacks on two large tankers carrying oil out of the strait on Monday night after a period of relative calm. Projectiles hit the Saudi Arabian-flagged crude carrier Sidr, followed minutes later by a Liberian-flagged vessel, Senegal Prosperity, which is owned by a South Korean company. The tankers each loaded 2 million barrels of ​Saudi crude at the Juaymah terminal last week, Kpler data showed. Saudi ⁠Aramco resumed oil loadings and sales from inside the strait in August.





“The security environment remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation,” the US embassy said. The price of oil spiked, with Brent crude futures trading above $US95 ($132) a barrel on Tuesday afternoon (New York time). US share markets also took a hit. With AP, Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Moa Point disaster caused by systemic leadership failures, damning report finds
World.content:
The catastrophic failure of the Moa Point wastewater treatment plant was caused by long-standing systemic failures of leadership by Wellington City Council, Wellington Water and the plant's operator Veolia, a damning report has found.

The plant, which flooded and shut down on February 4, has by now spewed approximately 14 billion litres of raw sewage into Wellington's south coast - pumping the waste close to the shore at Tarakena Bay after a heavy rain.

Some residents have stopped fishing, diving and swimming at the beaches regularly, while businesses have said they've been forced to the brink of closure due to the disaster.

While the report from the Crown Review team did not point to a single decision or event, it said the failure reflected "systemic governance failure" in how the treatment plant was managed.

Six recommendations were made, including improving communication and strengthening governance.

However, it paints a picture of a complicated management system where no single organisation acted as though it was in charge - and communication between Wellington City Council and Wellington Water was poor.

Lyall Bay beach and the rest of Wellington's south coast was initially off limits after the Moa Point treatment plant failed on 4 February RNZ / Krystal Gibbens

Six recommendations were made, including restoring compliance with consents, public communication, and improving risk management.

Wellington City Council, as the plant's owner and consent holder, "remained ultimately accountable" at the time of the incident.

The council maintained to the Crown Review team that it did not control the plant, the review team said.

"WCC relied on Wellington Water to notify it of issues or need for renewals, rather than define standards itself."

Wellington Water, in turn, did not have a detailed management plan for the plant, and no funding plan.

This meant Wellington Water did not make enough funding requests to the council.

The plan has spewed approximately 14 billion litres of raw sewage into Wellington's south coast. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Communication between the organisations was poor, the report said.

"Information flows between organisations were indirect and, at times, filtered."

Despite featuring heavily during the investigation, the review team noted that city council infrastructure leaders didn't meet the Crown Review to tell them about aspects of their role as owner of the plant - instead providing written submissions.

The report said this was despite requests for in-person meetings being made.

Crucial warnings missed, no staffing at the plant

The report explained, as a Wellington Review found in March, that during heavy rain trapped air in the plant's sewage bypass pipe caused wastewater to back up, flooding critical electrical equipment and the plant.

It said much more wastewater was being sent through the bypass because work was being done on the plant's UV disinfection system.

The report said Veolia told the Crown Review team it had warned about the bypass pipe risks, but Wellington Water said it was not aware this warning had been made.

An overflow event happened at 3pm on the afternoon before the major flooding event occurred, but the report said Veolia took no additional actions.

Air trapped in the plant's sewage bypass pipe caused wastewater to back up. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

A flooding event in July 2025 showed similar warning signs, the report said. The Crown Review team said Wellington Water was not aware this was raised by the operator.

There were also no staff on site at the plant - Veolia stated they were not instructed to increase monitoring or staffing with the UV system under upgrade.

No extra staff were required overnight as the conditions were considered typical.

Minister and organisations respond

Local Government Minister Simon Watts said the public deserved answers over what happened.

"The failure of the Moa Point Plant was one of the most significant wastewater infrastructure failures experienced in the Wellington region in recent decades."

He said lessons from the incident could strengthen management in the future.

"The review found the event was not caused by a single decision or isolated failure, but by longstanding weaknesses in governance, accountability, asset management, risk management and infrastructure resilience.

"The review's central finding is that preventing a similar event in the future depends on clear accountability throughout the system, supported by a strong understanding of risks and effective decision-making at every level.

Wellington Mayor Andrew Little has accepted the report's findings. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Wellington Mayor Andrew Little said the Crown Review team report into the failure of the Moa Point wastewater treatment plant in February was thorough.

"What happened at Moa Point is unacceptable. The bottom line is Wellingtonians deserve transparency, and to have assurance about the response and recovery. That is why I asked the central government to commission a suitably independent report," Little said.

"On behalf of Wellington City Council, I acknowledge and accept the report's findings."

Tiaki Wai, now owner of the water assets, said it welcomed the report.

Board Chair Will Peet said: "The failure of the plant on 4 February was devastating. As a south coast resident and frequent visitor of the affected beaches, I was as upset as many fellow Wellingtonians. We know that local residents, the business community and mana whenua have felt this very deeply."

World.title: Methanex to effectively close and sell off gas contracts
World.content:
New Zealand's largest gas user Methanex is to effectively close its plant and sell off its gas contracts.

Methanex said a lack of natural gas and a clear pathway to new supplies meant operations in New Zealand were no longer sustainable.

The Canadian-owned company said it had now entered into an agreement to sell all of its New Zealand natural gas contractual entitlements, commencing in the first quarter of next year.

It said it then planned to safely idle and preserve the facility for long-term optionality, should future circumstances support a restart of operations.

The company has in the past been responsible for taking around 30 to 40 percent of all of New Zealand's natural gas production.

ln recent years the country's natural gas production has declined rapidly with little new supply coming on board.

The company, which employs around 200 people, not including contractors and suppliers, said it would work closely with employees, contractors, suppliers, customers, and government stakeholders during the transition period.

Rich Sumner, president and CEO of Methanex Corporation, said the company had been preparing for this eventuality, given declining gas availability in the country.

World.title: Charity frustrated by haphazard nature of help for those bereaved by suicide
World.content:
Calls for more support for families of those who commit suicide Nine To Noon Download MP3 13m

The coroner who investigated the case of an Auckland woman who accidentally drowned after her husband committed suicide, is calling for more support for the families of those affected by self-inflicted deaths.

Coroner Alison Mills found Karen Hampson began drinking heavily after her husband's death in 2021. It contributed to her own death in January 2024, which the Coroner ruled was an accident.

She said services for loved ones of those who killed themselves were limited and funded grief counselling was difficult to access. She recommended the Ministry of Justice review the support offered to bereaved whānau dealing with the Coroners Court.

In response, the ministry acknowledged the potential benefits, but said funding constraints meant there were no plans for such services.

Coroner Mills also recommended Te Whatu Ora and the Ministry of Health review the funding and accessibility of grief counselling, particularly for those who have experienced loss through suicide. Neither Health New Zealand, nor the ministry, responded to the Coroner.

John Moore is the chief executive of Yellow Brick Road, which is a charity providing support to the families of those experiencing mental health struggles.

Yellow Brick Road CEO John Moore Supplied

He told Nine to Noon everyone going through the grief process like the woman who drowned needed someone alongside them to support them.

It was frustrating that his organisation's model for helping people in these situations, known as Waves, was not consistently rolled out around New Zealand.

How it works

The Waves programme aimed to link up with local suicide prevention coordinators, participants would be encouraged to wait around a year, and then placed in a group that would provide support.

Various health organisations referred relatives and Moore would like the system to be streamlined so that referrals were done in a more consistent way.

Victim Support used to support police in making referrals but has pulled out and no replacement organisation has been announced.

"I've seen it work and it's incredibly difficult to see that it is so haphazardly available around the country."

Consistency for delivery was vital.

"Identifying some leadership would be really important. We don't have it being driven. I don't see money and resources being the biggest barrier to this happening.

"There are existing services that are deilvering some of these services but because things aren't linked up we aren't getting to people in the right way at the right time."

One woman told Yellow Brick Road Waves had deterred her from wanting to join her dead son.

It was important that the charity met bereaved relatives early on and built a relationship with them, Scott said.

Moore agreed relatives could access support when their loved one died violently, however, this was not the case for those bereaved by suicide.

Group support a key

It was vital those people were able to grieve in a group, he said.

"Being alongside other people who can understand your loss helps you to feel less alone and feeling less alone I think is really key to getting through that experience."

As well, people needed help to navigate the legal experience. The time it took and the focus on finding fault rather than finding answers could make it "a drawn out and painful process".

Most families wanted answers, he said, however, the health services were often more focused on protecting themselves rather than finding the truth.

"That can make it particularly difficult in my experience."

The Justice Ministry told the coroner funding roles such as navigators to assist those grieving would take "significant investment" and it would reconsider its decision "when resources allowed".

Suicide prevention programmes would be "low hanging fruit" and not very expensive to put in place, Moore said in response.

Health agencies focused on diagnosis and treatment and suicides were "a way more complicated issue than that".

At present funding wasn't keeping up with the cost of delivering services.

"The ability to do something new is the stumbling block that I hear."

World.title: Rural Marlborough residents told to conserve water, as cause of leak not yet found
World.content:
Water is being trucked into rural Marlborough as supplies in Awatere and Seddon have been depleted due to a major leak.

Residents around Seddon are asked to urgently conserve water as the Rural Awatere water supply storage tanks are now empty and the Seddon water supply tank is only about 40 percent full.

The source of the leak is yet to be found.

Council engineers and contractors worked overnight but have not been able to find the source of the leak, which was discovered late Tuesday night.

Marlborough Waters chief executive Richard Coningham said replenishing the tanks would help maintain water supplies but did not remove the need for residents to conserve water.

"Trucking water into the area means we can begin replenishing both the rural Awatere tanks and the Seddon tank while crews continue working on the leak," Coningham said.

"However, we still need everyone connected to these supplies to use as little water as possible. Please keep water use to essential drinking, cooking and hygiene needs and avoid all non-essential use."

In Seddon people are advised to boil their water as a precaution and those on the rural Awatere supply remain under a long-standing boil water notice.

Coningham said while the trucked-in water was potable, some of the water trucks were food grade certified and not classed as potable grade under water regulations, which is why a precautionary boil water notice had been put in place for the Seddon supply.

Water should be brought to a rolling boil for at least one minute and allowed to cool naturally before use. The precautionary boil water notice will remain in place until the council advises otherwise.

The leak is believed to be in a section of pipe under the Awatere River bed, which could make the repair complex.

The pipe supplies Seddon, Seaview, Grassmere and rural areas south of the Awatere River.

World.title: Government shelves plans to ban hard-to-recycle plastic
World.content:
The Government has shelved plans to ban hard-to-recycle PVC and polystyrene from food and beverage packaging, and Zero Waste Aotearoa says big brands may be to blame.

The abandoned crackdown has been in the works for years and was originally due to come into force in mid-2025, but the deadline was shifted in late 2024.

A Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport (MCERT) spokesperson said the proposal would not proceed due to "other priorities being progressed in this election cycle."

Zero Waste Aotearoa's Director of External Affairs Sue Coutts told Nine to Noon she thinks it's the big global brands that are "dragging the chain."

Shelving plans to ban hard-to-recycle plastic Nine To Noon Download MP3 15m

"You know, we're seeing a lot of the New Zealand brands have already shifted... They've paid the cost. They've put the effort into shifting their business model and their systems."

"And then these last few, you know, companies that are dragging the chain are getting away with being able to not have to do that work."

She said this put the businesses who have already done the work at a disadvantage and the government needed to set clear rules that everyone should follow.

The hard-to-recycle PVC and polystyrene packaging being targeted by the policy included things like snap-apart yoghurt pots, which are number six polystyrene packaging.

"It makes it awkward, contaminates the recycling stream. It's not recyclable to kerbside at the moment."

Last week Johan Verbeek, University of Auckland director of the Centre of Advanced Materials Manufacturing and Design, told Afternoons the government's decision was disappointing but it may have been a matter of

priorities.

"I think it comes down to current priorities, you think what the government has to deal with and they have to decide 'all right what are we going to do next and maybe that just ended up in the not a priority right now unfortunately.'

Why PVC and polystyrene aren't going anywhere yet Afternoons Download MP3 7m

Verbeek said while PVC and polystyrene packaging was useful there were alternatives but cost was an issue many had to consider.

"That might cost a bit more, you have to change your equipment and that's probably what it came down to... companies don't have certainty.

"Because a bunch of companies were really invested in new technology, new materials to prepare for that and then government pulling back."

This was not the first crackdown to be reversed or put on hold with Labour pausing the container return scheme in 2023.

Coutts said "everyone's a bit sick of waiting" when it came to change being enforced.

"We're seeing things like the container return scheme get to the very last hurdle, and then for some reason they get pulled. And often it's because of lobbying and the background by the bigger companies."

Coutts said past research by the Ministry of Environment has shown that New Zealanders are willing to put the effort into following new rules.

She said a more recent Better Futures Kantar survey showed more than 70 percent of New Zealanders are committed to doing what they can to "use the systems that are there now".

"I think it's really about a lack of commitment to environmental protection and using resources efficiently."

Coutts said other countries have implemented similar policies such as the container return scheme including Lithuania, Romania and Austria.

"The people in our government haven't caught up. They haven't caught up with what's going on and what that means is that New Zealand is just falling so far behind our trading partners.

An MCERT spokesperson engagement would continue through international discussions on hard-to-recycle plastics, including negotiations on a global plastics treaty.

"The Ministry's focus continues on broader waste and resource efficiency initiatives including work to support product stewardship schemes for priority products such as agrichemicals and farm plastics."

World.title: US expected to announce major fuel security deal at Pacific Islands Forum
World.content:
RNZ's Teuila Fuatai in Koror, Palau

The United States is set to announce a fuel security deal worth US$60 million for the Pacific region, RNZ Pacific understands.

Details are yet to be finalised, but RNZ Pacific understands it was discussed at a closed dialogue partners meeting at the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) leaders' summit in Palau on Tuesday.

US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau is in Koror for the annual meeting. His trip to Palau comes after a raft of engagements in the region this year as the Trump administration's point-person for the Pacific.

The US is one of PIF's founding dialogue partners, alongside Canada, France, Japan and the United Kingdom. The PIF currently has 21 Dialogue Partners, which comprise external countries and organisations that have formal relationships with PIF and support Pacific regional priorities through political engagement.

Landau made a funding announcement with New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters and Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown about a new port in Penrhyn atoll, the Cook Islands' northern-most island.

Penrhyn, or Tongareva, is a former US military base. The US has committed US$50m to the major port upgrade, while New Zealand is contributing US$10m. The two countries are co-funding the infrastructure project.

US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown, and New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters mark the announcement of the Penrhyn Port Project in Palau. 1 September 2026 Facebook / US Embassy New Zealand

Peters said the idea of a new port for Tongareva was first discussed in April, when he met Landau and his boss, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Washington DC.

A potential fuel security deal was also raised as part of those meetings, he said. And while the financial contribution for the Tongareva port upgrade has been finalised, the fuel security deal, which is set to be worth US$60 million, is subject to congressional approval.

The Pacific region is heavily reliant on diesel for power generation.

A recent study from the UNSW Institute for Climate Risk and Response identified about 80 percent of the region's energy relied on imported oil products. Collectively, it estimated Pacific Island countries spent US$6 billion each year on imported oil products.

It also found that Palau, which is hosting this years PIF leaders meeting, spent 13 percent of its GDP (gross domestic product) on importing oil products, compared to about 10 percent of GDP on health, and 3 percent on education.

Other Pacific nations spent similar proportions of their GDP on importing oil products, the study found.

As a result, the surge in diesel prices due to the Iran War has left many Pacific nations economically exposed. After the Strait of Hormuz closed, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands announced emergency fuel conservation measures, while governments in Vanuatu, Cook Islands, Fiji, Federated States of Micronesia, Solomon Islands and Nauru passed national response measures.

Palau President Surangel Whipps Jr, who has now taken over as chair of the Forum troika, has been championing a push for the Pacific to be the first region in the world to be completely powered by renewable energy.

"The high cost of fuel, freight, and food shows how quickly events far from our shores and far from our reach affect every Pacific household, and our dependence on imported diesel fuels is an economic risk as well as a climate one," Whipps said in his opening ceremony address.

"The transition to renewable energy is therefore part of our sovereignty. It lowers our exposure and keeps more of our scarce resources working in our own economies."

Significant investment is critical to that transition. The UNSW study found to replace diesel generation with a renewable option, about US$650 million each year is needed for the region.

Peters said his ongoing work with the US, and other countries from outside the region, was a big part of ensuring incoming investment into the Pacific.

In regard to the US, he said discussions began about six months around its potential role in investing in the region.

"We talked about them having a good, hard look at where they should be making investments and giving some substance to what they were saying… because they were having an investment conference in Honolulu to which not many Pacific Island countries went.

"And so we were looking around for some real initiatives, and here comes this one here [Tongareva port]."

World.title: Who is responsible? Glaring lack of clarity over Fiji operation to remove street dwellers
World.content:
Authorities in Fiji are offering contradictory accounts of a nationwide effort to remove beggars and street dwellers from public spaces, with questions over warning notices and what support is available for those affected.

The agencies involved have been unable to clearly identify what those services are and who is responsible for providing them, or what happens to people after they are moved from their public places.

The ongoing lack of clarity has raised concerns among civil society organisations that the enforcement effort may be getting ahead of the support systems needed to make it work.

In August, The Fiji Times reported that city rangers were serving warning notices to individuals soliciting alms in public areas. The notices stated that behaviours such as persistent begging or obstructioning footpaths were offences and could lead to "enforcement actions".

The operation has been advertised as a joint effort between the Lautoka City Council, Fiji Police, and the Women, Children and Social Protection Ministry.

RNZ Pacific has repeatedly sought clarification on how the operation works in practice, on what would trigger a warning notice, what happens when someone refuses to leave, what support programmes are offered for street dwellers, and what role each agency plays.

The office of the Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection, Sashi Kiran, declined to comment on the ministry's role in supporting street dwellers or on what programmes being offered to people being moved from public spaces.

The office of Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu would only say police were there to "ensure the safety of all parties" and would "use necessary force" if required.

Fiji Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu Fiji Police Force

When RNZ Pacific asked what that meant in practice, and what powers police would use if people refused to leave public spaces, no detailed explanations were provided.

RNZ Pacific's specific questions to both the ministry and police remain unanswered.

'No forced relocation'

The Lautoka City Council chairman and acting CEO Ratu Tevita Momoedonu, however, was more forthcoming, and rejected suggestions people were being forcibly removed from streets.

"There is no forced relocation here. We can't force anybody," he said.

He described the initiative as welfare-led, saying street dwellers are being profiled and offered relocation to shelters and rehabilitation services.

"We don't warn people. We profile them, and we call them in meetings, and then we suggest to them the importance or the benefits of being relocated," he added.

When asked about the support programmes being offered by the ministry, Momoedonu said they could not help.

"I can't help you either, because the [Lautoka City] Council, we have our own jurisdictions here. We only help social welfare in profiling," he said.

"The rehabilitation part, the relocation part, it is their (ministry and police) responsibility, not us. If they are not answering to you people, then [they] neither do us," he said.

While Momoedonu denied that warning notices were being used as part of the relocation effort, he did acknowledge that council notices could be issued for breaches of bylaws, and that people involved in criminal activity could be removed.

"If there are bylaws that are violated, then we can issue directives? When there are criminal elements - drinking in public place, taking drugs in public place, disturbing the peace. These are criminal elements."

He said police assist the Lautoka City Council and welfare officers when street dwellers resist engagement, although he commented that police do not "enforce relocations".

A photograph of the Operation Loloma pamphlet Supplied image

In Nadi, Fiji's international gateway, there is a similar operation underway.

A pamphlet from social worker Mohenesh Singh describes "Operation Loloma" as an effort to take beggars off the streets, profile and screen them, and provide "alternative means of livelihood".

"Together, we can create lasting solutions that address the root causes of begging," the pamphlet reads.

"The information collected will see an an individual case plan drawn up for each beggar so that the welfare of the disadvantaged individuals are taken care of by the various networks we have in the country."

RNZ Pacific contacted Singh for comment, asking what street profiling looked like, and what support was offered for street dwellers. He declined to comment about their operation.

FCOSS 'caught by surprise'

Civil society groups which are also involved in working on the issue say they have been left in the dark about the Lautoka initiative.

The Fiji Council of Social Services (FCOSS) executive director Vani Catanasiga said she first learnt about Lautoka City Council's warning notice enforcement when contacted by RNZ Pacific.

"We were caught by surprise, so, I just heard that it was happening in Lautoka," Catanasiga said.

"I was aware about it in Suva, sort of, efforts or clean up ... but I wasn't aware about Lautoka."

Vani Catanasiga says the Fiji Council of Social Services was 'caught by surprise' about the operation. Facebook / Pacific Blue Line

Catanasiga said Fiji's civil sector has repeatedly raised concerns around the lack of co-ordination between Fijian agencies that are working with vulnerable people.

The Lautoka operation, she said, could serve as a "case study" in what happens when co-ordination between involved parties breaks down.

"Unfortunately, in this case, it has to do with a vulnerable group. They're already vulnerable, they're already confused, they're already in need of support, compassion," Catanasiga said.

"When we don't address persistent coordination challenges, it really just does a lot more harm. It exacerbates the harms that they already face."

In this case, Catanasiga said the issue is an absence of communication, and clarity in roles between the different agencies involved.

The additional lack of publicly available detail is concerning for organisations who are meant to be working with vulnerable people, she added.

She described the operations as "optics-led" and said while sympathised with the relevant authorities and people in authority trying to make a difference, the lack of transparency was concerning.

"It's not to penalise those who want to do something about it. It's about [asking], 'okay, have we applied the right processes?'

"Sometimes in our effort to to do this, we miss the more essential work of doing the due diligence. And sometimes we react ... a lot of our approaches are reactionary because it looks bad.

"It's not an excuse to miss the essential steps of safeguarding [and] due diligence that we must apply to our work, particularly around social protection [and] checking on the social safety nets that are supposed to be there."

'Unsustainable'

Catanasiga also suggested authorities were relying on Fiji's long-dormant law on minor offences to justify moving beggars and street dwellers from public places, targeting activities such as begging, loitering and drunk or disorderly behaviour.

"I understand there is a Minor Offences Act that was never operationalised. It was never applied.

"So, I think that they're using that to justify the removal of people from the streets. So begging, all those sorts of activities, loitering, it's covered under that act."

While Catanisaga said she fully supported efforts to move homeless individuals into dignified work and safe housing, the current operations will be unsustainable.

"I'm just concerned about the back end processes that are supposed to be in place, the support system. If not, our efforts to get people off the streets is not going to be sustainable," she said.

Moving forward, Catanasiga said the agencies involved to deal with the issue need to come together to complete the programme they have started.

"We always talk about dignity-centred approaches [to deal with vulnerable people]. This [initiative] is not dignity-centred approaches," she said.
